title: EduRiskX: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework with F-Logic Reasoning for Early Academic Risk Prediction
comment: Previously available on Research Square: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8877832/v1. This version presents the complete neuro-symbolic framework, EduRiskX, integrating temporal Transformers with F-Logic reasoning
summary: Predicting students' academic risk in online education is crucial for enabling timely interventions that can improve retention and learning outcomes. However, existing models often suffer from limited early detection capability and insufficient interpretability, leading to a "black-box" trust crisis that hinders their adoption in real-world pedagogical settings. To address these challenges, we propose EduRiskX, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates a temporal Transformer-based predictor with F-Logic symbolic reasoning. The neural component models longitudinal student activity sequences using temporal attention, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation. Acting as a data-driven expert system, an F-Logic rule base -- grounded in established educational theories (Engagement Theory and Student Integration Model) to mimic the diagnostic logic of human educators -- is constructed exclusively from the training data. The neural risk probability and the symbolic confidence score are then combined through a logistic regression-based fusion mechanism that learns the relative contribution of each signal. Experiments on the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) using a strict 80/10/10 student-level split show that EduRiskX achieves an accuracy of 0.900 and an F1-score of 0.894 at the end of the semester (Week 38), with an average early detection week of 9.32 and a detection rate of 94.30 percent. Compared with state-of-the-art time-series models (PatchTST, iTransformer) and common deep learning baselines (LSTM, CNN), EduRiskX yields improved recall and earlier risk identification under identical conditions. Beyond predictive performance, the F-Logic module provides structured rule-based explanations linking predictions to observable behavioral patterns and educational theories.

AI.tldr: EduRiskX is a neuro-symbolic framework combining a temporal Transformer predictor with F-Logic symbolic reasoning to predict students' academic risk in online education. It achieves 0.900 accuracy and 0.894 F1-score on OULAD by Week 38, with early detection averaging Week 9.32 and a 94.30% detection rate, while providing interpretable rule-based explanations grounded in educational theories.
AI.motivation: Existing student risk prediction models suffer from limited early detection capability and insufficient interpretability, creating a "black-box" trust crisis that hinders real-world adoption in pedagogical settings.
AI.method: EduRiskX integrates a temporal Transformer-based neural predictor (using temporal attention, class-weighted loss, and dynamic weekly truncation) with an F-Logic symbolic rule base constructed from training data and grounded in Engagement Theory and the Student Integration Model. The neural risk probability and symbolic confidence score are fused via logistic regression-based mechanism that learns the relative contribution of each signal.
AI.result: On OULAD with a strict 80/10/10 student-level split, EduRiskX achieves 0.900 accuracy and 0.894 F1-score at Week 38, with an average early detection week of 9.32 and a 94.30% detection rate. It outperforms PatchTST, iTransformer, LSTM, and CNN baselines in recall and early risk identification under identical conditions.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic fusion of neural prediction with F-Logic symbolic reasoning enables both improved predictive performance and interpretable, theory-grounded explanations that link predictions to observable behavioral patterns, addressing the trust crisis in educational risk prediction.

title: Standalone LLM and a Pre-specified Agentic Pipeline for Explaining ICU Mortality Predictions: a Feasibility Study on the eICU Demo Dataset
summary: Machine-learning models can predict ICU mortality accurately, but feature-attribution methods alone rarely provide the clinical narrative needed for bedside use. Large language models (LLMs) may bridge this gap, and multi-step agentic pipelines are a plausible extension because they separate data interpretation, guideline checking, and final explanation. This revised feasibility study preserves the original standalone-versus-agentic comparison while making the main clinical findings more explicit. Using the retained local eICU Demo artifact set (2,353 ICU stays; 8.1\% mortality), XGBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.855 (95\% CI 0.796--0.906) and an AUPRC of 0.332 (95\% CI 0.217--0.494). On a stratified 38-case explanation subset, the standalone LLM produced 1 explanation with explicit outcome leakage, whereas the four-step agentic pipeline produced none. Among the 14 cases that overlapped with the SHAP review subset, the standalone LLM showed higher SHAP alignment (mean Jaccard 0.171 versus 0.077) and higher direction consistency (92.9\% versus 78.6\%), while the agentic pipeline showed higher guideline grounding (0.762 versus 0.143), higher value specificity (0.236 versus 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 versus 0.671). Clinically, the results suggest that agentic decomposition may improve safety-relevant grounding and patient-specific detail, but it should be paired with attribution-based checks before use in high-stakes risk explanation.

AI.tldr: This revised feasibility study compares standalone LLM versus a four-step agentic pipeline for explaining ICU mortality predictions from an XGBoost model. The agentic pipeline eliminates explicit outcome leakage, improves guideline grounding and value specificity, but sacrifices SHAP alignment and direction consistency compared to the standalone LLM.
AI.motivation: Feature-attribution methods alone do not provide the clinical narrative needed for bedside ICU mortality prediction. LLMs may bridge this gap, and multi-step agentic pipelines are promising because they separate data interpretation, guideline checking, and final explanation. The study revises an earlier feasibility comparison to make clinical findings more explicit.
AI.method: Using a retained local eICU Demo artifact set (2,353 ICU stays; 8.1% mortality), an XGBoost model was trained (AUROC 0.855, AUPRC 0.332). On a stratified 38-case explanation subset, a standalone LLM was compared against a four-step agentic pipeline across metrics including outcome leakage, SHAP alignment (Jaccard similarity), direction consistency, guideline grounding, value specificity, and plausibility.
AI.result: The standalone LLM produced 1 explanation with explicit outcome leakage vs. none for the agentic pipeline. On 14 overlapping cases, the standalone LLM showed higher SHAP alignment (Jaccard 0.171 vs 0.077) and direction consistency (92.9% vs 78.6%), while the agentic pipeline showed higher guideline grounding (0.762 vs 0.143), value specificity (0.236 vs 0.143), and slightly higher plausibility (0.700 vs 0.671).
AI.conclusion: Agentic decomposition may improve safety-relevant grounding and patient-specific detail in ICU mortality explanations, but it should be paired with attribution-based checks before deployment in high-stakes risk explanation settings.

title: Large Models for Battery Prognostics and Health Management: A Review and Future Roadmap
comment: Published in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews
summary: Battery Prognostics and Health Management (BPHM) is critical for ensuring the safe, reliable, and cost-effective operation of batteries across electric vehicles, grid storage, and consumer electronics. Conventional BPHM approaches, including physics-based models and task-centric deep learning methods, face challenges in computational efficiency and parameterization, cross-domain generalization, dependence on extensive labeled run-to-failure data, and model interpretability. Recent Large Models (LMs), built upon Transformer architectures and self-supervised pre-training, offer a transformative new paradigm to overcome these long-standing bottlenecks. This review provides the first comprehensive survey of LM applications in BPHM, systematically examining how these models address challenges in the field. We begin by elucidating the foundational technologies enabling LMs, including Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, large-scale multimodal datasets, and PEFT techniques. We then categorize recent progress along four critical dimensions: mitigating data scarcity, enhancing generalization and robustness, integrating domain knowledge for interpretability, and enabling system-level automation. Despite promising results, significant challenges remain across data accessibility, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility. To guide future research, we propose a roadmap focused on building collaborative data ecosystems, validating intelligence for industrial applications, enhancing trustworthiness with physics-informed designs, and enabling efficient on-device deployment. This review establishes a systematic approach to understand and advance LM-driven BPHM, providing researchers and practitioners with essential insights for developing next-generation battery management systems capable of safe, reliable, and autonomous operation throughout battery lifecycles.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of Large Model (LM) applications in Battery Prognostics and Health Management (BPHM), systematically examining how Transformer-based, self-supervised pre-trained models address long-standing challenges such as data scarcity, cross-domain generalization, computational efficiency, and interpretability in battery health management.
AI.motivation: Conventional BPHM approaches (physics-based models and task-centric deep learning) face bottlenecks including computational inefficiency, poor cross-domain generalization, heavy reliance on extensive labeled run-to-failure data, and limited interpretability. Recent Large Models built on Transformer architectures offer a potentially transformative paradigm to overcome these issues, but no comprehensive survey has systematically examined their applications in BPHM.
AI.method: The review first elucidates the foundational technologies enabling LMs (Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, large-scale multimodal datasets, and PEFT techniques). It then categorizes recent progress along four critical dimensions: mitigating data scarcity, enhancing generalization and robustness, integrating domain knowledge for interpretability, and enabling system-level automation.
AI.result: The survey identifies promising results from LM applications across the four critical dimensions while revealing significant remaining challenges in data accessibility, intelligence validation, trustworthiness, and deployment feasibility. A research roadmap is proposed targeting collaborative data ecosystems, industrial intelligence validation, physics-informed trustworthiness enhancement, and efficient on-device deployment.
AI.conclusion: LM-driven BPHM represents a systematic and promising new paradigm for next-generation battery management systems. The proposed roadmap provides researchers and practitioners with essential guidance toward developing battery management systems capable of safe, reliable, and autonomous operation throughout battery lifecycles.

title: PICasso: An AI-Enabled Design Framework for Autonomous Optimization of Silicon Photonic Devices
comment: 5 Tables, 4 Figures
summary: We present PICasso, an AI-assisted framework for automated synthesis, verification, and optimization of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) from natural-language specifications. PICasso couples a structured NL -> YAML -> GDS generation pipeline with PDK aware knowledge injection, automated placement and routing, DRC/LVS validation, and SAX-based photonic simulation. To systematically evaluate AI-driven photonic design, we introduce PIC-Set, a benchmark of 36 parameterized PIC design tasks spanning core photonic primitives and multi-component circuits. Using PIC-Set, we benchmark several state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) under a unified evaluation protocol, including new metrics such as structural and functional $Spec@k$, optimization efficiency, and robustness under perturbations. Across the benchmark, PICasso significantly improves end-to-end specification satisfaction compared to vanilla LLM generation. Structural $Spec@3$ reaches up to 92.7% and functional $Spec@3$ up to 52% on high-complexity circuits. In addition, PICasso consistently reduces circuit insertion loss, lowering the mean loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (1.74 dB improvement) through simulation-guided optimization. These results demonstrate that structured domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback transform LLMs from brittle netlist generators into practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts with competitive runtimes relative to manual GUI-based workflows.

AI.tldr: PICasso is an AI-assisted framework that automates synthesis, verification, and optimization of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) from natural-language specifications, coupled with a PIC-Set benchmark of 36 design tasks. It achieves up to 92.7% structural and 52% functional Spec@3 on high-complexity circuits, and reduces mean insertion loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between natural-language-driven AI generation and manufacturable photonic integrated circuit design, addressing the brittleness of vanilla LLM netlist generation without structured domain constraints, physical verification, or simulation feedback.
AI.method: PICasso couples a structured NL → YAML → GDS generation pipeline with PDK-aware knowledge injection, automated placement and routing, DRC/LVS validation, and SAX-based photonic simulation. It introduces PIC-Set, a benchmark of 36 parameterized PIC design tasks, and evaluates LLMs under a unified protocol with new metrics including structural/functional Spec@k, optimization efficiency, and robustness under perturbations.
AI.result: PICasso significantly improves end-to-end specification satisfaction over vanilla LLM generation: structural Spec@3 reaches up to 92.7% and functional Spec@3 up to 52% on high-complexity circuits. It also reduces mean insertion loss from 4.98 dB to 3.25 dB (a 1.74 dB improvement) via simulation-guided optimization.
AI.conclusion: Structured domain constraints, physical verification, and simulation feedback transform LLMs from brittle netlist generators into practical PIC design agents capable of producing manufacturable layouts with competitive runtimes relative to manual GUI-based workflows.

title: WALL-SS: Scaling Long-horizon World Models via Next-Scale Autoregression
summary: Generative world models provide robots with predictive models of how the world evolves under interaction, with growing potential for simulation, planning, policy evaluation, and robot learning. Beyond clip-level future prediction, a unified generative formulation should relate actions to consequences, support flexible horizons and continuous interaction, and enable reward-driven optimization. We introduce WALL-SS, a world model that generates visual futures through Scale-wise autoregressive Scaling, enabling action-controllable and long-horizon robotic simulation. WALL-SS represents embodied trajectories as causal sequences of temporally interleaved observations and actions, making action-dependent state transitions explicit while naturally supporting variable-length generation, streaming extension through reusable causal states, and direct optimization through sequence probabilities. To make this formulation effective over long horizons, we generate each future observation in a coarse-to-fine manner and develop three complementary components within the same hierarchy. Action-conditioned next-scale prediction injects scale-aligned action representations to improve action-future coupling and model both successful and failed behaviors. Scale-compressed long-horizon memory retains recent interactions at fine resolution while compressing distant observations and actions, with scale-wise dream forcing enhancing robustness to self-generated context. Finally, on-policy alignment optimizes autoregressive visual dynamics with action-following and long-term consistency rewards while preserving the pretrained visual distribution. Experiments show that WALL-SS improves action following and trajectory accuracy, supports coherent minute-long streaming rollout under bounded memory, and consistently benefits from on-policy alignment in reducing action drift and long-horizon inconsistency.

AI.tldr: WALL-SS is a generative world model that uses scale-wise autoregressive scaling to enable action-controllable, long-horizon robotic visual simulation. It generates future observations in a coarse-to-fine manner with three key components: action-conditioned next-scale prediction, scale-compressed long-horizon memory with scale-wise dream forcing, and on-policy alignment. It supports coherent minute-long streaming rollouts under bounded memory and improves action following and trajectory accuracy.
AI.motivation: Generative world models for robots need to go beyond clip-level future prediction toward a unified formulation that relates actions to consequences, supports flexible horizons and continuous interaction, and enables reward-driven optimization for simulation, planning, policy evaluation, and robot learning.
AI.method: WALL-SS treats embodied trajectories as causal sequences of temporally interleaved observations and actions, enabling explicit action-dependent state transitions with variable-length generation and streaming extension via reusable causal states. Each future observation is generated coarse-to-fine using three complementary components in the same hierarchy: (1) action-conditioned next-scale prediction injects scale-aligned action representations; (2) scale-compressed long-horizon memory retains recent interactions at fine resolution while compressing distant observations/actions with scale-wise dream forcing; (3) on-policy alignment optimizes autoregressive visual dynamics with action-following and long-term consistency rewards while preserving the pretrained visual distribution.
AI.result: WALL-SS improves action following and trajectory accuracy, supports coherent minute-long streaming rollout under bounded memory, and consistently benefits from on-policy alignment in reducing action drift and long-horizon inconsistency.
AI.conclusion: WALL-SS demonstrates that a scale-wise autoregressive generative formulation can effectively support action-controllable and long-horizon robotic world modeling, with on-policy alignment serving as a reliable mechanism to mitigate drift and maintain consistency over extended interactions.

title: CIFQA: A Deterministic Tool-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Financial Query Answering
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, submitted for academic dissemination
summary: Calculation-intensive financial question answering requires exact reasoning over structured rates, temporal conditions, numerical formulas, and rule-based constraints. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on natural language tasks, they often produce numerically incorrect yet plausible answers when solving multi-step financial calculations. To address this limitation, we introduce CIFQA (Calculation-Intensive Financial Query Answering), a deterministic tool-grounded multi-agent LLM framework for financial question answering. CIFQA separates language understanding from numerical execution by assigning specialized agents to query interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, and response generation, while deterministic Python-based tools perform financial calculations and rule application. We instantiate CIFQA for fixed deposit query answering and evaluate it on a curated benchmark of fixed deposit queries. CIFQA achieves 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy, substantially outperforming direct LLM baselines even when provided with complete formulas, rate cards, and benchmark instructions. Ablation studies show that deterministic components such as exact rate lookup, tenure computation, rolling-year adjustment, and premature-withdrawal logic are critical contributors to performance. Notably, a 17B open-source backbone operating within CIFQA outperforms substantially larger frontier models evaluated with the same financial information, demonstrating that architectural design is a more important determinant of numerical reliability than model scale. While evaluated on fixed deposit queries, CIFQA provides a generalizable framework for calculation-intensive financial reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: CIFQA is a deterministic tool-grounded multi-agent LLM framework for calculation-intensive financial QA that separates language understanding from numerical execution, achieving 95.54% accuracy on fixed deposit queries and outperforming much larger frontier models.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce numerically incorrect yet plausible answers on multi-step financial calculations despite strong natural language performance, motivating a framework that separates reasoning from numerical execution.
AI.method: CIFQA uses specialized agents for query interpretation, routing, parameter extraction, computation planning, and response generation, with deterministic Python-based tools handling financial calculations and rule application. It is instantiated for fixed deposit query answering with exact rate lookup, tenure computation, rolling-year adjustment, and premature-withdrawal logic.
AI.result: CIFQA achieves 95.54% accuracy on calculation-intensive queries and 90.87% overall accuracy, substantially outperforming direct LLM baselines. A 17B open-source backbone within CIFQA outperforms larger frontier models, and ablations confirm deterministic components are critical.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design is a more important determinant of numerical reliability than model scale, and CIFQA provides a generalizable framework for calculation-intensive financial reasoning beyond fixed deposit queries.

title: Constraint-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Static Shape Estimation of Co-Manipulative Continuum Robots
summary: Static shape estimation of co-manipulative continuum robots (CCRs) is challenging because the continuum arms and manipulated flexible object form a closed chain that must satisfy both static equilibrium and geometric loop-closure constraints. This paper presents a constraint-aware physics-informed neural network (PINN) for static shape estimation of a tendon-driven CCR modeled using the geometric variable strain formulation. The proposed method incorporates a projected static equilibrium residual and a configuration-level geometric residual to enforce the governing mechanics and closed-chain geometry. In simulation, the PINN is compared with a purely data-driven artificial neural network (ANN) under limited and noisy training data. With 140 samples and 50% label noise, the PINN reduces the relative configuration error, equilibrium residual, and closed-chain residual by 67.88%, 67.35%, and 88.06%, respectively. Using the full dataset, the PINN achieves 0.1597% relative configuration error with an inference time of 0.1773 ms, compared with 17.97 s for an iterative nonlinear solver. Experimental fine-tuning reduces the marker RMSE from 2.657 mm to 0.497 mm and increases R2 from -0.788 to 0.937. These results demonstrate accurate, physically consistent, and computationally efficient static shape estimation of closed-chain CCRs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a constraint-aware physics-informed neural network (PINN) for static shape estimation of tendon-driven co-manipulative continuum robots (CCRs), where the continuum arm and manipulated object form a closed chain. The PINN integrates projected static equilibrium and geometric loop-closure residuals into the loss function. Results show superior accuracy, physical consistency, and computational efficiency compared to data-driven ANNs and iterative solvers.
AI.motivation: Static shape estimation of CCRs is challenging because the continuum arms and manipulated flexible object form a closed chain that must satisfy both static equilibrium and geometric loop-closure constraints simultaneously, making purely data-driven approaches insufficient.
AI.method: A constraint-aware PINN for tendon-driven CCRs modeled with the geometric variable strain formulation. The network incorporates a projected static equilibrium residual and a configuration-level geometric residual to enforce governing mechanics and closed-chain geometry. Experimental fine-tuning is also employed to adapt the model to real hardware.
AI.result: Under limited and noisy data (140 samples, 50% label noise), the PINN reduces relative configuration error by 67.88%, equilibrium residual by 67.35%, and closed-chain residual by 88.06% versus a purely data-driven ANN. With the full dataset, it achieves 0.1597% relative configuration error with 0.1773 ms inference time, versus 17.97 s for an iterative nonlinear solver. Experimental fine-tuning reduces marker RMSE from 2.657 mm to 0.497 mm and increases R2 from -0.788 to 0.937.
AI.conclusion: The proposed constraint-aware PINN demonstrates accurate, physically consistent, and computationally efficient static shape estimation for closed-chain CCRs, offering a strong alternative to iterative nonlinear solvers and data-driven baselines.

title: The Artificial Experimentalist: Discovery and Control of Self-Organizing Phenomena with Autotelic Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at ALIFE 2026. Companion website: https://developmentalsystems.org/carl/
summary: Existing methods for exploring cellular automata and other complex systems mostly operate in open loop: they set initial conditions, execute a full simulation, and observe the outcome, without intervening during execution. We introduce a closed-loop framework based on autotelic reinforcement learning, in which an agent autonomously samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene in a complex system through minimal, local perturbations. We instantiate this framework on Lenia, a continuous cellular automaton known for life-like self-organizing patterns, in an agentic system we call CARL, and demonstrate three capabilities. First, CARL discovers stable solitons across a wide range of Lenia update rules at a higher rate than heuristic baselines. Second, it learns to steer the movement direction of existing solitons with few interventions, showing that CARL can control self-organizing patterns, not only create them. Third, humans can use trained agents to guide solitons through maze environments in real time by specifying high-level directional commands that the agent translates into low-level interventions. Trained across diverse goals, update rules, and random initial states, the agents acquire policies that generalize zero-shot to various out-of-distribution conditions. These results suggest a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that, autonomously or with human guidance, discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CARL, a closed-loop framework based on autotelic reinforcement learning for controlling complex systems like Lenia (a continuous cellular automaton). CARL autonomously samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene via minimal local perturbations, demonstrating three capabilities: discovering stable solitons across various update rules, steering existing solitons' movement direction, and enabling humans to guide solitons through mazes in real time via high-level commands. The agents generalize zero-shot to out-of-distribution conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for exploring complex systems such as cellular automata operate in open loop—setting initial conditions, running full simulations, and observing outcomes without intervening during execution. This limits the agent's ability to actively discover, control, and shape emergent phenomena.
AI.method: The authors propose a closed-loop framework based on autotelic reinforcement learning, where an agent autonomously samples diverse goals and learns a goal-conditioned policy to intervene in a complex system through minimal, local perturbations. The framework is instantiated on Lenia (a continuous cellular automaton) in a system called CARL.
AI.result: CARL demonstrates three capabilities: (1) discovering stable solitons across a wide range of Lenia update rules at a higher rate than heuristic baselines; (2) steering existing solitons' movement direction with few interventions; (3) enabling real-time human guidance of solitons through maze environments via high-level directional commands. Trained across diverse goals, update rules, and random initial states, the agents generalize zero-shot to out-of-distribution conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a path toward artificial experimentalist agents that, autonomously or with human guidance, discover and control emergent phenomena in complex systems.

title: Dispersive Forward Tree Search for Optimal Control: Coverage, Complexity, and Computation
comment: 28 pages. Code: https://github.com/croshank/DFTSearch
summary: Steering-based planners require solutions to state-to-state boundary value problems, which can be inaccessible for nonlinear platforms. Forward propagation evades the steering requirement, but the finite-sample behavior of the associated planners remains uncharacterized and their implementations underperform in practice. This paper develops a propagation-based kinodynamic planner with deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees. We work within the large class of differentially flat nonlinear systems and show that a forward tree of locally dispersive control commands contains a near-optimal trajectory at a certified tree size. We provide a general mechanism to construct dispersive command sets for control-affine systems, which are necessary to implement the search algorithm prescribed by the theory. We show that covering the certified trajectory class irrespective of cost provably demands a tree exponentially sized in the problem horizon, and present a cost-conditioned dominance pruning procedure that retains near-optimality at a tree size polynomial in the horizon. We implement the resulting search algorithm, Dispersive Forward Tree search (DFT*), as breadth-first expansion of the forward tree, which maps naturally onto parallel hardware. We design efficient dispersive samplers for the unicycle, the trailer car, and the quadrotor and evaluate challenging planning tasks for these platforms. DFT* delivers consistently competitive and often substantially better solution quality than state-of-the-art kinodynamic planners at comparable solution times on embedded-tier processors, accelerating further as parallel compute is scaled. We also implement DFT* in a receding-horizon loop to demonstrate real-time planning in dynamic environments at embedded-tier compute budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DFT* (Dispersive Forward Tree search), a propagation-based kinodynamic planner with deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees for differentially flat nonlinear systems. It shows that a forward tree of locally dispersive control commands contains a near-optimal trajectory at a certified tree size, provides a general mechanism for constructing dispersive command sets for control-affine systems, and introduces a cost-conditioned dominance pruning procedure that retains near-optimality at a polynomial tree size. The algorithm is implemented as breadth-first expansion mapping onto parallel hardware and evaluated on unicycle, trailer car, and quadrotor platforms, demonstrating competitive or better solution quality than state-of-the-art kinodynamic planners.
AI.motivation: Steering-based planners require solving state-to-state boundary value problems, which is inaccessible for nonlinear platforms. While forward propagation avoids this steering requirement, the finite-sample behavior of forward-propagation-based planners has remained uncharacterized and their implementations underperform in practice. This gap motivates the need for a propagation-based kinodynamic planner with rigorous finite-sample guarantees.
AI.method: The method leverages the class of differentially flat nonlinear systems and builds a forward tree of locally dispersive control commands. Key components include: (1) a proof that this tree contains a near-optimal trajectory at a certified tree size; (2) a general mechanism to construct dispersive command sets for control-affine systems; (3) a cost-conditioned dominance pruning procedure that reduces tree size from exponential to polynomial in the horizon while retaining near-optimality; and (4) an implementation as breadth-first expansion of the forward tree (DFT*), which maps naturally onto parallel hardware, with efficient dispersive samplers for unicycle, trailer car, and quadrotor platforms.
AI.result: DFT* delivers consistently competitive and often substantially better solution quality than state-of-the-art kinodynamic planners at comparable solution times on embedded-tier processors. It accelerates further with parallel compute scaling. The algorithm is also demonstrated in a receding-horizon loop for real-time planning in dynamic environments at embedded-tier compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that propagation-based kinodynamic planning can achieve deterministic finite-sample near-optimality guarantees for differentially flat nonlinear systems, addressing a long-standing gap. The proposed DFT* algorithm is both theoretically grounded and practically effective, outperforming existing kinodynamic planners on embedded hardware and scaling with parallelism, while supporting real-time receding-horizon planning in dynamic environments.

title: The Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox Quantifying Net Energy Loss in on-Device Energy Forecasting
comment: The 5th International Conference on Mobile, Military, Maritime IT Convergence (ICMIC 2026)
summary: Energy forecasting aims to maximize accuracy to ensure energy efficiency by reducing energy waste, an objective that applies equally to on-device forecasting for mission-critical edge environments, including military systems. However, this paper identifies the Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox: high-precision energy forecasting models can ironically trigger a net energy deficit. This stems from both edge AI's inference energy consumption and battery aging. We propose a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework for energy forecasting, designed to minimize net energy loss. This framework treats not only inference energy consumption but also battery aging as a unified form of energy loss, as degradation represents a physical dissipation of the system's future energy-carrying capacity. We demonstrate that in thermally sensitive edge environments, energy saved by the superior precision of complex architectures is often outweighed by the total energy lost through their high operational intensity.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an "Accuracy-Efficiency Paradox" where high-precision energy forecasting models on edge devices can cause net energy loss due to inference energy consumption and battery aging. It proposes a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework that treats battery degradation as energy loss to minimize net energy deficit, demonstrating that complex architectures' precision gains are often outweighed by their operational energy costs in thermally sensitive edge environments.
AI.motivation: Energy forecasting aims to maximize accuracy for energy efficiency, especially in mission-critical edge environments like military systems. However, the paper reveals a paradox: more accurate models can ironically lead to net energy deficits due to the energy costs of running complex AI models on edge devices and the acceleration of battery degradation.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) framework that unifies both inference energy consumption and battery aging as forms of energy loss, as battery degradation represents a physical dissipation of the system's future energy-carrying capacity. This framework is designed to minimize net energy loss in energy forecasting systems.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates that in thermally sensitive edge environments, the energy saved by the superior forecasting precision of complex architectures is often outweighed by the total energy lost through their high operational intensity (inference cost plus battery aging).
AI.conclusion: High-precision forecasting models are not always the best choice for edge energy forecasting. A TCO-based evaluation that accounts for both inference energy and battery degradation should guide model selection to achieve genuine net energy efficiency.

title: Cross-Platform Benchmark of Neural 3D Reconstruction for Autonomous Laboratory Robots
comment: This manuscript is peer-reviewed from the committees in the workshop "VAxAutoSci: Visual Analytics in the Age of Autonomous Scientific Discovery" in conjunction with 2026 IEEE Visualization & Visual Analytics
summary: Autonomous robots performing laboratory tasks depend on 3D reconstruction pipelines that can turn raw camera streams into actionable object representations within the latency budget of a physical control loop. Neural 3D reconstruction methods have demonstrated high-quality view synthesis, but their real-time viability across the compute platforms on which laboratory robots actually run remains poorly characterized. In this work, we present a systematic compute-platform benchmark of neural 3D reconstruction methods, evaluating NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting training and rendering on GPU-enabled computing devices ranging from single-board computers to server-class nodes, and place Meta's SAM3D single-image reconstruction on the same axes to quantify its latency and fidelity gap relative to per-scene optimization. Our results show that Gaussian Splatting yields higher rendering quality than NeRF at greater GPU cost, and that onboard compute is insufficient for full per-scene optimization at interactive rates. Our preliminary assessment on SAM3D indicates that it delivers plausible object geometry within seconds, but with detail mismatches that can compromise downstream manipulation. Together, these findings motivate tiered pipelines in which lightweight feed-forward reconstruction sustains the real-time perception-and-tracking loop for laboratory robots, while heavier neural reconstruction is scheduled selectively on suitable compute.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic compute-platform benchmark of neural 3D reconstruction methods (NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, and SAM3D) across GPU devices from single-board computers to server-class nodes, revealing that Gaussian Splatting outperforms NeRF in quality at higher GPU cost, onboard compute is insufficient for real-time per-scene optimization, and proposing tiered pipelines combining fast feed-forward reconstruction with selective heavy neural optimization.
AI.motivation: Autonomous laboratory robots require real-time 3D reconstruction from raw camera streams, yet the real-time viability of neural 3D reconstruction methods across the actual compute platforms used by laboratory robots remains poorly characterized.
AI.method: A systematic compute-platform benchmark evaluating NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (both training and rendering) on GPU devices spanning single-board computers to server-class nodes, alongside a comparative assessment of Meta's SAM3D single-image reconstruction measured on latency and fidelity axes.
AI.result: Gaussian Splatting achieves higher rendering quality than NeRF but at increased GPU cost; onboard compute cannot support full per-scene optimization at interactive rates; SAM3D produces plausible object geometry in seconds but with detail mismatches that may compromise downstream manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate tiered pipelines where lightweight feed-forward reconstruction maintains the real-time perception-and-tracking loop for laboratory robots, while heavier neural reconstruction is selectively scheduled on appropriate compute resources.

title: LLMs for Academic Workflows: An Evaluation of Literature Reviews Generated with Short and Long Context Windows of LLMs
summary: Our research focuses on evaluating literature reviews generated in short and long context settings of large language models (LLMs) to investigate the impact of context window on the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and the role of AI in supporting literature review writing. Twenty AI-generated literature reviews based on research sources from Semantic Scholar and Arxiv were evaluated by two researchers across 15 dimensions. Our findings reveal that AI-generated literature reviews require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. As context windows increase, LLMs can incorporate broader information and maintain coherence across longer inputs, but they also exacerbate issues such as content repetition, omission of critical work, and a tendency towards descriptiveness over synthesis. Our work shows that AI-generated reviews can provide foundational overviews, but their output must be critically evaluated and refined by domain experts. Future research should consider integrating other LLMs and fine-tuned models in different domains with hybrid approaches that combine human expertise with AI capabilities to address the limitations identified in this study.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates AI-generated literature reviews produced by LLMs in short and long context settings, revealing that while LLMs can provide foundational overviews, their outputs require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. Longer context windows enable broader information incorporation but exacerbate issues like content repetition, omission of critical work, and descriptiveness over synthesis.
AI.motivation: To investigate the impact of context window size on the quality of AI-generated literature reviews and to understand the role of AI in supporting literature review writing.
AI.method: Twenty AI-generated literature reviews were produced based on research sources from Semantic Scholar and Arxiv, then evaluated by two researchers across 15 dimensions in short and long context settings of LLMs.
AI.result: AI-generated literature reviews require human oversight to meet academic publishing standards. Longer context windows allow broader information incorporation and coherence maintenance but worsen content repetition, omission of critical work, and descriptiveness over synthesis.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated reviews can serve as foundational overviews but must be critically evaluated and refined by domain experts. Future research should explore integrating other LLMs and fine-tuned models across domains using hybrid approaches combining human expertise with AI capabilities.

title: RTNav: Towards Real-Time Zero-Shot Object Navigation
summary: Navigation in unknown environments to find unforeseen objects has become increasingly feasible with capable vision and language foundation models. However, these models also introduce non-negligible inference latency, which becomes an important concern when agents must operate continuously in the real world. Most state-of-the-art methods are still developed in synchronous simulators, where the environment waits for the agent to act and inference time is effectively free. As a result, agents are often designed around the sequential execution of perception, reasoning, and action, with little regard for time constraints. Under real-time execution, where wall-clock time counts towards the task budget, the inefficiencies of these architectures become clear. We show that recent zero-shot object navigation methods suffer consistent performance degradation under such realistic timing conditions. Motivated by this observation, we propose RTNav, a simple but effective architecture that treats inference latency, asynchronous environment stepping, and bounded compute as explicit design considerations. Evaluated on real-time variants of HM3D-v1, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON, RTNav improves the success rate by up to 11% and the Success weighted by Completion Time by up to 5.1 points over prior work.

AI.tldr: RTNav is a real-time object navigation architecture that explicitly accounts for inference latency and asynchronous environment stepping, improving success rates by up to 11% over prior zero-shot navigation methods under realistic timing conditions.
AI.motivation: Most object navigation methods are developed in synchronous simulators where inference latency is effectively free, causing performance to degrade severely under real-time execution where wall-clock time counts toward the task budget.
AI.method: RTNav is an architecture that treats inference latency, asynchronous environment stepping, and bounded compute as explicit design considerations, in contrast to sequential perception-reasoning-action pipelines in existing methods.
AI.result: On real-time variants of HM3D-v1, HM3D-v2, and HM3D-OVON, RTNav improves success rate by up to 11% and Success weighted by Completion Time by up to 5.1 points over prior work.
AI.conclusion: Latency-aware architectural design is crucial for real-world object navigation, and RTNav demonstrates that explicitly accounting for timing constraints yields substantial performance gains over synchronous-simulator-tuned methods.

title: Methodological and Conceptual Framework for 5D Multi-Table Analysis: A Unified Approach for Complex Data Reuse
summary: Multi-table learning remains a major challenge in machine learning for healthcare and other complex information systems. Relational data combine several sources of complexity, including large data volume, high-dimensional variables, high-cardinality categorical features, complex inter-table dependencies, and repeated temporal observations. We introduce the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a unified architecture that represents relational databases as hypergraphs, learns pentadimensional embeddings (PentE), and performs sparse relational attention with complexity proportional to the average relational degree rather than the square of the number of entities. We formally define the architecture, derive the complexity of its attention mechanism, and provide an open-source reference implementation. We evaluate RHT on the public Synthea synthetic electronic health record dataset using multi-label prediction of SNOMED CT condition codes per encounter, a task characterized by high categorical cardinality and long-tailed label distributions. Comparisons with tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines show that RHT produces more semantically coherent embeddings while remaining computationally scalable. In this benchmark, the highest rare-code recall is achieved by XGBoost, whereas RHT attains the strongest embedding semantic coherence. We also report ablation studies quantifying the contribution of each architectural component. Clinical validation on MIMIC-IV is planned following PhysioNet credentialing. Source code and experimental protocols are provided in the accompanying repository.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Relational Hypergraph Transformer (RHT), a unified architecture that models relational databases as hypergraphs with pentadimensional embeddings (PentE) and sparse relational attention. RHT's attention complexity scales with the average relational degree rather than the square of entities, making it scalable for complex multi-table healthcare data. Evaluated on the Synthea dataset for multi-label SNOMED CT condition prediction, RHT achieves superior embedding semantic coherence compared to tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines, though XGBoost attains the highest rare-code recall.
AI.motivation: Multi-table learning in healthcare and complex information systems is challenging due to large data volume, high-dimensional variables, high-cardinality categorical features, complex inter-table dependencies, and repeated temporal observations. Existing approaches struggle to handle these combined complexities efficiently and coherently.
AI.method: RHT represents relational databases as hypergraphs, learns pentadimensional embeddings (PentE) for entities, and performs sparse relational attention whose computational complexity is proportional to the average relational degree rather than the square of the number of entities. The architecture is formally defined, and its attention complexity is derived, with an open-source reference implementation provided.
AI.result: On the public Synthea synthetic EHR dataset with multi-label SNOMED CT condition prediction (characterized by high categorical cardinality and long-tailed labels), RHT outperforms tabular, relational, and temporal graph baselines in embedding semantic coherence while remaining computationally scalable. XGBoost achieves the highest rare-code recall. Ablation studies quantify each architectural component's contribution.
AI.conclusion: RHT provides a scalable and semantically coherent unified architecture for relational/multi-table learning in healthcare. Clinical validation on MIMIC-IV is planned following PhysioNet credentialing, with source code and experimental protocols publicly available.

title: Closing the Loop on the Poppy Humanoid: Bipedal Locomotion with Linear-Quadratic Control and Learned Cost Functions
comment: Accepted by International Conference on the AI Revolution: Research, Ethics, and Society (AIR-RES 2026)
summary: The Poppy Humanoid is an open-source, low-cost robot suitable for research and education in artificial intelligence. However, we are unaware of any published methodology that achieves reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on the standard Poppy hardware. This paper contributes a functional closed-loop walking controller for Poppy, based on the linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) framework for trajectory tracking. Starting with data collected from open-loop playback of a nominal walking trajectory, our proposed method learns a quadratic cost function for an LQR controller that substantially improves the reliability of the motion. The closed-loop controller is validated empirically, demonstrating statistically significant improvements in walking performance compared to open-loop trajectory playback.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a closed-loop walking controller for the Poppy Humanoid robot based on LQR trajectory tracking, where the quadratic cost function is learned from data collected via open-loop playback of a nominal walking trajectory. The controller demonstrates statistically significant improvements in walking performance over open-loop playback.
AI.motivation: The Poppy Humanoid is an open-source, low-cost robot for AI research and education, but no published methodology achieves reliable, unassisted bipedal locomotion on the standard hardware. This gap motivates the need for a functional walking controller.
AI.method: The proposed method uses a linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) framework for trajectory tracking. Data collected from open-loop playback of a nominal walking trajectory is used to learn a quadratic cost function, which is then employed in the closed-loop LQR controller to improve motion reliability.
AI.result: Empirical validation demonstrates that the closed-loop LQR controller provides statistically significant improvements in walking performance compared to open-loop trajectory playback.
AI.conclusion: A closed-loop walking controller based on LQR with a learned cost function can enable reliable bipedal locomotion on the standard Poppy Humanoid hardware, filling a previously missing capability in this research platform.

title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Systematic Literature Review of Disease Spread Models
comment: To be published in the Winter Simulation Conference 2026
summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have created new opportunities to streamline and potentially automate many research processes, including systematic literature reviews (SLRs). This study reports an LLM pipeline development for extracting model-relevant information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers. We compare the results with those of a human-conducted SLR. Our results show paper-level accuracies of approximately 77.95% for GPT-4.1 and 81.67% for GPT-5.0. Field-level accuracy ranges from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex or subjective fields performing less reliably. Importantly, we find that agreement between LLMs is a potential indicator of output quality: low agreement may signal hallucinations, whereas high agreement combined with low accuracy may point to noise or errors in the human dataset. Overall, our study provides practical insights into prompt development and highlights both the potential and limitations of using LLMs for full-scale SLRs in the modeling and simulation domain.

AI.tldr: This study develops an LLM pipeline for extracting model-relevant information from 536 agent-based modeling papers and compares it against a human-conducted systematic literature review. GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.0 achieve paper-level accuracies of ~77.95% and ~81.67% respectively, with field-level accuracy ranging from 32.40% to 100.00% depending on field complexity. The study finds that LLM agreement can indicate output quality, where low agreement may signal hallucinations and high agreement with low accuracy may indicate human dataset errors.
AI.motivation: To explore whether LLMs can streamline and potentially automate systematic literature reviews, a time-consuming and labor-intensive research process, and to provide practical guidance on using LLMs for this purpose in the modeling and simulation domain.
AI.method: An LLM pipeline was developed to extract model-relevant information from 536 peer-reviewed agent-based modeling papers, and the outputs were compared against results from a human-conducted systematic literature review across both paper-level and field-level dimensions. Agreement patterns between LLMs were also analyzed as quality indicators.
AI.result: Paper-level accuracies of approximately 77.95% for GPT-4.1 and 81.67% for GPT-5.0. Field-level accuracy ranged from 32.40% to 100.00%, with more complex or subjective fields performing less reliably. LLM agreement was found to be a potential indicator of output quality—low agreement suggesting hallucinations, while high agreement with low accuracy pointing to possible human dataset errors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show significant potential for automating full-scale systematic literature reviews, but their performance varies substantially across field complexity and subjectivity. LLM agreement patterns can serve as diagnostic signals for output quality. The study offers practical insights into prompt development and delineates both the capabilities and limitations of LLM-based SLRs in the modeling and simulation domain.

title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
comment: 22 pages, 15 figures
summary: Robot policies deployed in the wild should have the capability to continually learn new tasks without forgetting existing behaviors. A common approach to combat such catastrophic forgetting is to train on new task data with a replay buffer of previously learned task data. Although this buffer is commonly sampled randomly from all prior experiences, we show that a small set of these experiences contributes greatly in anchoring past performance. We call these experiences Memory Anchors. We identify Memory Anchors in regions where representations of new-task observations collapse onto those of old-task observations even though the tasks require conflicting actions, like when a familiar object must be manipulated in a new way. Rehearsing old data in this region plays a key role in preventing destructive overwriting of past task knowledge, serving as this critical Memory Anchor role. Excluding only 10% Memory Anchors before sampling the buffer leads to more than a 4.5x increase in catastrophic forgetting on the LIBERO benchmark suites. Conversely, enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors can decrease high-conflict task forgetting by 63% and enables successful continual learning of two task sequences on a real robot. Videos and additional visualizations can be found at https://robot-adaptation.github.io/MemoryAnchors

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Memory Anchors"—a small set of prior experiences where new-task observations collapse onto old-task representations despite conflicting action requirements. These anchors critically prevent catastrophic forgetting in continual robot learning; excluding just 10% of them from replay buffers increases forgetting 4.5x on LIBERO benchmarks, while enriching buffers with them reduces high-conflict task forgetting by 63% and enables successful real-robot continual learning.
AI.motivation: Robot policies deployed in real-world settings need to continually acquire new skills without catastrophic forgetting, but standard replay-buffer approaches treat all prior experiences equally. The paper challenges this assumption by showing that a small subset of prior experiences disproportionately anchors past performance, and identifies a principled way to find these critical experiences.
AI.method: The authors identify Memory Anchors in representation space—regions where new-task observation representations collapse onto old-task observation representations even though the tasks require conflicting actions (e.g., familiar objects manipulated in new ways). They analyze the effect of selectively removing anchors from replay buffers and conversely enriching buffers with anchors, evaluating on LIBERO benchmark suites and a real robot.
AI.result: Removing only 10% of Memory Anchors from the replay buffer before sampling leads to over a 4.5x increase in catastrophic forgetting on LIBERO. Conversely, enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors reduces high-conflict task forgetting by 63% and enables successful continual learning of two task sequences on a physical robot.
AI.conclusion: Not all replay experiences are equally valuable for preventing catastrophic forgetting. Memory Anchors—experiences at the decision boundary between conflicting old and new tasks—are disproportionately critical for preserving past knowledge, suggesting that principled, anchor-aware buffer curation can substantially improve continual learning for robot policies.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Customer Churn Prediction in Telecommunications: A Framework for CRM Integration
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 1 table
summary: Subscriber attrition is a costly, persistent challenge for telecommunications providers, with monthly churn of roughly 1.9% in mature markets eroding billions in revenue annually. Predictive models can flag at-risk customers accurately, yet they are routinely excluded from frontline CRM workflows because high-performing ensemble and non-linear architectures are opaque: a retention specialist cannot design a personalised intervention from a probability score alone, without knowing why a subscriber is at risk. This paper addresses that gap. We benchmark four classifiers--Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM--on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (7,043 records; 19 features; 26.5% churn, balanced to 50% via SMOTE on the training partition only). Logistic Regression attains the strongest AUC-ROC (0.8411) and LightGBM the highest accuracy (78.42%); all four fall within a 0.011 AUC band (0.831--0.841), and 5-fold cross-validation confirms the leading models are effectively tied. Explanations are delivered at two granularities: a global SHAP ranking identifying tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract as the dominant churn signals, and instance-level SHAP and LIME decompositions that expose the drivers behind each prediction. Building on these outputs, we introduce a four-layer CRM integration architecture that converts risk scores and attribution vectors into tiered segmentation, maps top features to structured retention-action templates, and routes campaign outcomes into a retraining feedback loop. Targeting the highest-risk quintile is projected to cut overall churn by 3.3--5.3 percentage points, preserving an estimated $199K--$319K per campaign cycle.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks four classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, finding Logistic Regression achieves the best AUC-ROC (0.8411) and LightGBM the highest accuracy (78.42%), with all models statistically tied within a 0.011 AUC band. It delivers global and instance-level SHAP/LIME explanations and introduces a four-layer CRM integration architecture that converts risk scores into tiered segmentation and actionable retention templates, projecting 3.3-5.3 percentage point churn reduction worth $199K-$319K per campaign.
AI.motivation: High-performing predictive churn models are accurate but opaque, preventing retention specialists from designing personalized interventions. The paper addresses the gap between model performance and practical explainability in frontline CRM workflows.
AI.method: Benchmarks four classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) on the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records, 19 features, 26.5% churn balanced to 50% via SMOTE on training only). Uses 5-fold cross-validation, global SHAP ranking, instance-level SHAP and LIME decomposition, and proposes a four-layer CRM integration architecture with tiered segmentation, retention-action templates, and a retraining feedback loop.
AI.result: Logistic Regression achieves the strongest AUC-ROC (0.8411); LightGBM achieves the highest accuracy (78.42%). All models fall within a 0.011 AUC band (0.831-0.841) and cross-validation confirms they are effectively tied. Tenure, total charges, and month-to-month contract are the dominant churn signals. Targeting the highest-risk quintile projects 3.3-5.3 percentage point churn reduction, preserving $199K-$319K per campaign cycle.
AI.conclusion: Explainability combined with predictive performance enables practical deployment of churn models in CRM workflows. The four-layer integration architecture bridges model outputs to actionable retention interventions, yielding significant projected cost savings while maintaining model interpretability.

title: TrapVLA: Trapping Vision-Language-Action Models in Configured Failure Modes
summary: This work introduces Configured Failure Trapping, a novel backdoor attack task against Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which aims to activate attacks through stealthy textual triggers and induce configured failure modes. Unlike prior backdoor attacks that treat any task failure as a successful attack, Configured Failure Trapping requires the attacker to control how the robot fails (e.g., causing the robot to grasp with a specified positional offset), making it substantially more challenging and hard to detect. To support the new task, we propose an effective data engine for synthesizing high-quality target trajectories and an automated suite for measuring configured-failure fidelity. Then, based on this foundation, we construct two new benchmarks, namely Trap-LIBERO and Trap-RoboTwin, that instantiate Configured Failure Trapping across four representative failure modes. To address this task, we identify sparse action deviation as a critical challenge and accordingly propose a novel method named TrapVLA, which explicitly learns trigger-induced action residuals to steer the policy toward the configured failure behavior. Extensive experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic settings show that TrapVLA effectively injects configured failure modes into VLA models while largely preserving performance on clean data. Project page: https://john-liua.github.io/TrapVLA/

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Configured Failure Trapping, a novel backdoor attack task against Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that enables attackers to control how a robot fails (rather than just causing any failure) via stealthy textual triggers. The authors propose a data engine for synthesizing target trajectories, an automated evaluation suite, two benchmarks (Trap-LIBERO and Trap-RoboTwin) covering four failure modes, and TrapVLA—a method that learns trigger-induced action residuals to steer policy behavior toward configured failures while preserving clean-data performance.
AI.motivation: Prior backdoor attacks on VLA models only aim to cause task failure, but treating any failure as success ignores the attacker's need to control the specific failure mode. Configured Failure Trapping raises the bar by demanding that attackers dictate how the robot fails (e.g., grasping with a specific positional offset), which is more challenging, stealthier, and harder to detect, yet no prior work has addressed this task.
AI.method: The approach includes: (1) a data engine for synthesizing high-quality target trajectories tailored to configured failure modes; (2) an automated evaluation suite measuring configured-failure fidelity; (3) two benchmarks (Trap-LIBERO and Trap-RoboTwin) spanning four representative failure modes; and (4) TrapVLA, which identifies sparse action deviation as a core challenge and proposes explicit learning of trigger-induced action residuals to steer the policy toward the configured failure behavior while preserving clean-data performance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic settings demonstrate that TrapVLA effectively injects configured failure modes into VLA models while largely preserving performance on clean data.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes Configured Failure Trapping as a new, harder backdoor attack paradigm for VLA models, provides datasets and evaluation tools to support it, and demonstrates a viable attack method (TrapVLA) that controls failure modes precisely without sacrificing normal-task performance.

title: EEG-to-Report: An Annotation and Feature-Text Framework for Training Language Models on Clinical EEG
summary: Clinical electroencephalography (EEG) reporting remains largely manual and time-consuming, and current EEG software ecosystems do not produce the structured EEG-text supervision needed for training modern language models. Most toolboxes focus on visualization or preprocessing, providing limited support for workflows that generate high-quality datasets for AI. We introduce EEG-to-Report, a browser-based annotation and feature-text framework that links routine EEG review with the construction of AI-ready datasets. The framework integrates multi-format EEG ingestion, channel standardization, and an interactive viewer with a multimodal annotation layer that combines typed text and transcribed voice notes. For each annotated segment, a feature extraction engine computes a standardized set of spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, and spike-related descriptors, stored alongside clinical descriptions in a portable JSON schema. This yields aligned feature-text pairs designed to supervise multimodal EEG-language models. The framework also includes an auto-report module that couples an ensemble of convolutional networks with a large language model to draft clinical narratives for neurologist review. Using pilot annotations, we describe how EEG-to-Report streamlines annotation workflows and produces editable draft reports, providing a reusable foundation for automated EEG reporting systems.

AI.tldr: EEG-to-Report is a browser-based annotation and feature-text framework that integrates EEG ingestion, channel standardization, interactive viewing, multimodal annotation (typed text and voice), and automated feature extraction to create aligned feature-text pairs for training EEG-language AI models. It also includes an auto-report module combining CNNs with an LLM to generate draft clinical narratives.
AI.motivation: Clinical EEG reporting remains manual and time-consuming, and current EEG software ecosystems do not produce the structured EEG-text supervision data needed to train modern language models. Existing toolboxes focus on visualization or preprocessing rather than supporting workflows that generate high-quality AI-ready datasets.
AI.method: The framework integrates multi-format EEG ingestion, channel standardization, and an interactive viewer with a multimodal annotation layer combining typed text and transcribed voice notes. A feature extraction engine computes standardized descriptors (spectral, temporal, entropy, Hjorth, connectivity, spike-related) for each annotated segment, stored with clinical descriptions in a portable JSON schema. An auto-report module couples an ensemble of convolutional networks with a large language model to draft clinical narratives.
AI.result: Pilot annotations demonstrate that EEG-to-Report streamlines annotation workflows and produces editable draft reports, providing a reusable foundation for automated EEG reporting systems.
AI.conclusion: EEG-to-Report provides a reusable, browser-based framework that bridges clinical EEG review and AI dataset construction, enabling supervised training of multimodal EEG-language models and supporting the path toward automated EEG reporting.

title: SOLO: Stable Omni-terrain Long-Horizon Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
summary: Humans traverse complex terrain over long distances without losing balance, whereas perceptive humanoid policies become fragile as perception and control errors accumulate. We present SOLO, a unified framework addressing two compounding causes of this long-horizon fragility: dense terrain reconstruction smooths action-critical details, and pointwise imitation lacks temporal credit assignment. Its Query Reconstructor (QR) uses Fourier-encoded cell queries to retrieve spatially specific evidence from depth-proprioception tokens, preserving sharp terrain boundaries. Trajectory-Aware MSE (TA-MSE) Distillation adds next-state teacher-student disagreement to the PPO reward, enabling Generalized Advantage Estimation to propagate future disagreement penalties to preceding actions. In simulation, QR reduces height-map L1 error by factors of 3.3-4.0, while TA-MSE surpasses PPO and MSE+PPO in curriculum progression. On stress-test terrains, SOLO achieves 97.5% mean traversal success and 96% stepping-stone success, versus 75.0-75.6% and 0-3% for dense-reconstructor variants. Deployed zero-shot with only a chest-mounted depth camera and proprioception, SOLO completes a continuous 1.5-km outdoor route and an indoor mixed-terrain course. Project page: https://sunpihai-up.github.io/solo/

AI.tldr: SOLO is a unified framework for long-horizon legged locomotion that addresses two compounding causes of fragility in perceptive humanoid policies: dense terrain reconstruction that smooths action-critical details, and pointwise imitation lacking temporal credit assignment. It introduces a Fourier-encoded Query Reconstructor (QR) that preserves sharp terrain boundaries via spatially specific evidence retrieval from depth-proprioception tokens, and Trajectory-Aware MSE (TA-MSE) Distillation that adds next-state teacher-student disagreement to the PPO reward for temporal credit assignment. SOLO achieves over 97% traversal success on stress-test terrains with 96% stepping-stone success (vs 0-3% for dense-reconstructor variants) and completes a 1.5-km outdoor route and indoor mixed-terrain course zero-shot with only a chest-mounted depth camera and proprioception.
AI.motivation: Perceptive humanoid policies become fragile over long horizons as perception and control errors accumulate. Two compounding causes are identified: dense terrain reconstruction aggressively smooths action-critical terrain details, and pointwise imitation learning lacks temporal credit assignment, meaning errors are not attributed across time steps.
AI.method: SOLO comprises two components: (1) Query Reconstructor (QR), which uses Fourier-encoded cell queries to retrieve spatially specific evidence from depth-proprioception tokens, preserving sharp terrain boundaries; and (2) Trajectory-Aware MSE (TA-MSE) Distillation, which incorporates next-state teacher-student disagreement into the PPO reward so Generalized Advantage Estimation can propagate future disagreement penalties backward to preceding actions.
AI.result: In simulation, QR reduces height-map L1 error by factors of 3.3-4.0 and TA-MSE surpasses PPO and MSE+PPO baselines in curriculum progression. On stress-test terrains, SOLO achieves 97.5% mean traversal success and 96% stepping-stone success, versus 75.0-75.6% traversal and 0-3% stepping-stone success for dense-reconstructor variants. Deployed zero-shot with a chest-mounted depth camera and proprioception, SOLO completes a continuous 1.5-km outdoor route and an indoor mixed-terrain course.
AI.conclusion: SOLO demonstrates that addressing both perception fidelity (sharp terrain reconstruction) and temporal credit assignment (trajectory-aware distillation) together yields dramatically more robust long-horizon humanoid locomotion. The zero-shot real-world deployment confirms that the framework generalizes beyond simulation, achieving practical navigation over complex outdoor and indoor terrain.

title: Selection Bias Correction in Retail Intelligence
comment: Accepted to the 15th International Conference on Data Science, Technology and Applications (DATA 2026)
summary: Retail intelligence often relies on monitoring popular, high-velocity products, potentially biasing economic indicators by ignoring the "long tail" of niche items. This simulation study investigates selection bias in inflation estimation and compares correction methods across diverse data-generating processes. Through 400 Monte Carlo replications spanning four scenarios--aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, and polynomial relationships--we test the robustness of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) with five specifications against stratification with varying strata counts. Our findings reveal fundamental limits of weighting methods in retail long-tail contexts: stratification achieves superior performance in three of four scenarios, maintaining sub-0.04pp median error even when boundaries deliberately misalign with population breaks (116x advantage over IPW). However, IPW with spline propensity models wins under smooth polynomial relationships (median error 0.007pp vs. 0.013pp), demonstrating context-dependency. Critically, even an oracle IPW specification with perfect structural knowledge achieves 6.06pp error compared to stratification's 0.008pp in step-function scenarios. This reflects violation of the Positivity Assumption--a fundamental causal inference requirement--rather than IPW methodological inferiority. When selection probabilities differ dramatically (90% vs. 1%), weighting methods operate outside their theoretical design envelope. These results demonstrate that stratification provides a safer engineering choice in retail long-tail distributions with severe positivity violations.

AI.tldr: A Monte Carlo simulation study (400 replications, 4 data-generating scenarios) comparing Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) with five specifications against stratification for correcting selection bias in inflation estimation from retail "long-tail" data. Stratification outperforms IPW in 3 of 4 scenarios (maintaining sub-0.04pp median error, with up to 116x advantage), while IPW with spline propensity models wins under smooth polynomial relationships. The study attributes IPW's failure in step-function scenarios to violation of the Positivity Assumption rather than methodological inferiority, concluding stratification is a safer engineering choice under severe positivity violations.
AI.motivation: Retail intelligence systems monitoring only popular, high-velocity products may introduce selection bias in economic indicators like inflation estimation by ignoring the "long tail" of niche items. The study aims to systematically evaluate and compare bias-correction methods under diverse data-generating processes to identify robust solutions for real-world retail applications.
AI.method: The study employs 400 Monte Carlo simulations across four scenarios: aligned step functions, smooth gradients, misaligned breaks, and polynomial relationships. Five IPW specifications (including an oracle specification with perfect structural knowledge) are tested against stratification with varying strata counts. Performance is measured via median error in inflation estimation.
AI.result: Stratification achieves superior performance in three of four scenarios, maintaining sub-0.04pp median error even with deliberately misaligned boundaries (116x advantage over IPW). IPW with spline propensity models wins under polynomial relationships (0.007pp vs 0.013pp median error). Critically, even the oracle IPW achieves only 6.06pp error vs stratification's 0.008pp in step-function scenarios, reflecting Positivity Assumption violation when selection probabilities differ dramatically (90% vs 1%).
AI.conclusion: Stratification is the safer engineering choice for retail long-tail distributions characterized by severe positivity violations and extreme selection probability imbalances. IPW's poor performance in step-function scenarios stems from a fundamental violation of causal inference assumptions rather than implementation shortcomings, making its applicability context-dependent in retail settings.

title: Relaxation-Aware Multimodal Sensing of Soft Gripper Driven by Structure-Perception-Learning
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures. Published in Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS 2026)
summary: Achieving stable, sustained grasping with soft robotic hands remains a fundamental challenge. Compliance enables safe and adaptive contact, yet the intrinsic viscoelasticity of soft polymers leads to stress relaxation and a continuous decay of grasping force during holding. Inspired by human grasping, which combines phase-dependent stiffness regulation with continuous sensing and feedback, this paper presents an integrated structure--perception--learning framework. We develop a variable-stiffness soft gripper that uses onboard vision and infrared thermography to track deformation and the temperature field in real time, preserving continuous tracking of the interaction state. To mitigate relaxation-induced force decay, we propose a temperature-coupled viscoelastic force representation, together with a physics-informed learning model, to reconstruct the force trend and provide explicit compensation during holding. Experiments show that, in a 280s force-controlled grasp-and-hold task, the proposed method maintains the desired force with a mean absolute error of 0.066N, outperforming fixed-aperture and instantaneous-only baselines by 80% and 95%, respectively. Overall, the results support a mechanism--AI co-design view: mechanisms shape feasible interactions, while learning compensates remaining uncertainty in viscoelastic dynamics, together enabling stable, sustained grasping.
