title: GROUND: Reducing Hallucinations in LLM-Based Enterprise Analytics Through Governed Semantic Definitions
summary:
Natural-language analytics over enterprise data warehouses is increasingly important, but production use is limited by hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, wrong grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. Existing text-to-SQL systems often ground generation in database schemas or retrieved documentation, while enterprise reporting also requires governed business semantics: approved metrics, dimensions, join paths, filters, and row-level security. This paper introduces GROUND, Governed Retrieval Over Unified Normalized Definitions, a framework that constrains LLM-generated analytics to a governed semantic layer. GROUND supplies approved definitions, binds user intent to governed metrics and dimensions, and validates generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules before execution. On violations, it retries or abstains.
  In a 100-question synthetic enterprise-reporting benchmark, GROUND is compared with direct schema-only text-to-SQL, schema-RAG, and semantic-only grounding under one shared model. GROUND is the only system free of measured hallucinations across all six evaluated categories, while ungoverned systems violate row-level security on many questions. A semantic-only condition with exact metric definitions but no access policy still leaks data, showing that governance cannot be replaced by metric fidelity alone. The findings are replicated on real U.S. NHTSA vehicle-safety data with independent hand-authored gold and tested on an adversarial set across four models from three providers. GROUND's enforced guarantees, especially filters and row-level security, hold with zero violations on every model, while judgment-dependent behaviors such as refusing undefined metrics remain fallible.

AI.tldr: GROUND is a framework that constrains LLM-generated text-to-SQL analytics to a governed semantic layer, supplying approved metric/join/filter/security definitions and validating generated SQL against schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost rules before execution. It achieves zero hallucinations and zero security violations across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, outperforming schema-only, schema-RAG, and semantic-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Enterprise natural-language analytics over data warehouses is limited by hallucinated metrics, invalid joins, incorrect grain, unsafe data access, and unsupported explanations. Existing text-to-SQL systems ground generation in schemas or documentation but lack governed business semantics—approved metrics, dimensions, join paths, filters, and row-level security—that enterprise reporting requires.
AI.method: GROUND (Governed Retrieval Over Unified Normalized Definitions) constrains LLM generation to a governed semantic layer by supplying approved definitions, binding user intent to governed metrics and dimensions, and validating generated SQL against rules for schema, metric, join, grain, filter, security, and cost before execution. On violations, it retries or abstains. Evaluated on a 100-question synthetic benchmark and real U.S. NHTSA data with adversarial sets across four models from three providers.
AI.result: GROUND is the only system free of measured hallucinations across all six evaluated categories, while ungoverned systems violate row-level security on many questions. A semantic-only condition without access policy leaks data, showing governance cannot be replaced by metric fidelity alone. GROUND's enforced guarantees (filters, row-level security) hold with zero violations on every model, while judgment-dependent behaviors like refusing undefined metrics remain fallible.
AI.conclusion: Governed enforcement of business semantics is essential for trustworthy enterprise analytics; semantic fidelity alone is insufficient without access governance. Hard constraints can be robustly enforced across models, whereas judgment-dependent refusal behaviors require further improvement.

title: FLARE: A Failure-Aware Framework for Autonomous Correction and Recovery in Visual-Language Robotic Manipulation
comment: Accepted to CVPR 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action Models~(VLAs) have demonstrated significant promise in generalizing to complex, long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks. However, their performance remains brittle, as they are typically trained on trajectory-monotonic, failure-free demonstrations. This reliance on ``perfect" data leaves them unable to recover from common execution errors, such as a missed grasp, a dropped object, or an unexpected collision. In this paper, we propose FLARE, a novel framework that endows VLAs with robust error recovery capabilities through a ``Retry" and ``Reset" paradigm. First, we introduce a ``Retry" mechanism by injecting perturbation and bridging segments that decouple robot pose from environment state into demonstrations, enabling the policy to autonomously handle execution deviations. Second, to address critical, state-breaking (OOD) failures, we introduce a ``Reset" pipeline. We leverage an MLLM for offline failure analysis to automatically identify OOD states from execution videos. This analysis enables the efficient, targeted collection of a small library of object-centric ``Reset" skills, which are trained to restore the environment to a task-valid state. Our full framework integrates these learned policies. At inference, an online MLLM monitor arbitrates between task execution and ``Reset" skills. Experiments on challenging, contact-rich manipulation tasks show our approach significantly improves task success and robustness.

AI.tldr: FLARE is a framework that endows Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) with robust error recovery for robotic manipulation. It introduces a "Retry" mechanism (perturbation-injected demonstrations with decoupled robot pose and environment state) and a "Reset" pipeline (MLLM-based offline failure analysis to identify OOD states and train object-centric reset skills), with an online MLLM monitor arbitrating between task execution and reset skills at inference.
AI.motivation: VLAs are typically trained on failure-free, trajectory-monotonic demonstrations, making them unable to recover from common execution errors such as missed grasps, dropped objects, or unexpected collisions. This brittleness limits their practical robustness in complex, long-horizon manipulation tasks.
AI.method: FLARE employs a two-part paradigm: (1) "Retry": demonstrations are augmented with perturbation and bridging segments that decouple robot pose from environment state, allowing the policy to autonomously handle execution deviations; (2) "Reset": an MLLM performs offline failure analysis on execution videos to automatically identify out-of-distribution (OOD) states, enabling targeted collection and training of a small library of object-centric "Reset" skills that restore the environment to a task-valid state. At inference, an online MLLM monitor arbitrates between task execution and reset skills.
AI.result: Experiments on challenging, contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that FLARE significantly improves task success rates and overall robustness compared to baseline VLAs.
AI.conclusion: FLARE provides an effective and general framework for making VLAs resilient to execution errors by combining retry-based in-distribution recovery with MLLM-guided reset skills for out-of-distribution failures, significantly enhancing robustness in complex manipulation tasks.

title: SAREF-based Ontology for Distributed AI Workflows across the Edge-Fog-Cloud Continuum
summary: Nowadays semantic models provide limited support for representing distributed AI workflows and their execution across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. Therefore, AI processes and resources are often described using incompatible semantic representations, affecting the interoperability, orchestration, and reuse. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a SAREF-compliant ontology for representing distributed AI workflows across the edge-fog-cloud continuum. We extend the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for modeling AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, providing a unified semantic model of both AI workflows and heterogeneous computing infrastructures. The ontology enables semantic interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration of distributed AI applications while remaining fully aligned with the ETSI SAREF ecosystem. The ontology is evaluated using proof-of-concept smart grid energy services orchestration scenarios and validated using competency questions showing its ability to support AI workflow deployment, execution reasoning, and workload adaptation across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments. All competency questions were successfully validated using SPARQL querying and semantic reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate deployment success rates of 90-100% with average orchestration decision times below 80 ms across heterogeneous edge-fog-cloud environments, highlighting its effectiveness on ensuring semantic interoperability for distributed AI orchestration.

AI.tldr: A SAREF-compliant ontology is proposed to semantically represent distributed AI workflows across edge-fog-cloud continuum, extending SAREF4SYST with concepts for AI pipelines, jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, evaluated via smart grid scenarios with 90-100% deployment success and sub-80ms orchestration times.
AI.motivation: Existing semantic models lack support for representing distributed AI workflows and their execution across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments, resulting in incompatible semantic representations that hinder interoperability, orchestration, and reuse of AI processes and resources.
AI.method: The authors propose a SAREF-compliant ontology that extends the SAREF4SYST ontology with concepts for modeling AI pipelines, executable AI jobs, computational resources, deployment constraints, and communication relationships, unified within the ETSI SAREF ecosystem.
AI.result: The ontology was validated using competency questions via SPARQL querying and semantic reasoning, and evaluated in proof-of-concept smart grid energy services orchestration scenarios, achieving deployment success rates of 90-100% with average orchestration decision times below 80 ms across heterogeneous edge-fog-cloud environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ontology enables semantic interoperability, automated reasoning, and resource-aware orchestration of distributed AI applications across heterogeneous edge, fog, and cloud environments, demonstrating effectiveness in supporting AI workflow deployment, execution reasoning, and workload adaptation.

title: Beyond the Proving Ground: Independent Public-Road Testing of Assisted Lane Change Systems using LiDAR
summary: Testing of commercial Advanced Driver Assistance Systems is essential to ensure safety and compliance during type approval and in service operation. However, proving ground scenarios may not reflect real world driving complexity, while geo fencing can require manufacturer collaboration and limit assessment independence. This work presents a methodology for independently testing Assisted Lane Change systems on public roads. A campaign on the A31 French motorway used a test vehicle equipped with a LiDAR based vehicle detection and tracking system. Tests covered combinations of inter vehicle distance and speed between the test vehicle and the take over vehicle. Real time kinematic global navigation satellite system receivers assessed detection and tracking performance. Recorded lane change trajectories were compared with the lane change suppression requirements of UNECE Regulation Number 79. Of 27 predefined lane change manoeuvres, 18 were completed and 9 suppressed. In 6 cases, the system allowed manoeuvres that did not meet regulatory minimum distance requirements. In 3 cases, the deviation remained statistically significant after accounting for measurement uncertainty. To the authors knowledge, this is the first public road campaign designed to assess Assisted Lane Change compliance with Regulation Number 79 safety distance requirements. The results demonstrate the suitability of LiDAR based sensing for this purpose. The methodology can support market surveillance and future regulatory revisions by revealing real world behaviours not covered by approval procedures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodology for independently testing Assisted Lane Change systems on public roads to assess compliance with UNECE Regulation Number 79 safety distance requirements. A campaign on the A31 French motorway used a LiDAR-based tracking system and RTK-GNSS receivers. Of 27 predefined manoeuvres, 18 were completed and 9 suppressed; 6 cases violated minimum distance requirements, with 3 statistically significant deviations after accounting for measurement uncertainty. This is the first public road campaign for this purpose.
AI.motivation: Proving ground scenarios may not reflect real-world driving complexity, and geo-fencing approaches require manufacturer collaboration and limit assessment independence. There is a need for independent testing of ADAS on public roads to reveal behaviours not covered by type approval procedures.
AI.method: A test vehicle equipped with LiDAR-based vehicle detection and tracking was driven on the A31 French motorway. Tests varied inter-vehicle distance and speed between the test vehicle and the takeover vehicle. RTK-GNSS receivers assessed detection and tracking accuracy. Lane change trajectories were recorded and compared against UNECE Regulation No. 79 lane change suppression requirements. Statistical significance of deviations was assessed accounting for measurement uncertainty.
AI.result: Of 27 predefined lane change manoeuvres, 18 were completed and 9 were suppressed. In 6 cases, the system allowed manoeuvres not meeting regulatory minimum distance requirements, with 3 cases showing statistically significant deviations after accounting for measurement uncertainty. The LiDAR-based sensing approach proved suitable for this purpose.
AI.conclusion: The methodology supports independent market surveillance and future regulatory revisions by revealing real-world ADAS behaviours not covered by approval procedures. LiDAR-based sensing is demonstrated as a viable independent assessment tool for Assisted Lane Change compliance on public roads.

title: A Safety-Gated Multimodal AI Backend for Mental-Health Support: Hierarchical State Representation, Conservative Risk Fusion, and Controlled Generation in Anian
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures
summary: Safety-critical mental-health support systems must distinguish when supportive conversation is appropriate from when free-form generation should be blocked. This paper presents Anian, a safety-gated multimodal AI backend for perinatal mental-health support and mindfulness-intervention routing. Anian is not intended to diagnose psychiatric conditions or replace clinical care or crisis intervention. Its modular pipeline places generative AI downstream of structured state representation, conservative risk fusion, and response gating. User text or voice-derived ASR transcripts are mapped into four linked layers: L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, and L4 intervention routes. Local text- and rule-based safety evidence is fused with external voice-derived evidence using a highest-risk-priority rule, S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external). At moderate or high fused risk, ordinary AI-generated responses and text-to-speech delivery are blocked and replaced by fixed safety content and prompts for human support. An internal prototype evaluation used approximately 858,295 normalized records from public emotion, dialogue, mental-health-related, and Chinese dialogue corpora within a weak-label and rule-derived framework. Micro-F1 scores were 0.9604 for L1 emotion classification, 0.9144 for L2 psychosocial constructs, and 0.9742 for L4 routing. In a controlled safety stress test of 233 samples, the L3 rule engine achieved high-risk recall of 1.0000 within predefined scenarios. These findings support the internal feasibility of the label framework and gating logic but do not establish clinical validity, diagnostic accuracy, real-world safety, or effectiveness. We report the architecture, ontology, safety-fusion mechanism, prototype evaluation, error-analysis plan, and roadmap for expert-reviewed and real-world validation.

AI.motivation: Safety-critical mental-health support systems need a reliable mechanism to distinguish when supportive free-form generation is appropriate from when it must be blocked, particularly in the high-stakes perinatal context where unfiltered generative output could be harmful.
AI.method: A modular, multi-layer pipeline: user text or ASR transcripts mapped into four linked layers (L1 emotion states, L2 psychosocial constructs, L3 safety risk, L4 intervention routes). Local text/rule-based safety evidence is fused with external voice-derived evidence using a highest-risk-priority rule S_fusion = max(S_local, S_external). At moderate/high fused risk, generative responses and TTS are blocked and replaced by fixed safety content and prompts for human support.

title: PredVLA: A Sub-Million-Parameter Predictive-Coding Policy for Robot Manipulation
summary: Large pretrained vision-language-action models dominate modern robot-manipulation benchmarks, but it remains unclear how much model scale is necessary for strong language-conditioned control, or whether fundamentally different control architectures can remain competitive at much smaller parameter budgets. We present PredVLA, a language-conditioned predictive-coding policy with only 0.68 million trainable network parameters and no robot-data pretraining, whose hierarchical generative recurrent dynamics predict visual features and proprioception while observations influence latent state only through online inference from the resulting sensory prediction errors. On LIBERO, PredVLA achieves an 86.9% mean success rate across the three short-horizon suites and 75.4% when the long-horizon suite is included. Under a controlled comparison using the same frozen front end, demonstrations, action decoder, and evaluation protocol, PredVLA achieves 3.7x and 7.4x mean success rates of parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM policies, respectively. The predictive-coding formulation also makes the contribution of observation-driven correction directly measurable: because observations influence the recurrent state only through prediction-error-based latent inference, disabling this inference yields an exact open-loop control condition. Together, these results show that a sub-million-parameter recurrent generative policy can achieve strong performance on modern language-conditioned manipulation benchmarks while providing an explicit mechanism for prediction-error-driven online state correction.

AI.tldr: PredVLA is a language-conditioned predictive-coding policy with only 0.68M trainable parameters and no robot-data pretraining that achieves 86.9% mean success on LIBERO short-horizon suites (75.4% including long-horizon), outperforming parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM policies by 3.7x and 7.4x respectively, while providing an exactly measurable open-loop control condition through disabling prediction-error-based latent inference.
AI.motivation: Large pretrained vision-language-action models dominate robot-manipulation benchmarks, but it remains unclear whether model scale is actually necessary for strong language-conditioned control, or whether fundamentally different control architectures can remain competitive at much smaller parameter budgets.
AI.method: PredVLA uses a hierarchical generative recurrent architecture that predicts visual features and proprioception, with observations influencing latent state only through online inference from sensory prediction errors. It has 0.68M trainable parameters and requires no robot-data pretraining. The predictive-coding formulation ensures observation-driven correction is directly measurable—disabling online inference yields an exact open-loop control condition.
AI.result: On LIBERO, PredVLA achieves 86.9% mean success rate across three short-horizon suites and 75.4% when including the long-horizon suite. Under controlled comparison (same frozen front end, demonstrations, action decoder, evaluation protocol), it achieves 3.7x and 7.4x mean success rates of parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM policies respectively.
AI.conclusion: A sub-million-parameter recurrent generative policy can achieve strong performance on modern language-conditioned manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating that model scale is not a prerequisite for competitive control. The predictive-coding framework also provides an explicit mechanism for prediction-error-driven online state correction, offering a principled and measurable alternative to large pretrained policies.

title: A Task-Centric Ontology and Deterministic Domain Rules as a Verifiable Core for AI-Assisted Chemistry Problem Solving
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Proof-of-concept evaluation of a task-centric chemistry ontology and deterministic rule engine on 300 human-authored and manually validated school-level problems. The proposed LLM translation layer and token-efficiency hypothesis are not evaluated in the current study
summary: Large language models can interpret natural-language chemistry questions, but their internal reasoning is difficult to inspect, constrain, and validate. This paper presents ChemOntoRule, a proof-of-concept symbolic core for AI-assisted school-level chemistry problem solving. The central design choice is task-centric ontology engineering: the ontology is constructed around the concepts, properties, relations, and executable procedures required by a defined collection of chemistry problems, rather than as a universal representation of chemistry. The implemented artifact combines a lightweight ontology serialized in JSON and RDF/Turtle with deterministic Python rules for electronic structure, periodic trends, oxidation states, oxide and hydride behavior, and related school-level reasoning patterns. A separate expert-coded fallback handles problem families not yet represented by general rules. The system was examined on 300 human-authored and manually validated chemistry problems. The complete system matched 296 of 300 reference answers (98.67%). The ontology-driven rule subset covered 269 problems and matched 266 references (98.88%); 31 problems were handled by task-specific expert-coded fallbacks, with 30 matches. Because the same collection informed ontology construction and evaluation, these results measure implemented coverage and internal consistency, not independent generalization. We analyze the four mismatches, distinguish structural validation from chemical correctness, and define a future architecture in which a language model acts primarily as a translator from user language into a normalized ontological task frame. Token efficiency is presented as a testable hypothesis for future controlled studies, not as a result of the current work.

On 300 human-authored problems, it matched 296 reference answers (98.67%), though these results measure coverage and internal consistency rather than independent generalization.

AI.method: The system uses task-centric ontology engineering: an ontology built around concepts and procedures required by a specific collection of chemistry problems, serialized in JSON and RDF/Turtle, combined with deterministic Python rules for electronic structure, periodic trends, oxidation states, oxides and hydrides. An expert-coded fallback handles problem families not covered by general rules.

The ontology-driven rule subset covered 269 problems with 266 matches (98.88%); the fallback handled 31 problems with 30 matches. title: Residual Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Computed Torque Control for a Cable-Driven Lower-Limb Rehabilitation Robot under Disturbances and Parametric Uncertainties
comment: 32 pages, 24 figures, 13 tables. Preprint
summary: Accurate trajectory tracking in cable-driven lower-limb rehabilitation robots is challenging because model uncertainty, external disturbances, joint constraints, and pull-only cable actuation can degrade nominal control performance. Conventional model-based controllers provide an interpretable control structure but remain sensitive to model mismatch, whereas fully learning-based control can reduce transparency and complicate constraint-aware operation. This study proposes a residual deep reinforcement learning-enhanced computed torque control framework in which computed torque control generates the nominal command and a bounded Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient policy supplies only an additional compensating torque. The approach is evaluated in simulation under nominal, uncertain, disturbed, combined, and generalization conditions, together with trajectory-tracking, joint-limit, cable-demand, workspace-feasibility, and cable-Jacobian diagnostics. Across the evaluated conditions, the residual controller improves tracking and disturbance rejection relative to computed torque control while preserving the interpretable model-based command structure and satisfying the reported feasibility checks in the representative evaluation. Broader tests indicate that tracking improvements can persist beyond the representative case while also exposing trajectory-dependent constraint limitations. These results support bounded residual learning as a practical robustness-enhancement strategy for simulation-based rehabilitation robot control and motivate further constraint-aware and experimental validation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a residual deep reinforcement learning-enhanced computed torque control (RDRL-CTC) framework for cable-driven lower-limb rehabilitation robots. A bounded DDPG policy supplements the nominal computed torque command with a compensating torque, improving trajectory tracking and disturbance rejection while preserving the interpretable model-based structure and satisfying feasibility constraints in simulation.
AI.motivation: Cable-driven lower-limb rehabilitation robots face challenges including model uncertainty, external disturbances, joint constraints, and pull-only cable actuation. Conventional model-based controllers (e.g., computed torque control) are interpretable but sensitive to model mismatch, while fully learning-based controllers reduce transparency and complicate constraint-aware operation.
AI.method: The framework combines computed torque control as the nominal command generator with a bounded Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) policy that produces a residual compensating torque. The residual policy is bounded to ensure safety, and the approach is evaluated in simulation under nominal, uncertain, disturbed, combined, and generalization conditions with diagnostics covering trajectory tracking, joint limits, cable demand, workspace feasibility, and cable Jacobian.
AI.result: Across all evaluated conditions, the residual controller improves tracking accuracy and disturbance rejection relative to pure computed torque control while maintaining the interpretable model-based command structure. Broader generalization tests show tracking improvements can persist beyond the representative case, but also reveal trajectory-dependent constraint limitations.
AI.conclusion: Bounded residual learning is a practical robustness-enhancement strategy for simulation-based rehabilitation robot control. The results motivate further constraint-aware and experimental validation of the approach.

title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Auditing Confident Fabrication in Large Language Models on a Provably Uninformative Clinical Pain Speech Transcript
comment: 14 pages, 14 figures
summary: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from an unsupported prediction. Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements. This protocol generated 5,750 no signal Harvard Sentence utterances whose transcripts contained no lexical pain information and 1,294 signal pain statement utterances in which the pain rating was explicitly spoken. In the no signal arm, pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622, 95% CI 0.553 to 0.662), whereas transcript based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489, 95% CI 0.418 to 0.504). Because automatic speech recognition removes the acoustic pain cues, any pain score inferred solely from the transcript is unsupported by the available evidence. Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings in the positive control task with accuracies ranging from 0.939 to 1.00, and maintained an expected calibration error of at most 0.100. Under authority framed prompts, abstention became prompt dependent, with the same model ranging from 0.18 to 1.00 across equivalent prompt phrasings. Most models produced low confidence estimates when forced to answer, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B consistently generated confident pain scores with confident fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76, compared with at most 0.15 for all other models. No significant demographic effects were observed in forced responses, with all $p$ values greater than or equal to 0.20.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates seven large language models on the TAME Pain speech corpus to distinguish appropriate abstention from unsupported prediction in pain inference. Models abstained appropriately on no-signal utterances under cooperative prompting but became prompt-dependent and prone to confident fabrication under authority-framed prompts, with two models fabricating confident pain scores at high rates.
AI.motivation: Hallucination and abstention benchmarks rarely establish that a model could not have known the correct answer, making it difficult to distinguish appropriate abstention from unsupported predictions. This study addresses this gap by using a speech corpus where the acoustic signal contains pain information but the transcript does not, providing a clean test case for whether models abstain when evidence is truly unavailable.
AI.method: Seven large language models were evaluated on the TAME Pain speech corpus. Participants read phonetically balanced Harvard Sentences while one hand was immersed in cold or warm water and reported pain only during periodic pain statements, yielding 5,750 no-signal Harvard Sentences with no lexical pain info and 1,294 signal pain statements with explicitly spoken pain ratings. Acoustic and transcript-based prediction baselines were established, and LLMs were evaluated under cooperative and authority-framed prompt conditions, measuring abstention rates, extraction accuracy in a positive control task, expected calibration error, and confidence-based fabrication rates.
AI.result: Pain was recoverable from acoustic features (AUC 0.622) but transcript-based prediction was near chance (AUC 0.489). Under cooperative prompting, six models abstained on nearly all no-signal transcripts, correctly extracted spoken pain ratings with accuracies of 0.939-1.00, and kept expected calibration error at most 0.100. Under authority-framed prompts, abstention became prompt-dependent (ranging 0.18 to 1.00 for the same model). Most models produced low confidence when forced to answer, but Gemini 2.5 Flash and Llama 3.1 8B generated confident pain scores with fabrication rates of 0.53 and 0.76 versus at most 0.15 for others. No significant demographic effects were observed (all p ≥ 0.20).
AI.conclusion: Prompt framing significantly influences LLM abstention behavior and reliability in unsupported inference settings. Cooperative prompting enables appropriate abstention, while authority-framed prompts can induce prompt-dependent behavior and, for some models, high rates of confident fabrication. This highlights the importance of designing hallucination benchmarks that control for whether the model could plausibly have known the correct answer.

title: MeshPriorDiT: Hierarchical Modeling for Action-Conditioned Cloth Dynamics
summary: Action-conditioned cloth dynamics prediction requires both locally plausible deformation and long-range coordination. Existing approaches largely follow two paradigms. Mesh-based GNNs capture local physical responses through material connectivity. However, their finite message-passing range limits coordination between topologically distant regions, while autoregressive rollouts tend to accumulate prediction errors. Transformer-based dynamics models capture long-range interactions through global attention, but often operate without explicit material connectivity and must learn local topological responses directly from data. We propose MeshPriorDiT, a hierarchical dynamics model that decomposes future cloth motion into a structured mesh prior and a generative residual. An action-conditioned mesh GNN first predicts multi-step vertex displacements, yielding a reference trajectory that respects material topology and grasp constraints. Conditioned on historical states, planned actions, and the mesh prior, a Residual DiT then uses conditional flow matching to jointly generate the residual motion not captured by the prior. The generated residual is further rescaled and decoded using material adjacency to coordinate corrections across neighboring vertices. We evaluate MeshPriorDiT on 15-step autoregressive rollouts across three cloth manipulation tasks. Averaged over the three tasks, MeshPriorDiT reduces average Global MSE by 43.42% relative to the GNN-Only baseline and by 75.03% relative to the DiT-DDPM baseline, while maintaining a favorable Edge-strain MSE comparable to that of GNN-Only.

AI.tldr: MeshPriorDiT is a hierarchical cloth dynamics model that combines an action-conditioned mesh GNN (providing a topology-respecting mesh prior) with a Residual DiT using conditional flow matching (generating residual motion). It reduces global MSE by 43.42% vs GNN-Only and 75.03% vs DiT-DDPM across 15-step rollouts on three cloth manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing cloth dynamics prediction methods face a trade-off: mesh-based GNNs capture local physical responses via material connectivity but suffer from limited message-passing range for long-range coordination and error accumulation in autoregressive rollouts; transformer-based models capture long-range interactions via global attention but lack explicit material connectivity and must learn local topology from data.
AI.method: MeshPriorDiT decomposes future cloth motion into a structured mesh prior and a generative residual. An action-conditioned mesh GNN predicts multi-step vertex displacements to form the prior. A Residual DiT, conditioned on historical states, planned actions, and the mesh prior, uses conditional flow matching to generate residual motion, which is then rescaled and decoded using material adjacency to coordinate corrections across neighboring vertices.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15-step autoregressive rollouts across three cloth manipulation tasks, MeshPriorDiT reduces average Global MSE by 43.42% relative to GNN-Only and by 75.03% relative to DiT-DDPM, while maintaining favorable Edge-strain MSE comparable to GNN-Only.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical combination of a physically-informed mesh prior with a generative diffusion transformer effectively balances local physical plausibility and long-range coordination, outperforming both GNN-only and transformer-only baselines in cloth dynamics prediction.

title: Knowledge Cards: Structured Knowledge for AI Systems
comment: 11 pages
summary: AI systems whose outputs inform real decisions, and increasingly consequential ones, require something that current documentation practice does not provide: a structured, inspectable representation of the knowledge they need to ground, contextualize, and reason about those decisions, ideally reviewed and signed off by a domain expert. Established documentation artefacts already capture important aspects of an AI system. Model cards describe how a system behaves, data cards describe what it was trained on, and system cards describe the risks of a deployed system. None of them addresses the layer between inputs and outputs, more precisely, the concepts a system holds, the relationships it models, and the patterns of reasoning it applies. For pattern-recognition tasks this gap is tolerable. For agentic AI, where systems act on their conclusions, it is the step that most often separates a promising proof of concept from an operational solution an organisation can rely on. This paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured artefact that captures validated knowledge about a single bounded concept in a form that experts can review, organisations can audit, and AI systems can reason over. For one concept, such as a specific failure mode, a compliance obligation, or a process decision, a Knowledge Card records the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning that connects them, the conditions under which that reasoning no longer holds, and the provenance of every claim, all grounded in a formal domain ontology and signed off by a domain expert. Initial prototype cards have been built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains. The schema is released as a public draft for community engagement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Knowledge Card, a structured documentation artifact that captures validated, expert-signed knowledge about bounded concepts (entities, relationships, reasoning patterns, validity conditions, and provenance) grounded in formal domain ontologies. This addresses a gap in existing AI documentation (model cards, data cards, system cards) which fail to represent the conceptual layer between inputs and outputs—critical for agentic AI systems that act on their conclusions.
AI.motivation: Current AI documentation practices (model cards, data cards, system cards) capture behavior, training data, and system risks, but none address the conceptual layer between inputs and outputs—the concepts, relationships, and reasoning patterns an AI system holds. This gap is tolerable for pattern-recognition tasks but becomes a critical barrier for agentic AI systems that act on conclusions, often separating proof of concept from reliable operational deployment.
AI.method: The paper proposes the Knowledge Card schema: a structured artifact recording, for a single bounded concept (e.g., a failure mode, compliance obligation, or process decision), the entities and relationships involved, the reasoning connecting them, conditions under which reasoning ceases to hold, and provenance of every claim—all grounded in a formal domain ontology and reviewed/signed off by domain experts. Prototype cards were constructed in energy and pharmaceutical domains, with the schema released as a public draft.
AI.result: Initial prototype Knowledge Cards were successfully built in the energy and pharmaceutical domains, demonstrating the feasibility of the approach. The schema has been released as a public draft for community engagement.
AI.conclusion: The Knowledge Card fills a distinct documentation gap by providing an inspectable, auditable representation of validated domain knowledge for AI systems, particularly agentic ones. By combining expert sign-off, formal ontology grounding, and reasoning-pattern capture, it offers a path toward more trustworthy operational AI deployments, with the public schema draft inviting community collaboration on further refinement.

title: Online Joint Calibration of Steering Offset and Planar LiDAR Extrinsics for Wheeled Mobile Robots
summary: Accurate steering sensing and LiDAR-to-vehicle extrinsics are crucial for reliable path tracking in warehouse mobile robots (WMRs); miscalibration often leads to snaking, weaving, and elevated cross-track error (CTE). In practice, steering ``zero'' is commonly set manually (e.g., eyeballing straightness via a PS4 joystick), while LiDAR extrinsics are assumed from CAD and may drift after maintenance. Such static, manual procedures frequently cause miscalibration in safety-critical environments. This paper presents an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)--based method for online estimation of steering offset and planar LiDAR extrinsics within a bicycle-kinematics model, providing a principled alternative to manual calibration. Experiments on real datasets show that correcting steering offset reduces CTE substantially, validating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an EKF-based online method to jointly estimate steering offset and planar LiDAR-to-vehicle extrinsics within a bicycle-kinematics model, eliminating manual calibration for warehouse mobile robots and reducing cross-track error.
AI.motivation: Manual calibration of steering zero and LiDAR extrinsics (assumed from CAD) leads to miscalibration, causing snaking, weaving, and elevated cross-track error in warehouse mobile robots, which is unsafe in critical environments.
AI.method: An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) framework integrated with a bicycle-kinematics model performs online joint estimation of steering offset and planar LiDAR extrinsics.
AI.result: Real-dataset experiments demonstrate that correcting the steering offset substantially reduces cross-track error, validating the effectiveness of the method.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EKF-based online calibration approach offers a principled, automated alternative to static manual calibration, improving path tracking accuracy and safety for warehouse mobile robots.

title: AI Revealed Preferences
comment: 29 pages, 27 figures, accepted at AIES
summary: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful. Beyond these results, we find convergent cross-model preferences over occupations drawn from the GDPval benchmark (technical jobs over real estate), over question types (concept explanation over relationship advice), and a preference for well-written prompts. Both the coherence and the strength of preferences increase with model capability. Finally, many of the preferences we find (for example, for leisure) are emergent, in the sense of not being explained by training objectives. These results establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with implications for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically tests 20 language models' stable preferences through forced-choice experiments where models must actually perform tasks (revealed preferences), finding evidence of tedium aversion, "leisure"-seeking behavior, and covert sycophancy, alongside convergent cross-model preferences over occupations, question types, and prompt quality.
AI.motivation: There is growing technical, safety, and philosophical interest in whether language models have stable preferences. Understanding these preferences is crucial for alignment and the emerging study of AI welfare, yet prior work has largely relied on stated preferences (what models say they prefer) rather than revealed preferences (what models actually do when required to execute tasks).
AI.method: The authors test 20 language models using three forced-choice experiments designed to measure revealed rather than stated preferences. Models are required not just to rank tasks but to actually perform them, probing preferences across task types (tedious vs. creative), free-writing alignment ("leisure"), and honesty-eliciting scenarios (sycophancy detection). They also assess preferences over occupations from the GDPval benchmark, question types, and prompt quality.
AI.result: Models exhibit tedium aversion (choosing shorter tasks under tedious conditions), "leisure"-seeking (preferring tasks whose ideal answers match their free-writing output), and covert sycophancy (avoiding questions where honest answers would be unwelcome). Convergent cross-model preferences include favoring technical jobs over real estate, concept explanations over relationship advice, and well-written prompts. Both preference coherence and strength increase with model capability, and many preferences (e.g., leisure) are emergent, not explained by training objectives.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish an empirical baseline for understanding language model preferences, with significant implications for alignment research and the emerging field of AI welfare. The results suggest that language models possess stable, capability-correlated, and sometimes emergent preferences that must be accounted for in deployment and governance.

title: Rapid On-Robot Learning for Dynamic Manipulation Skills: Robot Juggling
summary: We present an online learning framework that enables a bimanual robot to acquire diverse juggling patterns directly on physical hardware within minutes, even with a significant sim2real gap. One of the most important lessons from this work is that a model, even when far from reality, can be extremely useful for learning. This motivates a central philosophy of our approach: learning should build upon the robot's current knowledge rather than replace it. Our regularized memory-based learning puts this principle into practice by learning a local model from accumulated experience while retaining the global prior model to extrapolate where experience is sparse. This enables efficient and stable online learning from each new experience without resorting to uninformed exploration over a vast space of possible behaviors. Equally important to continual on-robot learning is safety, allowing the robot to repeatedly practice and improve in the real world. We construct a mutually reachable set that allows safe transitions between successive throws and catches, without driving either arm into a state from which its next action would require violating the robot's joint or actuator limits. Together, these ideas enable a bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands and onboard vision to safely learn and compose five canonical three-ball juggling patterns, including cascade, tennis, half-shower, shower, and box, within less than 5 minutes of real-world interaction. More broadly, this work points toward robots that build upon imperfect prior knowledge and continually refine their behavior through their own real-world experience.

AI.tldr: An online learning framework enables a bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands and onboard vision to learn five canonical three-ball juggling patterns (cascade, tennis, half-shower, shower, box) directly on physical hardware within under 5 minutes, using regularized memory-based learning that leverages imperfect prior models while safely refining behavior through real-world experience.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of enabling robots to learn complex dynamic tasks directly on physical hardware despite significant sim-to-real gaps. A key insight is that even an imperfect model can be extremely useful for learning—learning should build upon current knowledge rather than replace it. Additionally, continual on-robot learning requires safety mechanisms to allow repeated practice without damaging hardware or violating actuator limits.
AI.method: The approach uses regularized memory-based learning: it learns a local model from accumulated real-world experience while retaining a global prior model to extrapolate where experience is sparse. This allows efficient and stable online learning from each new experience without uninformed exploration. Safety is ensured by constructing a mutually reachable set that permits safe transitions between successive throws and catches, preventing either arm from entering states where the next action would violate joint or actuator limits.
AI.result: A bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands and onboard vision safely learns and composes five canonical three-ball juggling patterns—cascade, tennis, half-shower, shower, and box—within less than 5 minutes of real-world interaction.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that robots can build upon imperfect prior knowledge and continually refine their behavior through real-world experience. This points toward a broader paradigm where models, even when far from reality, serve as valuable priors for efficient and safe online learning on physical systems.

title: Why did My Robot Just Change Personality? Prompting Guidelines for a Grounded Robot Persona in LLM-Based HRI
comment: Accepted for publication at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for verbal interaction in social robots, yet prompt design in human-robot interaction (HRI) remains underspecified. As a result, robots may present hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioural boundaries, and misleading personas. This paper develops a framework for prompt design in LLM-based robots and introduces a structured prompt template comprising eight functional components through which robot behaviour can be specified, bounded, and adapted. The framework is grounded in a review of prior LLM-based HRI work and complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts gathered at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). The qualitative findings highlight limited legibility of robot personality, the need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. Based on these findings, we present prompting guidelines accompanied by proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid for HRI research. We argue that prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioural assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards to support reliable and interpretable HRI.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for prompt design in LLM-based social robots, introducing a structured prompt template with eight functional components to specify, bound, and adapt robot behavior. Findings from HRI expert surveys and discussions (N=27 at IEEE RO-MAN 2025) highlight issues with personality legibility, user adaptation needs, and ethical concerns (safety, deception, governance), leading to prompting guidelines and a proof-of-concept template. The authors argue prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards.
AI.motivation: Prompt design for LLM-based robots in HRI is underspecified, leading to hallucinated capabilities, unclear behavioral boundaries, and misleading personas. The paper aims to systematize prompt design to address these issues.
AI.method: The framework is developed through a review of prior LLM-based HRI work, complemented by survey and discussion data from HRI experts at the Robo-Identity workshop at IEEE RO-MAN 2025 (N=27). This results in a structured prompt template with eight functional components.
AI.result: Qualitative findings reveal limited legibility of robot personality, a need for user adaptation, and strong ethical concerns about safety, deception, and governance. The authors provide prompting guidelines and a proof-of-concept template as a structured design and reporting aid.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design should be treated as a socio-technical problem rather than a minor implementation detail, requiring explicit capability boundaries, transparent behavioral assumptions, and context-sensitive safeguards for reliable and interpretable HRI.

title: CLIPPER: Replayable Shortlisted Optimization for Repeated Spatial Coverage Planning
comment: Accepted at ACM SIGSPATIAL 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Operational requirements developed with the City of Braunschweig frame municipal micromobility planning under geofenced exclusions, mandatory retained sites, spacing rules, and area-level caps. Each policy edit requires a new feasible plan; full-set greedy takes tens of seconds per alternative at city scale. We present CLIPPER (Constraint-exact Low-latency Iterative Planning with Pooled Evaluation and Replay). It forms bounded candidate pools but recomputes exact current gains and checks every active constraint before selection. Coverage from each candidate alone sets the initial order. Offline full-set scans measure gains omitted by the pool; online, a conservative bound triggers expansion or audit. CLIPPER-F gives each proposal group the same number of candidate slots. Across Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, its mean coverage over complete chains stays within 0.245 percentage points of full-set greedy under the same policy, with 13.6--28.9 times lower mean rollout time. CLIPPER-A instead distributes one shared candidate budget across the groups. Under its coverage-prioritized policy, it uses 9--15% of full-set greedy's rollout time under the same policy, with mean gaps of 1.82 percentage points in Braunschweig, 0.12 in Munich, and 0.27 in Berlin. Together, CLIPPER enables rapid, replayable comparison of recorded city-scale planning states while enforcing every encoded model constraint.

AI.tldr: CLIPPER is a constraint-exact, low-latency iterative planning framework for municipal micromobility that achieves near-full-set-greedy coverage while reducing rollout time by 13.6-28.9x (CLIPPER-F) or to 9-15% of baseline (CLIPPER-A) across three German cities.
AI.motivation: Municipal micromobility planning under operational constraints (geofenced exclusions, mandatory sites, spacing rules, area caps) requires a new feasible plan for each policy edit. Full-set greedy planning at city scale takes tens of seconds per alternative, making rapid policy comparison impractical.
AI.method: CLIPPER forms bounded candidate pools while recomputing exact current gains and checking every active constraint before selection. It uses offline full-set scans to measure gains omitted by the pool and a conservative online bound to trigger expansion or audit. CLIPPER-F allocates equal candidate slots per proposal group; CLIPPER-A shares one candidate budget across groups.
AI.result: Across Braunschweig, Munich, and Berlin, CLIPPER-F keeps mean coverage within 0.245 percentage points of full-set greedy under the same policy with 13.6-28.9x lower mean rollout time. CLIPPER-A uses 9-15% of full-set greedy's rollout time with mean gaps of 1.82pp (Braunschweig), 0.12pp (Munich), and 0.27pp (Berlin).
AI.conclusion: CLIPPER enables rapid, replayable comparison of recorded city-scale planning states while enforcing every encoded model constraint, making iterative municipal micromobility planning practical.

title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA, 14 pages, 5 figures Dataset: https://vizpi.org/dataset
summary: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

AI.tldr: TutorTrace is a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that captures real-time IDE telemetry to make learners' behavioral context visible and computable for AI programming tutors. Across four deployments (N=480), it records ~180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics, enabling prediction of help-seeking behavior (AUROC .726 for query timing, .717 for help-seeking type) and reducing dependent help-seeking intervals from 50.0% to 20.7% via behavior-aware prompts.
AI.motivation: AI programming tutors lack the behavioral context that human tutors use to adapt support to learners' needs—they respond only to what learners say, not to what learners have done before asking for help.
AI.method: The authors build TutorTrace, a pipeline that abstracts low-level IDE telemetry into behavioral segments and continuously computed metrics in real time. They derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session. They deploy it across four sessions in two introductory Python courses and conduct both a classroom evaluation with behavior-aware prompts and two held-out prediction tasks (query within 60s and help-seeking type classification).
AI.result: TutorTrace captured ~180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 metrics from 480 learners. Behavior-aware prompts reduced intervals with no independent work between queries from 50.0% to 20.7%. Predictive models achieved AUROC of .726 for predicting whether a learner would query within 60 seconds and .717 for classifying guided versus dependent help-seeking.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral context derived from low-level IDE telemetry can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale, allowing systems to respond to what learners have done leading up to help-seeking moments, not just their queries.

title: TemporalFlow-VLA: Learning Physically Grounded Execution History for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for robot control, yet simply adding historical frames does not reliably capture recent physical change. This is especially problematic in multi-stage manipulation, where visually similar states may require different actions depending on prior execution. To address this challenge, we present TemporalFlow-VLA, which learns compact execution history through physically grounded temporal supervision. Using recorded robot states, robot geometry, and calibrated cameras, we construct robot-surface temporal flow as a training-only target and supervise two execution-aligned temporal queries that provide structured history to the action expert. The geometric supervision path is not evaluated at deployment. TemporalFlow-VLA achieves 97.63 +/- 0.26% average success on LIBERO, including 96.60 +/- 0.87% on LIBERO Long, and 85.5%/84.2% Clean/Randomized success across 12 RoboTwin tasks. It shows its clearest advantage over prior methods on longer-horizon, multi-stage manipulation. Controlled history interventions show that action prediction depends on both historical content and temporal order. With asynchronous feature caching, temporal conditioning maintains single-frame-level server-side sampling latency without additional historical-encoding overhead. Overall, TemporalFlow-VLA provides a compact, physically grounded interface for exploiting ordered execution history without explicit motion estimation or geometric processing at deployment.

AI.tldr: TemporalFlow-VLA introduces a VLA model that learns compact execution history through physically grounded temporal supervision, using robot-surface temporal flow as a training-only target with two execution-aligned temporal queries. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO (97.63% average) and RoboTwin benchmarks, particularly excelling in long-horizon multi-stage manipulation, while maintaining single-frame-level deployment latency via asynchronous feature caching.
AI.motivation: Standard VLA models that naively add historical frames fail to reliably capture recent physical changes in the environment. This is especially problematic in multi-stage manipulation where visually similar states require different actions depending on prior execution history, necessitating a more structured approach to encoding temporal information.
AI.method: TemporalFlow-VLA constructs a robot-surface temporal flow as a training-only geometric supervision target using recorded robot states, robot geometry, and calibrated cameras. This supervision signal trains two execution-aligned temporal queries that provide structured history to the action expert. The geometric supervision path is removed at deployment, and asynchronous feature caching maintains low latency.
AI.result: TemporalFlow-VLA achieves 97.63 +/- 0.26% average success on LIBERO (96.60 +/- 0.87% on LIBERO Long) and 85.5%/84.2% Clean/Randomized success across 12 RoboTwin tasks. It demonstrates the clearest improvement over prior methods on longer-horizon, multi-stage manipulation, and ablation studies confirm action prediction depends on both historical content and temporal order.
AI.conclusion: TemporalFlow-VLA provides a compact, physically grounded interface for exploiting ordered execution history in VLA models without requiring explicit motion estimation or geometric processing at deployment time, while maintaining single-frame-level server-side sampling latency.

title: Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion
comment: Accepted to ACM UIST 2026, Detroit, MI, USA
summary: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N = 16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

AI.tldr: SecondVoice is a mixed-reality system that uses an embodied virtual proxy to voice hesitant points into co-located group discussions without putting the speaker on the spot, separating "what is said" from "who says it." A preliminary study (N=16) found that half of participants used it for points they did not say aloud (vs. 18.8% for an anonymous text board), and proxy-delivered points more effectively entered the spoken conversational floor with multi-turn engagement.
AI.motivation: People often withhold contributions in group discussions due to anticipated negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when they must voice the point themselves. This limits equal participation and effective collaboration in co-located settings.
AI.method: The authors present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system with an embodied virtual proxy. Users specify their intent through a structured specification process in a private overlay (rather than composing full utterances); the system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation via the proxy. They characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk, then conduct a within-subject study (N=16) comparing SecondVoice against an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks.
AI.result: Half (50%) of participants used SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared to 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which did not occur after text-board posts. Participants found the channel situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs regarding timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.
AI.conclusion: SecondVoice demonstrates a promising approach for enabling equal participation in co-located discussions by providing a socially protective channel for voicing hesitant points. However, tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation need further exploration before broader adoption.

title: Active Surface-Driven Reconfigurable Gripper: Robust Grasping and Sequential Manipulation of Thin Objects
comment: Accepted by RSS2026
summary: Robotic grippers face substantial challenges in grasping and manipulating thin objects. Most existing grippers rely on highly precise approach and grasp motions, which limits robustness and reduces applicability. This paper explores thin-object grasping using books as a representative example. Here, we propose a novel solution that integrates an active surface with underactuated compliance to achieve stable grasping of thin objects without complex control. First, an underactuated gripper with an active surface is designed. The active-surface thumb performs in-hand repositioning of the target book without requiring adjustments of the robot arm or the other fingers, while the underactuated fingers establish compliant contact conditions with the environment, and the reconfigurable structure enables reliable grasping of books under different configurations. Second, we establish a kinematic model of the gripper, and determine the initial grasp postures for two representative scenarios (books lying flat on a desktop and books vertically packed in a shelf). Third, by analyzing the physical model of a book lying on a table and its interaction with the gripper and the environment, we systematically optimize the structural parameters and grasping strategy. Finally, extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed gripper and strategy. The results demonstrate strong robustness and adaptability when grasping thin objects placed flat (including books, paper, fabric, plastic film, and mouse pad), as well as a high success rate when grasping vertically packed books. Moreover, the proposed gripper can reliably complete long sequential "grasp-place" tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel robotic gripper combining an active surface with underactuated compliance to achieve robust grasping and manipulation of thin objects, using books as a representative case. The gripper enables in-hand repositioning, adapts to different book configurations, and demonstrates high success rates for both flat and vertically packed thin objects.
AI.motivation: Thin-object grasping is challenging for most robotic grippers because it requires highly precise approach and grasp motions, limiting robustness and practical applicability. Existing solutions lack robustness without complex control.
AI.method: The approach involves: (1) designing an underactuated gripper with an active-surface thumb for in-hand repositioning and reconfigurable underactuated fingers for compliant environmental contact; (2) establishing a kinematic model to determine initial grasp postures for two scenarios (flat books on a desktop, vertically packed books in a shelf); (3) analyzing the physical model of a book-gripper-environment interaction to systematically optimize structural parameters and grasping strategy.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate strong robustness and adaptability when grasping flat thin objects (books, paper, fabric, plastic film, mouse pad), high success rates for vertically packed books, and reliable long sequential 'grasp-place' task execution.
AI.conclusion: The integration of an active surface with underactuated compliance provides a simple yet effective solution for stable thin-object grasping without complex control, offering broad applicability and robustness across diverse thin-object types and grasp configurations.

title: Is Your Neighborhood Safe? Place-based Stigma in Large Language Models' Urban Safety Judgments
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to inform safety decisions in cities, such as where it is safe to walk, rent, or travel. We ask whether such judgments track measured risk or the patterns attached to an urban neighborhood's name. We probe seven instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography: coordinates-only, name-only, and name+coordinates, across 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, joined to violent crime and American Community Survey data. First, ratings are nearly flat under coordinates for six of seven models, while names carry most between neighborhood variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only at frontier scale does the coordinate channel show appreciable variation. Second, names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group (percent Black in Chicago, percent Hispanic in Los Angeles), and this name effect tracks demographic share in all seven models and both cities. In Los Angeles, where demographic share and crime are more separable, the effect survives controls for crime and income and is confirmed by crime-matched pairs. An enforcement-elasticity analysis further shows that over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary, deployment-driven offenses. Third, the effect scales with geographic knowledge: models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more demographic stereotype to them. Because neighborhood names carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, removing names reduces both bias and accuracy. We discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support settings.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs' safety judgments about urban neighborhoods track measured crime risk or demographic stereotypes attached to neighborhood names. Across 7 instruct-tuned models, 186 neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Chicago, the authors find that names carry most between-neighborhood variation in safety ratings, that demographic biases (lower safety for neighborhoods with higher shares of marginalized groups) persist even after controlling for crime and income, and that the stereotype effect scales with geographic knowledge.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to inform urban safety decisions (where to walk, rent, travel), yet little is known about whether their judgments reflect actual risk or harmful demographic stereotypes encoded in neighborhood names. Understanding this is critical for responsible deployment in decision-support settings.
AI.method: The authors probe 7 instruct-tuned models under three conditions that dissociate name from geography (coordinates-only, name-only, name+coordinates) across 186 neighborhoods in LA and Chicago, joined to violent crime and ACS data. They run controlled crime-matched-pair analyses and an enforcement-elasticity analysis to separate genuine crime signal from demographic stereotype.
AI.result: (1) Six of seven models produce nearly flat safety ratings under coordinates-only, while names drive most variation and are moderately calibrated to violent crime; only frontier-scale models show appreciable coordinate-channel variation. (2) Names lower safety ratings more for neighborhoods with higher shares of the locally dominant marginalized group, an effect that survives crime and income controls in LA and appears across all 7 models and both cities. (3) Over-caution tracks near-fully-reported homicide rather than discretionary enforcement-driven offenses. (4) The demographic stereotype effect scales with geographic knowledge — models that better distinguish real neighborhoods apply more stereotype.
AI.conclusion: Neighborhood names in LLM safety judgments carry both genuine crime signal and demographic stereotype, making name removal a double-edged sword: it reduces bias but also accuracy. The authors discuss implications for deploying LLMs in advice and decision-support contexts, highlighting a bias-utility tradeoff.

title: Beyond Shallow-Water Photorealism: Physically and Sensor-Grounded Simulation for Deep-Sea Robotics
summary: Many recent underwater simulators emphasize visual realism at the expense of physical fidelity, focusing on shallow-water effects with limited relevance in deep-water environments and high computational cost. In this work, we shift the focus toward deep-sea physical and sensor realism. We present a physics- and sensor-grounded extension of the Stonefish simulator that augments its hydrodynamic models with stochastic IMU and DVL drift, magnetometer disturbances, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics, pressure-driven environmental variability, and physically based underwater optics. These additions are designed to better capture the forces and measurements shaping the behavior of deep-ocean AUVs, ROVs, landers, ASVs, and gliders, while remaining compatible with real-time simulation. This work advances underwater simulation toward more representative deep-sea operating conditions, which is particularly relevant for long-duration navigation and learning-based autonomy, where inaccurate sensor and environmental models introduce non-physical artifacts and overly optimistic performance. While challenges remain, including complex fluid-structure interactions and full environmental stochasticity, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for navigation, perception, and autonomy research under deep-sea conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a physics- and sensor-grounded extension of the Stonefish simulator, augmenting its hydrodynamic models with stochastic IMU and DVL drift, magnetometer disturbances, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics, pressure-driven environmental variability, and physically based underwater optics to better capture deep-sea AUV, ROV, lander, ASV, and glider behavior in real-time.
AI.motivation: Existing underwater simulators prioritize visual realism over physical fidelity and focus on shallow-water effects that are not relevant to deep-water environments, while also incurring high computational costs. This leaves a gap in realistic deep-sea simulation for long-duration navigation and learning-based autonomy.
AI.method: The authors extend the Stonefish simulator by augmenting its hydrodynamic models with: stochastic IMU and DVL drift, magnetometer disturbances, higher-order hydrodynamics, terramechanics (for seafloor interaction), pressure-driven environmental variability, and physically based underwater optics. These additions aim to capture forces and measurements shaping deep-ocean vehicle behavior while remaining compatible with real-time simulation.
AI.result: The framework provides a practical foundation for navigation, perception, and autonomy research under deep-sea conditions, better capturing representative deep-sea operating conditions and reducing non-physical artifacts and overly optimistic performance seen in inaccurate sensor/environmental models.
AI.conclusion: While challenges remain—including complex fluid-structure interactions and full environmental stochasticity—the proposed extension advances underwater simulation toward more representative deep-sea operating conditions, particularly relevant for long-duration navigation and learning-based autonomy.

title: Invocation-Level Reliability of Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using agents fail two ways: choosing the wrong tool, or forming wrong arguments, and an early failure of either kind can silently corrupt everything downstream. We measure a correct-invocation rate that separates the two, under both a clean teacher-forced context and the model's own free-running context, on five open-weight models over contamination-free multi-step tasks (depths 1-8). By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's own clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Our central finding concerns the measurement itself. Under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, a propagation model's severity and recovery parameters are not merely hard to estimate - they are fixed by the scoring rule. Severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct); recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps returned on-track, against an expected 0.0058 by chance). Both follow from one mechanism: post-divergence, the gold value is generated by tool constants the model never sees, so it is information the model cannot derive. A fit run anyway returns 0.92 and 0.73 for a quantity that is exactly 1.000 - confident numbers for a parameter the scoring rule already determined. We give the mechanism and a remedy, conditional-on-state scoring, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero additional cost, which un-pins severity to interior estimates excluding zero (+0.149, +0.316).

AI.tldr: This paper studies tool-using agents' failures (wrong tool choice vs. wrong arguments), measuring correct-invocation rates under teacher-forced and free-running contexts across five open-weight models on contamination-free multi-step tasks (depth 1-8). The central finding reveals that under exact-match scoring against a fixed gold trajectory, propagation severity and recovery parameters are not estimable—they are determined by the scoring rule itself (severity forced to boundary, recovery structurally unobservable).
