The authors propose conditional-on-state scoring as a remedy, applied post-hoc to cached completions at zero cost, which un-pins these parameters to interior estimates.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents fail in two distinct ways—choosing the wrong tool or forming wrong arguments—and early failures silently corrupt all downstream steps. The authors aim to properly separate and measure these failure types, and more importantly, expose a fundamental flaw in how propagation models are evaluated under standard exact-match scoring against gold trajectories.
AI.method: The study measures correct-invocation rates under both clean teacher-forced contexts and the model's own free-running context across five open-weight models on multi-step tool-using tasks (depths 1-8). The authors analyze the statistical properties of exact-match scoring against fixed gold trajectories, demonstrating that post-divergence, gold values derive from tool constants the model cannot observe, making recovery information-theoretically impossible. They propose conditional-on-state scoring as a remedy, applied retrospectively to cached completions at zero cost.
AI.result: By depth 6, roughly 70% of a model's clean-context capability is lost to its own earlier mistakes (L6 = 0.686, 0.684). Under exact-match scoring, severity is forced to its boundary (0 of 869 poisoned steps correct) and recovery is structurally unobservable (0 of 580 poisoned steps on-track vs. 0.0058 expected by chance). A fit run produces confident estimates (0.92, 0.73) for a quantity that is exactly 1.000. Conditional-on-state scoring un-pins severity to interior estimates (+0.149, +0.316).
AI.conclusion: Standard exact-match scoring against fixed gold trajectories makes propagation severity and recovery parameters statistically unidentifiable—they are predetermined by the scoring rule. The proposed conditional-on-state scoring provides a free (retrospective, zero-cost) remedy that yields interior, meaningful estimates of propagation parameters.

title: Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization for Underwater Sampling
summary: Accurate state estimation for autonomous underwater vehicles performing close-range seafloor sampling remains challenging. In low-altitude operation, down-looking cameras over featureless planar seabeds produce scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy, and inconsistent feature tracking. Meanwhile, inertial-Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) fusion alone provides no mechanism for structural drift correction. We propose a Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that treats physical interaction as an informative geometric constraint within a smoothing-based localization formulation. The method tightly fuses suction-based manipulator contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors. Visual odometry relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors are uncertainty-scaled according to inlier statistics to prevent visually weak frames from destabilizing the estimator, while contact events are modeled as high-confidence factors that induce implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition. Furthermore, the system can fully initialize online during motion. Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulation environments demonstrates that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations. These results highlight the role of embodied physical interaction as a localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) performing close-range seafloor sampling, which fuses suction-based manipulator contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors in a smoothing-based formulation. Contact events serve as high-confidence geometric constraints inducing implicit loop closures, while visual factors are uncertainty-scaled by inlier statistics. Experiments in tanks, harbor, and simulation show reduced trajectory drift and improved object revisit accuracy.
AI.motivation: Accurate state estimation for AUVs during close-range seafloor sampling is challenging due to: (1) down-looking cameras over featureless planar seabeds causing scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy, and inconsistent feature tracking; and (2) inertial-DVL fusion lacking structural drift correction mechanisms.
AI.method: A Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that: (1) models physical interaction (suction-based manipulator contact) as informative geometric constraints within a smoothing-based localization formulation; (2) tightly fuses contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors; (3) scales visual odometry relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors by inlier statistics to prevent visually weak frames from destabilizing estimation; (4) models contact events as high-confidence factors inducing implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition; (5) supports full online initialization during motion.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulation environments demonstrates that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations.
AI.conclusion: Embodied physical interaction serves as an effective localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments, highlighting a novel paradigm where task-related physical contacts are exploited as geometric constraints for state estimation.

title: Predicting Consequences and Reinforcing Navigation Policies with Latent World Models
summary: World models enable agents to reason about future outcomes and learn policies from their knowledge of state transition, but existing approaches primarily focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making. In this work, we propose a compatibility prediction Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility rather than reconstructing observations. Our key insight is that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity, enabling action consequences to be evaluated directly in latent space. To support counterfactual training, our model leverages action sequences sampled across trajectories and learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the learned world model can supervise policy learning from unlabeled video data and further improve policies through reinforcement learning entirely within the world model. This imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show that our approach significantly outperforms prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance. The code, pretrained models, and additional materials are available at https://wzm206.github.io/latent-world-model-nav.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Latent World Model (LWM) for robot navigation that predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility instead of reconstructing observations, enabling policy learning from unlabeled video without action annotations or environment interaction.
AI.motivation: Existing world models focus on reconstructing future observations or features, which introduces unnecessary complexity and limits their effectiveness for decision making in robotics.
AI.method: LWM predicts action-conditioned latent feature compatibility based on the insight that spatial proximity correlates with latent feature similarity. It uses action sequences sampled across trajectories for counterfactual training, learns to predict which sequences lead closer to the goal, and supervises policy learning from unlabeled video data with reinforcement learning conducted entirely within the world model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world robot navigation datasets show significant improvements over prior world model and imitation learning methods in prediction accuracy, policy learning, and real-world navigation performance.
AI.conclusion: The imagination-driven framework eliminates the need for action annotations and additional environment interaction, providing an effective and scalable approach for robot navigation.

title: 4DSynth: Controllable Procedural World Synthesis for Dynamic Embodied Simulation
summary:
Embodied agents need environments that are visually diverse, physically interactive, and changing over time. Procedural simulators can generate large interactive scene collections, and recent 4D generators produce compelling visual dynamics. Combining these properties in one environment, however, still demands extensive manual effort, and the result is rarely editable or controllable enough to reuse at scale.
  We present 4DSynth, a controllable procedural system that turns a natural-language description, a blueprint mask, or a single photograph into an editable 4D environment with explicit geometry, animated actors, collision-free trajectories, and physics-ready simulation state. Multiple scene routes share one geometry-grounded representation, so the same pipeline handles animation, camera planning, rendering, and task generation.
  To validate the full pipeline, we construct 4DSynth-Nav, an interactive navigation benchmark generated entirely from 4DSynth's procedural scenes. Two vision-language models evaluated across three difficulty tiers both fail the majority of tasks and stall after early subtasks. The same procedural controllability that produces these environments also makes each failure reproducible and each difficulty axis independently tunable. This paper presents both a controllable generation pipeline and the scalable benchmark it enables, offering a practical foundation for developing and evaluating embodied agents.

AI.tldr: 4DSynth is a controllable procedural system that generates editable 4D environments from natural language, blueprint masks, or a single photograph. It also introduces 4DSynth-Nav, a navigation benchmark built from these procedurally generated scenes, where state-of-the-art vision-language models fail a majority of tasks.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents require visually diverse, physically interactive, and temporally changing environments. While procedural simulators and 4D generators exist separately, combining these properties into one controllable, editable, and reusable environment remains extremely difficult and demands extensive manual effort.
AI.method: 4DSynth is a controllable procedural system that converts a natural-language description, blueprint mask, or single photograph into an editable 4D environment with explicit geometry, animated actors, collision-free trajectories, and physics-ready simulation state. Multiple scene routes share one geometry-grounded representation, enabling unified animation, camera planning, rendering, and task generation. The system is validated via 4DSynth-Nav, an interactive navigation benchmark generated entirely from procedural scenes.
AI.result: Two vision-language models evaluated across three difficulty tiers in 4DSynth-Nav both fail a majority of tasks and stall after early subtasks. The procedural controllability ensures each failure is reproducible and each difficulty axis is independently tunable.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents both a controllable 4D environment generation pipeline and a scalable navigation benchmark it enables, providing a practical foundation for developing and evaluating embodied agents.

title: Structured Evidence Routing for Incident Risk Prediction from Multimodal Longitudinal EHRs
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories. We propose structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow that separates full-record access from disease-specific assessment. The router organizes the complete pre-index EHR into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form an evidence-linked risk assessment, which the reviewer critiques. For comparison with supervised EHRSHOT baselines, we pair the routed evidence summaries with a supervised classifier readout. Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, our method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC, while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal pre-readout ablations further suggest that routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces structured evidence routing, a router-predictor-reviewer workflow for incident risk prediction from longitudinal EHRs. The router compresses full patient histories into evidence slices, the predictor forms evidence-linked risk assessments, and the reviewer critiques them. The method matches supervised EHRSHOT baselines on AUROC and remains competitive on AUPRC across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks while providing patient-specific evidence trails.
AI.motivation: Incident risk prediction from longitudinal EHRs is challenging because relevant signals are multimodal, weak in isolation, and distributed across irregular patient histories, necessitating a method that can effectively organize and leverage dispersed clinical evidence.
AI.method: A router-predictor-reviewer workflow is proposed. The router organizes full pre-index EHR data into a compact summary and targeted evidence slices; the predictor uses this evidence to form evidence-linked risk assessments, which the reviewer critiques. The routed evidence summaries are paired with a supervised classifier readout for benchmarking against supervised EHRSHOT baselines.
AI.result: Across five 1-year incident diagnosis tasks, the method reaches the AUROC range of established supervised EHRSHOT baselines and remains competitive on AUPRC while exposing a patient-specific evidence trail. Internal ablations show routing, laboratory evidence, task guidance, and review each contribute to performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured evidence routing achieves performance comparable to established supervised baselines while offering interpretability through patient-specific evidence trails, with ablation studies confirming the contribution of each workflow component.

title: Arbitrary-Order Hermite Interpolation of Rigid-Motion Jets via Hyper-Multidual Quaternions
comment: 21 pages, 1 figure
summary: We study bilateral interpolation of finite-order rigid-motion jets represented by unit dual quaternions. An order-$n$ multidual (MD) algebra is the truncated polynomial algebra $\mathbb{R}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{n+1})$; hyper-multidual (HMD) quaternions are dual quaternions with coefficients in this algebra. Temporal HMD transforms encode a pose and its derivatives, whereas a generic HMD curve need not be the temporal jet of its pose projection; we call this requirement holonomicity. We show that a temporal transform and its relative descriptor are unitary and derive recursive coefficient constraints, together with a local realizability converse in an admissible logarithm chart. We then extend screw linear interpolation (ScLERP) algebraically to unit HMD quaternions. Although it matches complete endpoint transforms, direct HMD--ScLERP is generically non-holonomic for arbitrary endpoint jets. We give a coefficient criterion and explicit endpoint and first-order interior contact defects. A holonomic alternative is obtained by mapping endpoint transforms to logarithmic dual-quaternion coordinates, applying the degree-$(2n+1)$ Hermite polynomial that matches derivatives through order $n$, and lifting by the exponential. HMD arithmetic also recovers higher-order rigid-motion acceleration fields without explicit differentiation of $\mathrm{dexp}$. Rotation and full $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ tests through second order, with an additional third-order polynomial check, reproduce the stated defects and endpoint jets.

AI.tldr: This paper studies bilateral interpolation of finite-order rigid-motion jets represented by unit dual quaternions using hyper-multidual (HMD) quaternion algebra. It shows temporal transforms are unitary, derives recursive coefficient constraints with a local realizability converse, extends ScLERP algebraically to unit HMD quaternions (which is generically non-holonomic), and proposes a holonomic alternative via Hermite interpolation in logarithmic dual-quaternion coordinates. HMD arithmetic also provides higher-order acceleration fields without explicit dexp differentiation.
AI.motivation: To develop a consistent algebraic framework for higher-order interpolation of rigid-motion trajectories (jets) in dual quaternion space, while addressing the holonomicity requirement — ensuring that a curve in dual-quaternion space genuinely represents the temporal jet of a pose trajectory rather than an arbitrary curve.
AI.method: The paper uses multidual (MD) algebra R[ε]/(ε^{n+1}) to build hyper-multidual (HMD) quaternions. It proves unitarity of temporal transforms and relative descriptors, derives recursive coefficient constraints for realizability, and introduces an algebraic HMD-ScLERP extension. For a holonomic alternative, it maps endpoint transforms to logarithmic dual-quaternion coordinates, applies degree-(2n+1) Hermite polynomials matching derivatives through order n, and lifts via the exponential map. HMD arithmetic computes higher-order acceleration fields without explicit dexp differentiation.
AI.result: Direct HMD-ScLERP matches complete endpoint transforms but is generically non-holonomic for arbitrary endpoint jets; the paper provides coefficient criteria and explicit first-order interior contact defects. The Hermite-logarithmic-exponential approach yields a holonomic alternative. Numerical tests in rotation and full SE(3) through second order (plus a third-order polynomial check) verify the stated defects and endpoint jets.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes that while algebraic extension of ScLERP to HMD quaternions fails to preserve holonomicity in general, a holonomic high-order interpolation scheme can be constructed through Hermite interpolation in logarithmic coordinates followed by exponential lifting, with HMD arithmetic efficiently recovering higher-order motion fields.

title: AffectOmni: RL-Verifiable People-Centric Grounded Affective Reasoning for Social and Art-Related Scenes
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on VQA and scene understanding, yet affective reasoning remains vulnerable to shortcut behavior. Models may predict correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues such as micro expressions and body language, which weakens traceability and external verification. Prior reinforcement learning approaches mainly reward context or logical coherence without explicitly enforcing attention to human evidence. In addition, LLM as a Judge scoring often suffers from score clustering, which reduces reward discriminability. We propose AffectOmni, a GRPO trained framework for verifiable affective reasoning. AffectOmni introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to encourage people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, and it adopts within-group comparative scoring to produce more stable and discriminative reward signals. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free form rationales into executable evidence instructions, which are grounded into pixel level evidence regions via SAM3 to provide an externally auditable interface outside the training loop. Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open source 7B scale baselines, including gains of 4.66% on emotion recognition and +14.29% on temporally sensitive tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/eliot127825-rgb/AffectOmni_nobody.

AI.tldr: AffectOmni is a GRPO-trained multimodal large language model framework for verifiable affective reasoning that introduces People Focus and Temporal Order rewards to enforce people-centric evidence selection and temporally structured reasoning, uses within-group comparative scoring for more discriminative reward signals, and grounds free-form rationales into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3 for external verification, achieving consistent gains on emotion recognition and temporally sensitive benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs perform well on VQA and scene understanding but exhibit shortcut behavior in affective reasoning by predicting correct answers while neglecting people-centric cues (micro expressions, body language), which hampers traceability and external verification. Prior RL approaches don't explicitly enforce attention to human evidence, and LLM-as-a-Judge scoring suffers from score clustering that reduces reward discriminability.
AI.method: AffectOmni is trained with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). It introduces two novel rewards: People Focus reward to encourage selection of people-centric evidence, and Temporal Order reward to promote temporally structured reasoning. It also adopts within-group comparative scoring to yield more stable and discriminative reward signals than absolute scoring. For verification, a Thinking Summarizer converts free-form rationales into executable evidence instructions that are grounded into pixel-level evidence regions via SAM3, providing an externally auditable interface outside the training loop.
AI.result: Experiments on IntentBench, Daily Omni, and WorldSense show consistent improvements over open-source 7B-scale baselines, including a 4.66% gain on emotion recognition and a +14.29% improvement on temporally sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: AffectOmni demonstrates that explicitly rewarding people-centric evidence selection and temporal reasoning, combined with discriminative comparative scoring, improves both affective reasoning performance and verifiability in MLLMs, providing an externally auditable grounding mechanism through pixel-level evidence.

title: Riemann-1.0: An Embodied World Action Model for Physical AI
summary: We introduce Riemann-1.0, a fully causal autoregressive World Action Model for embodied intelligence. Riemann-1.0 jointly models multi-view visual observations, robot states, and embodiment-specific actions within a unified causal autoregressive sequence, representing robot actions and world evolution as causal state transitions. Unlike existing WAMs based on joint generation, video-first prediction, or decoupled modeling paradigms, Riemann-1.0 unifies online robot policy execution and action-conditioned world simulation within a single model, enabling it to function as both an executable robot policy and a multi-embodiment visual world simulator. To scale embodied experience across heterogeneous data sources, we further develop a progressive embodied pretraining framework that unifies learning from egocentric human videos, handheld-gripper demonstrations, and heterogeneous robot trajectories under a shared World Action Modeling objective. Built upon 200K+ hours of interaction data, Riemann-1.0 progressively transfers large-scale embodied experience into executable robot manipulation capabilities. Riemann-1.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance across both simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. It achieves success rates of 94.3% on RoboTwin2.0, 99.0% on LIBERO, and 62.6% on the long-horizon compositional benchmark RoboCasa-365, outperforming the previous best method by 8.4% On long-horizon real-world manipulation tasks, Riemann-1.0 achieves a Success Rate (SR) of 85.0% and a Progress Success Rate (PSR) of 94.4%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 15% in SR. These results demonstrate that unified World Action Modeling together with progressive embodied pretraining effectively transforms large-scale embodied experience into generalizable robot manipulation capabilities.

AI.tldr: Riemann-1.0 is a fully causal autoregressive World Action Model (WAM) that unifies multi-view visual observations, robot states, and embodiment-specific actions into a single sequence, functioning as both an executable robot policy and a multi-embodiment visual world simulator. Built on a progressive embodied pretraining framework with 200K+ hours of heterogeneous interaction data, it achieves state-of-the-art results across simulation (94.3% on RoboTwin2.0, 99.0% on LIBERO, 62.6% on RoboCasa-365) and real-world manipulation (85.0% SR, 94.4% PSR) benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing World Action Models rely on joint generation, video-first prediction, or decoupled modeling paradigms, which fail to unify online robot policy execution with action-conditioned world simulation in a single architecture. The authors aim to bridge this gap by proposing a unified model that can simultaneously act as a robot policy and an embodied world simulator, while scaling embodied experience across heterogeneous data sources (egocentric human videos, handheld-gripper demonstrations, heterogeneous robot trajectories).
AI.method: Riemann-1.0 models robot actions and world evolution as causal state transitions within a unified causal autoregressive sequence that jointly represents multi-view visual observations, robot states, and embodiment-specific actions. It employs a progressive embodied pretraining framework that unifies learning from egocentric human videos, handheld-gripper demonstrations, and heterogeneous robot trajectories under a shared World Action Modeling objective, trained on 200K+ hours of interaction data to progressively transfer large-scale embodied experience into executable robot manipulation policies.
AI.result: Riemann-1.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance on both simulation and real-world benchmarks: 94.3% success rate on RoboTwin2.0, 99.0% on LIBERO, 62.6% on the long-horizon compositional benchmark RoboCasa-365 (outperforming the previous best by 8.4%), and on long-horizon real-world manipulation tasks, 85.0% SR and 94.4% PSR, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 15% in SR.
AI.conclusion: Unified World Action Modeling combined with progressive embodied pretraining effectively transforms large-scale embodied experience into generalizable robot manipulation capabilities, demonstrating that a single causal autoregressive model can serve both as an executable policy and a multi-embodiment visual world simulator while outperforming existing decoupled or generation-based approaches.

title: Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization
summary: Operating a scientific instrument such as an atomic force microscope (AFM) requires continuous expert decision-making. A trained user defines the experimental intent, translates it into instrument commands, assesses incoming data, adjusts imaging parameters, and post-processes the final image. Existing automation usually addresses only parts of this workflow through hard-coded routines, task-specific controllers, or trained machine-learning models. Here we present an agentic-AI framework that operates the executable part of the AFM workflow using a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework consists of 3 MCP-based agents: AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; AFM Pilot assesses image quality through a large language model (LLM) and, if necessary, adapts imaging parameters; and AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. Because the language model performs image assessment rather than a fixed scalar objective or external optimizer, the same strategy can be applied across sample types and imaging modes without specific retraining. Safe hardware operation is enforced through an ambiguity check layer before execution. Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that this guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time, with no significant difference. These results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an agentic-AI framework for fully automated atomic force microscope (AFM) operation using a tool-augmented large language model connected to instrument functions via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The framework uses three MCP-based agents (AFM Messenger, AFM Pilot, AFM Doctor) to handle command translation, image-based tuning, and artifact post-processing, respectively. A guarded execution layer eliminates wrong-command execution entirely, and live experiments show AFM Pilot matches expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time.
AI.motivation: Operating scientific instruments like AFM requires continuous expert decision-making, and existing automation only addresses parts of the workflow through hard-coded routines or task-specific controllers. There is a need for a general-purpose, safe, and adaptable automation framework that handles the full executable workflow without requiring retraining for different sample types or imaging modes.
AI.method: The framework consists of three MCP-based agents built on a general-purpose, tool-augmented large language model: (1) AFM Messenger converts natural-language instructions into checked instrument commands; (2) AFM Pilot assesses image quality via LLM and adapts imaging parameters when needed; (3) AFM Doctor diagnoses image artifacts and applies transparent post-processing from a pre-approved tool set. An ambiguity check layer enforces safe hardware operation before execution.
AI.result: Benchmarking against fine-tuned and off-the-shelf tool-using models shows that the guarded execution layer, rather than model capability alone, reduces wrong-command execution to zero. In live experiments on different samples, AFM Pilot matched expert operators in image quality, iteration count, and tuning time with no significant difference.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a safe route to agentic operation of scientific instruments, where experimental intent remains human-defined while command execution, image-based tuning, and post-processing are delegated to AI agents.

title: GRAFT: Grounded and Efficient Online Reinforcement Adaptation for Fine-Grained Robot Manipulation
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide strong priors for robot manipulation, yet adapting them online to fine-grained biomedical tasks remains challenging. Task success often hinges on subtle, view-dependent visual cues, while task-level rewards provide little guidance about which regions matter, making it difficult to learn task-relevant visual grounding from limited real-robot interaction. Online adaptation is further constrained by the computational cost of VLA inference and replay-based updates. We introduce GRAFT (Grounded Reinforcement Adaptation for Fast Task Learning), a framework for efficient online VLA adaptation through grounded perception. GRAFT uses region-level supervision to learn view-specific visual anchors that focus perception on task-relevant local cues without requiring region proposals at deployment. It further combines single-step action generation with cached visual-language prefix reuse to accelerate online learning. Across four biomedical manipulation tasks, GRAFT improves success rates by 25 percentage points under matched adaptation budgets, while reducing the computational overhead of online policy updates.

AI.tldr: GRAFT is a framework for efficient online adaptation of pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies to fine-grained biomedical manipulation tasks. It learns view-specific visual anchors via region-level supervision, enabling task-relevant visual grounding without region proposals at deployment, and accelerates online learning via single-step action generation and cached visual-language prefix reuse. It improves success rates by 25 percentage points across four biomedical tasks under matched adaptation budgets while reducing computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained VLA policies online to fine-grained biomedical manipulation is challenging because: (1) task success depends on subtle, view-dependent visual cues; (2) task-level rewards offer little guidance on which regions matter; and (3) online adaptation is constrained by the high computational cost of VLA inference and replay-based updates.
AI.method: GRAFT introduces three key components: (1) region-level supervision to learn view-specific visual anchors that focus perception on task-relevant local cues without requiring region proposals at deployment; (2) single-step action generation to streamline policy updates; and (3) cached visual-language prefix reuse to reduce the computational cost of online adaptation.
AI.result: Across four biomedical manipulation tasks, GRAFT improves success rates by 25 percentage points compared to baselines under matched adaptation budgets, while also reducing the computational overhead of online policy updates.
AI.conclusion: GRAFT demonstrates that grounded perception via learned visual anchors, combined with computational optimizations such as single-step action generation and prefix caching, enables efficient and effective online adaptation of VLA policies for fine-grained biomedical manipulation tasks.

title: Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling
summary: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations---such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections---through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. title: Pass the Bucket: Efficient, Robust, Local Load Balancing for Teams of Heterogeneous Robots
comment: This paper was submitted to IROS 2026 on March 2nd and accepted on June 17th
summary: We study the problem of decentralized, self-organized task sharing for a swarm of heterogeneous robots that collaborate in transportation or other objectives that require coordinated motion planning. To this end, we present theoretical and practical results for the simple but effective mechanism of \emph{bucket brigades} for load balancing, in which a team of heterogenous robots share a spatial task in a confined, one-dimensional space, while only being able to sense collisions with neighbors or walls. The goal is to optimize throughput of the overall system, without central control or information, aiming at an interval partition proportional to robot velocities. We address possible chaotic system behavior by developing a stabilization mechanism based on simple local aid, a ``token'', that temporarily decelerates robots after an encounter. This purely local change eliminates persistent oscillations, resulting in convergence towards a stable system state. We accelerate system convergence by comparing a single boundary token to ubiquitous two-directional tokens and optimizing the deceleration factor. Event-driven simulations report convergence times and robustness: For a large variety of perturbations (such as robot deletion, position or velocity jittering), the system reliably re-converges. The results suggest a local, practical mechanism for robust load balancing for heterogeneous teams of robots that promises an effective tool as basis for more complex scenarios.

Event-driven simulations demonstrate robust convergence under various perturbations including robot deletion and jittering.

Simple bucket brigade mechanisms can exhibit chaotic behavior and persistent oscillations, preventing convergence to an optimal throughput state. The goal is to achieve a stable interval partition proportional to robot velocities purely through local sensing (collision detection) and minimal communication.
AI.method: The authors develop a stabilization mechanism based on a local "token" that temporarily decelerates robots following an encounter. They compare a single boundary token against ubiquitous two-directional tokens and optimize the deceleration factor. Both theoretical analysis and event-driven simulations are used to study system convergence and stability under perturbation scenarios.

The two-directional token approach and optimized deceleration factors accelerate convergence. Event-driven simulations show the system reliably re-converges under a wide range of perturbations, including robot deletion and position or velocity jittering.
AI.conclusion: The proposed local mechanism provides a robust, practical solution for load balancing in heterogeneous robot swarms and serves as an effective foundation for more complex multi-robot coordination scenarios in confined spaces.

title: GameWAM: A World Action Model for Video Games
comment: 44 pages, 23 figures, 7 tables
summary: Modern video games combine first-person perception, rapid visual changes, persistent world state, and heterogeneous native controls. Existing game agents map visual and task context directly to actions but lack explicit world dynamics modeling, whereas interactive game world models predict visual futures from supplied actions but do not serve as task policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) unify these objectives, but remain largely unexplored under the dynamics and open-ended interaction of video games. We introduce GameWAM, to our knowledge the first WAM for native closed-loop gameplay and GUI control. GameWAM jointly generates future visual observations and executable keyboard-mouse trajectories through parallel visual and action generative processes with block-causal conditioning and flow matching. To support joint world-action learning, we construct synchronized gameplay and GUI trajectories. To handle heterogeneous native control, GameWAM predicts a gameplay/GUI mode at each action step and generates actions with mode-specific prediction distributions and continuous-action normalization. For long-horizon interaction, block-cycle control predicts beyond the committed horizon, executes only a short action prefix, and replans from new observations, while fine-grained within-cycle context and hierarchical cross-cycle history preserve temporal continuity. Experiments demonstrate competitive task success with fewer executed native actions than the compared agents. We further uncover Low-Frequency Action Source Imprinting (LASI), in which low-frequency components of the sampled action source systematically steer coarse generated camera motion under fixed conditioning, revealing a source-sensitivity failure mode in generative control. Project page is available at https://yunncheng.github.io/GameWAM/.

title: Active sensing to characterize the heterogeneity of plant stress
summary:
While most phenotyping platforms rely primarily on image-based measurements, advanced plant characterization requires the integration of active physiological sensing modali- ties such as chlorophyll fluorescence. We present an autonomous robotic platform designed to perform targeted fluorescence measurements on plant leaves. The system combines 3D plant reconstruction, geometric analysis, and motion planning to localize suitable measurement points and generate collision-free trajectories for a robotic manipulator.
  A dense 3D model of the plant is reconstructed from multi-view data and used to extract candidate leaf surfaces based on orientation, accessibility, and sensing constraints. These targets are then integrated into a task-level planning framework that guides the end-effector to precise contact or near-contact configurations required for point-based fluorescence acquisition. The platform enables automated, repeatable, and spatially resolved physiological measurements that go beyond passive imaging. By tightly coupling perception, geometric reasoning, and manipulation, the proposed system provides a robotics-driven approach to high-resolution plant phenotyping and opens new directions for autonomous agricultural inspection and plant-aware manipulation.

AI.tldr: An autonomous robotic platform that integrates 3D plant reconstruction, geometric analysis, and motion planning to perform targeted chlorophyll fluorescence measurements on plant leaves, enabling automated, repeatable, spatially resolved physiological phenotyping beyond passive imaging.
AI.motivation: Most phenotyping platforms rely purely on image-based measurements, which limits characterization to passive observations. Advanced plant characterization requires active physiological sensing modalities such as chlorophyll fluorescence, which has not been integrated into autonomous robotic platforms.
AI.method: The system reconstructs a dense 3D model of the plant from multi-view data, extracts candidate leaf surfaces based on orientation, accessibility, and sensing constraints, then uses a task-level planning framework to generate collision-free trajectories for a robotic manipulator that positions an end-effector at precise contact or near-contact configurations for point-based fluorescence acquisition.
AI.result: The platform demonstrates automated, repeatable, and spatially resolved physiological measurements that go beyond passive imaging by tightly coupling perception, geometric reasoning, and manipulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robotics-driven approach provides high-resolution plant phenotyping capabilities and opens new directions for autonomous agricultural inspection and plant-aware manipulation.

title: Same Model, Different Harness: Different Coding-Agent Results
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Software and study artifacts: https://github.com/sydches/yuj
summary:
A coding agent combines a model with a harness, which decides what the model sees, which tools it can use, and how the work continues. We ask whether changing the harness changes the result when the model and task stay fixed. We compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks. The control supplies the full conversation in time order, while the treatment keeps the same record but mechanically shortens older tool results as the context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work.
  Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. The tight-window Verified comparison uses 169 tasks, a 20,480-token window, and a fixed 480-second attempt endpoint; on this cohort, treatment raises mean per-task F2PF from 28 percent to 49 percent and complete solutions from 43 to 72. Without model-specific retuning, the same frozen treatment also raises both endpoints on the same cohort for three additional models with different designs. In the wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, observed arm outcomes are close on Verified and Pro, while FeatureBench retains a higher mean per-task F2PF under treatment. On the wide-window Verified cohort, treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn. Because changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver.

AI.tldr: A coding agent's harness—not just the model—significantly affects performance. Under tight context windows, automatically shortening older tool results and responding to stalled/repeated work raised fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72 on SWE-bench Verified across 169 tasks, and improved results across three additional models without retuning. This shows the harness and model must be evaluated together as the solver.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the harness component of a coding agent—independent of the model weights—affects benchmark outcomes, given that evaluations typically focus on model choice while the harness (context management, tool access, workflow control) may confound results.
AI.method: The authors compare two configurations of the same harness on three coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, FeatureBench) with the model fixed. The control supplies the full conversation in time order; the treatment mechanically shortens older tool results as context fills and responds to repeated or stalled work. Comparisons include a tight-window setting (169 tasks, 20,480-token window, 480-second endpoint) and wide-window settings, plus cross-model generalization tests with four models of different designs.
AI.result: Under tight context, the treatment raises mean per-task fail-to-pass fraction (F2PF) in all three pressure comparisons and increases complete solutions on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro. On the tight-window Verified cohort, F2PF rises from 28% to 49% and complete solutions from 43 to 72. The frozen treatment also improves both endpoints for three additional models with different designs. In wide-window Qwen3.6 comparisons, arms are close on Verified and Pro, but FeatureBench retains higher F2PF under treatment; treatment also serves fewer prompt tokens per turn in wide-window Verified.
AI.conclusion: Changing the harness changed what unchanged model weights could accomplish, so coding-agent evaluations should treat the model and harness together as the tested solver rather than evaluating the model in isolation.

title: Planning a Shared Modular Fixture Layout Across Robotic Disassembly Stages
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering (T-ASE)
summary: Stable support remains challenging in robotic disassembly of irregularly shaped products. As components are progressively removed, the available support surfaces, mass distribution, and task loads change throughout the process. A fixture layout designed for one workpiece state may therefore become infeasible at later stages, motivating unified support planning over the complete disassembly sequence. This paper presents a modular vacuum-based fixturing system that plans one shared support configuration for the complete disassembly sequence of a screwdriver or shaver, allowing each sequence to proceed without fixture reconfiguration. To search the mixed continuous--discrete layout space under repeated cross-stage evaluation, a denoising diffusion probabilistic model generates physics-informed initial configurations that are refined through Bayesian optimization. Robotic screw and component-removal experiments verified the disassembly feasibility of the planned layouts, while 11 directional-load tests quantified their stability. Comparisons between the measured operational loads and directional responses yielded mean empirical stability margins of 66.9% for the screwdriver and 81.6% for the shaver. These results demonstrate that a product-specific shared layout can provide stable support throughout the tested robotic disassembly sequence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular vacuum-based fixturing system that plans a single shared support configuration for the complete robotic disassembly sequence of irregularly shaped products (screwdriver and shaver), using a denoising diffusion probabilistic model for physics-informed initial layout generation refined via Bayesian optimization. Experiments validated feasibility and stability, achieving mean empirical stability margins of 66.9% (screwdriver) and 81.6% (shaver).
AI.motivation: Stable support during robotic disassembly of irregularly shaped products is challenging because support surfaces, mass distribution, and task loads change as components are removed. A fixture layout optimized for one workpiece state may become infeasible at later stages, motivating the need for unified support planning across the entire disassembly sequence.
AI.method: The approach consists of a modular vacuum-based fixturing system that plans one shared support configuration for the complete disassembly sequence. Layout search operates over a mixed continuous-discrete space under repeated cross-stage evaluations, where a denoising diffusion probabilistic model generates physics-informed initial configurations that are subsequently refined via Bayesian optimization.
AI.result: Robotic screw and component-removal experiments confirmed disassembly feasibility of the planned layouts, and 11 directional-load tests quantified stability. Comparisons between measured operational loads and directional responses yielded mean empirical stability margins of 66.9% for the screwdriver and 81.6% for the shaver.
AI.conclusion: A product-specific shared fixture layout can provide stable support throughout the tested robotic disassembly sequence without requiring mid-process fixture reconfiguration, demonstrating the viability of unified support planning for robotic disassembly of irregularly shaped products.

title: Agent Mesh: Reliability Primitives for Non-Idempotent Agent Delegation - Identity Adequacy and Evidence Adequacy
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables; 5-page ancillary supplement
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly perform bounded software tasks under an orchestrator that retries, resumes, and budgets them. The machinery such orchestrators reach for is the service mesh's: retry, timeout, and error-rate circuit breaking. We report a failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform over 147 numbered incidents spanning 81 runs, each with a measured cost and, in most cases, a mutation proof reproducing the failure. All three assumptions those primitives rest on are violated in practice, and we quantify the consequences: a loop of fifty-four consecutive successful tool calls no error-rate breaker could see; a progress signal constant by construction, guaranteeing a false trip on the third repair round and driving one run from six of six components to three; twenty-one events accumulated across six invocations of one delegation, making a correct, idempotent component unwinnable; a misrouted failure that woke five components for a two-component fault, leaving three bystanders regressing working code; and twelve incidents in which the enforcement layer blocked correct work, the most expensive costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes. We find one cross-cutting cause and its dual. Identity adequacy: in five separate subsystems an identity that failed to discriminate produced a confident wrong answer, and two of them derived the corrective rule independently. Evidence adequacy: a reliability decision may be taken only on evidence capable of moving, attributable to what it measures, and deterministic under identical conditions. From the findings we derive seven reliability primitives whose enforcement unit is the delegation rather than the message, and specify the controlled evaluation the study motivates but does not constitute.

AI.tldr: A failure study of a production agentic software-delivery platform across 147 incidents in 81 runs shows that service-mesh primitives (retry, timeout, error-rate circuit breaking) rest on assumptions violated in practice, revealing cross-cutting causes of identity inadequacy and evidence inadequacy, and motivating seven delegation-level reliability primitives.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents perform bounded software tasks under orchestrators that use service-mesh primitives (retry, timeout, error-rate circuit breaking) for reliability control. This paper investigates whether the assumptions underlying these primitives hold in real agentic software-delivery platforms, and quantifies the consequences when they do not.
AI.method: The study analyzes 147 numbered incidents across 81 runs of a production agentic software-delivery platform, each with measured cost and, in most cases, a mutation proof reproducing the failure. The authors examine how the three service-mesh primitives' assumptions are violated and identify cross-cutting root causes.
AI.result: Key findings include: 54 consecutive successful tool calls undetectable by error-rate breakers; a progress signal that is constant by construction causing a false trip on the third repair round; 21 accumulated events making an idempotent component unwinnable; a misrouted failure waking five components for a two-component fault; and 12 incidents where the enforcement layer blocked correct work (worst costing 107 agent turns and zero accepted writes). Two cross-cutting causes were identified: identity inadequacy (in five subsystems) and evidence inadequacy.
AI.conclusion: The service-mesh reliability primitives are fundamentally mismatched for agentic delegation boundaries. The authors derive seven reliability primitives anchored at the delegation level rather than the message level, and specify a controlled evaluation that this study motivates but does not itself constitute.

title: Task-space model-based control of pneumatic soft actuators
comment: 11 pages, 14 figures
summary: Soft actuators enable dexterous and compliant interaction, but closed-loop task-space control remains challenging due to strong nonlinearities, distributed deformation, and uncertainty in their dynamics. This paper presents a real-time dynamic-model-based task-space feedback and estimation framework based on a non-minimal coordinate discrete elastic rod model formulated in absolute coordinates with holonomic constraints. The resulting structure preserves distributed mechanics while maintaining computational efficiency through sparse system matrices, enabling real-time control with up to 10 discretized rods. A quasi-static feedforward inverse model is combined with a task-space PI controller and a dynamic observer that fuses measurement residuals as virtual forces, enabling full-state estimation from sparse sensing. The approach is experimentally validated on three planar pneumatic soft actuators with varying geometries. Across five tasks, including drawing the digits 0-9 across the workspace (3-18 mm/s tip speed), tracking periodic motion (up to 37 cm/s), cross-platform generalization, reduced sensing conditions, and real-time user-defined references, our method achieves 1.5-2.3 mm root mean square error (RMSE) for precision motions and 5.5-12.4 mm RMSE at 1-2 Hz. Results demonstrate that structured, non-minimal dynamic models can enable real-time, high-precision, moderate-bandwidth task-space control of planar soft pneumatic actuators in free space.

AI.motivation: Closed-loop task-space control of soft actuators is challenging due to strong nonlinearities, distributed deformation, and dynamic uncertainty. Existing approaches lack a real-time dynamic-model-based framework that can preserve distributed mechanics while remaining computationally tractable for control.
AI.method: The framework is built on a non-minimal coordinate discrete elastic rod model in absolute coordinates with holonomic constraints, enabling sparse system matrices for computational efficiency (up to 10 discretized rods in real time). A quasi-static feedforward inverse model provides the reference, a task-space PI controller handles tracking, and a dynamic observer fuses measurement residuals as virtual forces for full-state estimation from sparse sensing.

AI.conclusion: Structured, non-minimal dynamic models can enable real-time, high-precision, moderate-bandwidth task-space control of planar soft pneumatic actuators in free space, demonstrating the viability of physics-based dynamic modeling for soft robot control.

title: LLM Agents for Time-Series: A Survey
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly being developed for time-series problems, but their design choices vary substantially across task settings. This survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that organizes these systems by the time-series problems they address rather than by isolated technical components. We group existing systems into four categories: forecasting and reasoning, augmentation and synthesis, anomaly detection and diagnosis, and decision support. Within each category, we examine how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design. We further summarize representative datasets and environments, and compare reported model performance under shared or closely related settings. Overall, this survey offers a task-oriented guide to designing LLM-based agents for time-series problems and identifies open gaps for future work.

AI.tldr: A problem-driven survey of LLM-based agents for time-series problems, organizing systems into four categories (forecasting/reasoning, augmentation/synthesis, anomaly detection/diagnosis, decision support) and examining how task requirements shape agent architecture, tool use, and memory design.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents for time-series problems have diverse design choices across different task settings, and existing surveys lack a coherent framework for organizing these systems. A problem-driven taxonomy provides a task-oriented guide to better understand and compare these agents.
AI.method: The survey adopts a problem-driven taxonomy that categorizes LLM-based agent systems by the time-series problems they solve: (1) forecasting and reasoning, (2) augmentation and synthesis, (3) anomaly detection and diagnosis, and (4) decision support. Within each category, the survey analyzes how task requirements influence agent architecture, tool use, and memory design, and summarizes representative datasets, environments, and model performance.

title: Tensegrity Continuum Robots Enable Task-Adaptive Morphologies for Cooperative Behaviors
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, Accepted to Nature Machine Intelligence
summary: Robots that can change their morphologies and behaviors for different tasks and environments hold great promise for adaptable, multifunctional systems. Modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) can achieve such functionalities by docking and rearranging individual units, but most rely on rigid modules that lack structural compliance, resulting in limited capabilities. Continuum robots offer compliance through flexible backbones, yet they cannot self-reconfigure into task-adaptive multi-robot configurations. Here, we introduce an MRR that unifies the advantages of both architectures by combining a tensegrity-based compliant body with claw-based connection mechanisms. Each robot can manipulate and locomote independently, and multiple robots can self-reconfigure into different morphologies (e.g., chains, loops, branches) for cooperative manipulation and locomotion. We demonstrate the robots' capability across diverse tasks and environments, including coordinated object manipulation and transport, multimodal locomotion, and loco-manipulation in real-world scenarios. These results lay a foundation for adaptable and multifunctional robotic collectives, with broad potential applications in manufacturing, space exploration, and search-and-rescue operations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel modular reconfigurable robot (MRR) that combines tensegrity-based compliant bodies with claw-based connection mechanisms, unifying the advantages of MRRs and continuum robots. The robots can operate independently or self-reconfigure into various morphologies (chains, loops, branches) for cooperative manipulation, locomotion, and loco-manipulation in real-world scenarios, with applications in manufacturing, space exploration, and search-and-rescue.
AI.motivation: Existing modular reconfigurable robots (MRRs) rely on rigid modules lacking structural compliance, which limits their capabilities, while continuum robots offer compliance but cannot self-reconfigure into task-adaptive multi-robot configurations. This work aims to unify the strengths of both architectures.
AI.method: The approach combines a tensegrity-based compliant body with claw-based connection mechanisms, enabling each robot unit to manipulate and locomote independently while allowing multiple units to self-reconfigure into different morphologies such as chains, loops, and branches for cooperative tasks.
AI.result: The robots demonstrate coordinated object manipulation and transport, multimodal locomotion, and loco-manipulation across diverse tasks and environments in real-world scenarios.

title: The Reasoning Tax: Token Economics of LLM Reasoning Across Task Types and Deployment Contexts
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures and tables, accepted at the 2026 TPCTC Conference and will be published at Performance Evaluation and Benchmarking (Springer)
summary: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable large language models misses a central deployment question: when do extended thinking tokens earn their cost? We introduce the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric that measures the accuracy gain of a reasoning model over a non-reasoning baseline, normalized by the generated-token multiplier. We define paired and approximated TES variants for model families with reasoning toggles and frontier models without direct non-reasoning counterparts. We then conduct an empirical benchmarking analysis across 151 model-benchmark evaluation runs on seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, science reasoning, instruction following, expert knowledge, knowledge recall, and research-level physics. The analysis examines three deployment-facing dimensions: which task structures yield positive marginal reasoning efficiency, how increasing reasoning effort changes TES within model families, and how deployment context changes economic viability. Results show that task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty: sequential inferencechain tasks such as AIME 2025 and LiveCodeBench show high TES, while knowledge-recall tasks such as MMLU-Pro show low TES despite their difficulty. We also find systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. Finally, Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) shows that inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) shows how on-premises deployment can change the economics of otherwise costly reasoning workloads. These findings support a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule: enable reasoning selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treating it as a universally beneficial mode.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Token Economy Score (TES), a marginal benchmarking metric measuring accuracy gain of reasoning models over non-reasoning baselines normalized by token multiplier, with empirical analysis across 151 evaluation runs on 7 benchmarks showing task structure predicts reasoning efficiency better than nominal difficulty.
AI.motivation: Accuracy-only benchmarking of reasoning-capable LLMs fails to address the key deployment question of when extended thinking tokens are worth their cost. There is a need for a metric that captures the marginal value of reasoning in economic terms.
AI.method: Defines TES (paired and approximated variants) for model families with and without reasoning toggles. Conducts empirical benchmarking across 151 model-benchmark runs on seven benchmarks, analyzing three dimensions: task-structure-driven reasoning efficiency, reasoning effort scaling within model families, and deployment context economics. Introduces Reasoning Cost Share (RCS) and Deployment Cost Multiplier (DCM) for cost analysis.
AI.result: Sequential inference-chain tasks (AIME 2025, LiveCodeBench) show high TES while knowledge-recall tasks (MMLU-Pro) show low TES despite difficulty. Systematic diminishing returns at higher reasoning effort levels are found, including cases where additional thinking reduces accuracy. RCS shows inference spend is often dominated by internal thinking, while DCM shows on-premises deployment changes economics of reasoning workloads.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning should be enabled selectively by task type, effort level, and deployment context rather than treated as a universally beneficial mode. This supports a benchmarking-driven model-selection rule for deployment decisions.

title: STEP: State-Aware Task Estimation and Planning with Multi-Modal LLMs for Human-Robot Collaboration
comment: Published in IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN), 2026, 8 pages, 4 figuers, 5 tables
summary: Effective human-robot collaboration in industrial settings requires robots to understand human intentions and assist with task planning, reducing workload. Recent works have explored the use of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MM-LLMs) for task planning in such data-scarce scenarios, leveraging in-context learning to interpret user actions and generate long-horizon action plans in natural language. However, MM-LLMs inherently lack an understanding of system states and do not track state transitions, often leading to hallucinated actions that deviate from the intended goal. Additionally, generating action plans in natural language tends to limit the generated plans to a high level, introducing ambiguity in action execution. To address these limitations, we propose the State-aware Task Estimator and Planner (STEP), which prompts a MM-LLM to explicitly estimate the state of the system and predict the state transitions resulting from executed actions. By forecasting future states alongside actions, STEP ensures task-convergent planning while also providing additional assistance parameters necessary for executing the predicted actions. We evaluate STEP in a simulated environment using a robot assembly task. Our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art by 32.8% in action executability and 14.8% in final-state error.

AI.tldr: STEP is a State-aware Task Estimator and Planner that prompts a Multi-modal Large Language Model to explicitly estimate system states and predict state transitions alongside action generation, improving task-convergent planning for human-robot collaboration. It outperforms SOTA by 32.8% in action executability and 14.8% in final-state error in a simulated robot assembly task.
AI.motivation: MM-LLMs used for task planning in human-robot collaboration lack an understanding of system states and do not track state transitions, leading to hallucinated actions that deviate from the intended goal. Additionally, natural language action plans are often too high-level, introducing ambiguity in execution.
AI.method: STEP prompts a MM-LLM to explicitly estimate the system state and predict state transitions resulting from executed actions. By forecasting future states alongside actions, it ensures task-convergent planning and provides additional assistance parameters needed for executing predicted actions.
AI.result: STEP outperforms the state-of-the-art by 32.8% in action executability and 14.8% in final-state error in a simulated robot assembly environment.

title: 6.5% of the Neuro-Symbolic Literature Can Be Reproduced from Its Published Artifacts, a Six-Stage Audit Framework and First Instantiation
summary: We present a six-stage framework for auditing the reproducibility of scientific claims across a research literature within the computer science domain, and instantiate our framework for the neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI) subdomain. Instantiating the framework on the NSAI subdomain produced a multi-year audit. Stage one retrieved 5,497 records and removed 3,018 duplicates. Stage two screened the 2,479 unique records at title and abstract, identifying 1,365 self-identified NSAI records, then removed a further 61 at full text for off-topic, non-research, no-quantitative-evaluation, or inaccessible-full-text reasons. Stage three sought a verifiable public code artifact for each of the 1,304 eligible records and found none for 849, leaving 455 to enter the artifact inventory and bounded rerun of stages four and five. We fully or partially reproduced 85 studies, 6.52% of the eligible corpus and 18.68% of attempted reruns. We found that 321 attempted reruns were blocked by missing non- code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories. These figures quantify a persistent reproducibility deficit that survives even nominal "code available" declarations, and signal the need for enforced, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles in future NSAI publications. We argue that empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a six-stage framework for auditing reproducibility of scientific claims in computer science and applies it to neuro-symbolic AI (NSAI), finding that only 6.52% of 1,304 eligible studies were fully or partially reproducible, with most failures caused by missing non-code artifacts or unusable code repositories.
AI.motivation: To quantify the persistent reproducibility deficit in NSAI research despite nominal "code available" declarations, and to identify systemic barriers preventing the reproduction of scientific claims.
AI.method: A six-stage audit framework: (1) retrieval of records and deduplication, (2) title/abstract screening for NSAI identification, (3) full-text screening and code artifact verification, (4-5) bounded rerun of eligible studies with artifact inventory, and (6) analysis. Applied to the NSAI subdomain over multiple years.

Of attempted reruns, 85 studies (6.52% of eligible corpus, 18.68% of attempted) were fully or partially reproduced. 321 reruns were blocked by missing non-code artifacts and 42 by missing or unusable code repositories.
AI.conclusion: Empirical NSAI papers should be required at submission time to provide complete, versioned, and permanently archived artifact bundles to address the reproducibility deficit.

title: Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026. Project page: https://bit-pie.github.io/ESRP/ Code: https://github.com/BIT-PIE/ESRP Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/serendipity800/ESRP-PD
summary: This paper introduces Embodied Scene Rearrangement Planning (ESRP), a novel task requiring embodied agents to rearrange furniture in 3D scenes to match a target configuration using only egocentric observations and a top-down target layout. title: SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills
comment: accepted at EMNLP
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents executing complex, long-running procedural skills. Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history. Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

AI.tldr: SKILL.state is a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history in LLM agents with an explicit, mutable execution state, discarding intermediate reasoning after each validated state update. This improves task accuracy and substantially reduces cumulative token consumption across diverse datasets, models, and environments for long-horizon procedural skills.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent runtimes suffer from latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons because they maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history.
AI.method: SKILL.state changes the runtime architecture to feed the model only three components at each step: the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history.
AI.result: Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption compared to append-only conversation history approaches.
AI.conclusion: Explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

title: FlashVLA: Streaming Action Decoding for Fast and Asynchronous VLA Inference
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are increasingly promising for robotic manipulation, yet their real-world deployment remains bottlenecked by high inference latency and unstable asynchronous execution. This challenge is particularly pronounced in flow-matching-based VLA models, where action decoding requires multiple iterative steps conditioned on the VLM context. While efficient inference methods improve control frequency and asynchronous methods reduce execution idle time, existing approaches often fail to jointly achieve low-latency inference and accurate, temporally consistent asynchronous execution. We introduce \textbf{FlashVLA}, a streaming action decoding framework that addresses both challenges in a unified formulation. FlashVLA maintains a streaming action buffer with multiple chunks at different noise levels and decodes them using chunk-wise causal attention. This design allows FlashVLA to produce one executable action chunk per inference step. Moreover, its chunk-wise autoregressive formulation implicitly preserves action continuity, enabling smooth asynchronous execution without extra future-state conditioning. Across extensive simulated and real-world experiments, FlashVLA substantially improves inference speed while maintaining strong task performance. It can achieve $\geq$30\,Hz control frequency on a single GPU with smooth asynchronous inference in real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: FlashVLA is a streaming action decoding framework for Vision-Language-Action models that enables low-latency inference and smooth asynchronous execution by maintaining a streaming action buffer with multiple chunks at different noise levels and decoding them via chunk-wise causal attention, achieving ≥30 Hz control frequency on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: VLA models face real-world deployment bottlenecks due to high inference latency and unstable asynchronous execution, especially in flow-matching-based models requiring multiple iterative decoding steps. Existing efficient inference and asynchronous methods fail to jointly achieve low-latency inference and accurate, temporally consistent execution.
AI.method: FlashVLA maintains a streaming action buffer containing multiple chunks at different noise levels, decoding them using chunk-wise causal attention. This unified formulation produces one executable action chunk per inference step, and the chunk-wise autoregressive design implicitly preserves action continuity without needing extra future-state conditioning, enabling smooth asynchronous execution.
AI.result: In extensive simulated and real-world experiments, FlashVLA substantially improves inference speed while maintaining strong task performance. It achieves ≥30 Hz control frequency on a single GPU with smooth asynchronous inference in real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: FlashVLA demonstrates that jointly addressing inference latency and asynchronous execution consistency is feasible through a unified streaming decoding framework, enabling practical real-world deployment of flow-matching-based VLA models at high control frequencies.

title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
comment: 46 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary information available on request from the authors
summary: Mentalization - the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions to guide one's own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.
