LLMs showed behavioral and computational signatures of mentalizing that varied by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance, and GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive reasoning depth to opponent sophistication, outperforming humans.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have been shown to behave consistently with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, it remains unknown whether these models can actually use mentalization to guide adaptive behavior in strategic decision-making contexts. The paper aims to uncover the latent cognitive strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs and provide a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

Human participants (N=251) were benchmarked as a comparative measure, and recursive depth of reasoning was analyzed as a key cognitive parameter.

title: CLAP: Cross-Embodiment Video World Models are Zero-Shot Physical Simulators
summary: State-of-the-art action-conditioned video models are typically restricted to a single robot embodiment, preventing them from leveraging the vast corpus of heterogeneous video data that contains rich signals for learning generalizable physics. To bridge this gap, we introduce CLAP, a framework for cross-embodiment action-conditioned video generation capable of being trained on diverse, internet-scale videos across human and robotic agents. CLAP is grounded in the insight that universal physical laws govern spatiotemporal dynamics regardless of the actor. However, cross-embodiment learning is non-trivial because action representations vary sharply across robot platforms and are typically absent in human videos. CLAP addresses this fundamental challenge through the following core contributions. First, CLAP reconciles disparate action spaces using end-effector poses, language instructions, and latent actions. Second, to resolve their individual limitations, CLAP introduces a curriculum-based cross-embodiment learning recipe that first learns foundational physical priors across unlabeled video data using latent actions and subsequently grounds them in end-effector action spaces for zero-shot deployment to real-world tasks. Crucially, CLAP approaches or surpasses state-of-the-art single-embodiment video models in challenging environments like DROID. These performance advantages compound via few-shot adaptation to establish a novel paradigm for training single-embodiment video world models. Ultimately, CLAP delivers the most comprehensive suite of action-conditioned video world models to date - spanning diverse action-conditioning spaces (end-effector, language, and latent) and robot morphologies (including cross-embodiment, DROID, Bridge, bimanual YAM robots, and G1 humanoids). We open-source all code and models. Project Website at https://omni-clap.github.io .

AI.tldr: CLAP is a framework for cross-embodiment action-conditioned video generation that trains on diverse internet-scale videos across humans and robots, using end-effector poses, language instructions, and latent actions to reconcile disparate action spaces, with a curriculum-based learning recipe that first learns physical priors from unlabeled video via latent actions then grounds them in end-effector action spaces for zero-shot deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing action-conditioned video models are restricted to a single robot embodiment, preventing them from leveraging heterogeneous video data that contains rich signals for learning generalizable physics. Cross-embodiment learning is challenging because action representations vary sharply across robot platforms and are typically absent in human videos.
AI.method: CLAP reconciles disparate action spaces using three conditioning modalities: end-effector poses, language instructions, and latent actions. It introduces a curriculum-based cross-embodiment learning recipe that first learns foundational physical priors across unlabeled video data using latent actions, then grounds them in end-effector action spaces for zero-shot deployment to real-world tasks.
AI.result: CLAP approaches or surpasses state-of-the-art single-embodiment video models in challenging environments like DROID. Performance advantages compound via few-shot adaptation, establishing a novel paradigm for training single-embodiment video world models. It delivers the most comprehensive suite of action-conditioned video world models to date, spanning diverse action-conditioning spaces and robot morphologies including cross-embodiment, DROID, Bridge, bimanual YAM robots, and G1 humanoids.
AI.conclusion: Cross-embodiment training with a curriculum that separates learning physical priors from action grounding enables video world models to leverage heterogeneous data sources and outperform single-embodiment models, with all code and models open-sourced.

title: Approved Too Late: Verdict Staleness in LLM-Guarded Self-Adaptive Systems
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Autonomic Computing and Self-Organizing Systems (ACSOS 2026)
summary: A large language model (LLM) guardrail for a self-adaptive system (SAS) may issue an approval that is correct at check time but stale by actuation. This creates an Execute-stage time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) hazard. We study verdict freshness: whether a guardrail verdict remains valid when used. We distinguish three quantities that answer different questions: all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. Across five reproducible SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. We introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon from its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without an explicit plant-dynamics model. Using fixed settings documented in the artifact, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. A separate audit of four LLM judges finds nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream. We formulate a freshness contract: every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and addresses the TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) hazard in LLM-based guardrails for self-adaptive systems, where an approval can be correct when issued but stale by the time it is actuated. The authors introduce three distinct freshness metrics, empirically measure verdict staleness across five SAS environments (5.3-48.4% all-candidate verdict change rates), and propose the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS) which reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8%. They also audit LLM judges and formalize a freshness contract requiring approvals to be correct at check time and remain valid at use time.
AI.motivation: LLM guardrails in self-adaptive systems may approve actions that are valid at the moment of checking but become invalid by the time the action is executed, creating a TOCTOU hazard at the Execute stage. Verdict freshness—whether a guardrail's verdict remains valid when used—has not been systematically studied, despite being critical for safety-critical adaptive systems.
AI.method: The authors define three distinct freshness quantities: (1) all-candidate verdict change under fixed-action replay, (2) oracle-labeled approval expiry on recorded closed-loop trajectories, and (3) judge-conditioned use-time invalidity. They evaluate these across five reproducible SAS environments. They then introduce the Freshness-Bounded Shield (FBS), which estimates each approval's validity horizon based on its safe-side margin and recent feature volatility, without requiring an explicit plant-dynamics model. They also conduct a separate audit of four LLM judges.
AI.result: Across five SAS environments, all-candidate verdict-change rates span 5.3-48.4% at a common replay shift of eight simulator steps. With fixed documented settings, FBS reduces oracle-labeled approval-expiry rates from 3.4-24.7% to 0-1.8% at the same shift. The audit of four LLM judges found nonzero judge-conditioned use-time invalidity in every approval stream.
AI.conclusion: Verdict staleness is a real and measurable problem in LLM-guardrailed SAS, but it can be substantially mitigated via the Freshness-Bounded Shield without explicit plant models. The authors formalize a freshness contract—every approval must be correct at check time and remain valid at use time—as a normative requirement for trustworthy LLM guardrails in self-adaptive systems.

title: FaithSieve: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Math Proofs with Faithful Formal Evidence
comment: 32 pages, 3 figures; preprint with appendix and supplementary experimental details
summary: Large language models can now generate complex, multi-step mathematical proofs, but reliably determining their correctness and localizing early logical errors remains a critical challenge. Existing evaluation approaches largely depend on model-based natural-language judgments, which often overlook local reasoning gaps. While formal theorem provers like Lean offer a path to rigorous verification, using them to evaluate informal text requires solving locality and semantic mismatches: a prover might bypass a local flaw by proving an overly broad target, or validate an auto-formalized statement that drifts from the original mathematical intent. To address this, we introduce FaithSieve, a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs. FaithSieve decomposes coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracts typed proof obligations, and verifies them through a formal evaluation agent. Formal validation is gated by semantic alignment scoring, so Lean evidence is incorporated only when the formal statement faithfully preserves the context, objects, and logical form of the original claim. We construct two expert-verified datasets, ProofLoc-Olympiad and ProofLoc-University, to benchmark first-error localization. On the 350-problem Olympiad dataset, FaithSieve using a GPT-5.4 backbone achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy, outperforming the direct-judging baseline of 72.29%. Furthermore, on the 200-problem ProofLoc-University benchmark spanning six advanced domains, FaithSieve reaches 84.5% exact accuracy, compared to 75.0% for the direct judge. Our work demonstrates that decomposing proofs into fine-grained units and grounding them with faithful formal evidence significantly improves reliable evaluation of natural-language reasoning.

AI.tldr: FaithSieve is a Lean-assisted framework for fine-grained evaluation of natural-language mathematical proofs, decomposing coarse proof steps into local reasoning units, extracting typed proof obligations, and verifying them through a formal evaluation agent gated by semantic alignment scoring. It achieves 81.43% exact first-error accuracy on an Olympiad dataset and 84.5% on a university-level benchmark, outperforming direct-judging baselines.

While formal theorem provers like Lean offer rigorous verification, they face locality and semantic mismatch challenges: a prover may bypass local flaws by proving an overly broad target, or validate auto-formalized statements that drift from the original mathematical intent.

title: Decoupling Planning and Control for Instructable Agents
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. Project page: https://zinengtang.github.io/instruct-to-act/
summary: Recent work shows that pre-trained, instruction-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) perform well at mapping from instructions and observations to high-level plans, but struggle to realize such plans as reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments. At the same time, world-model controllers excel at fast observation-to-action control, but lack open-ended task guidance. In this work, we combine these strengths into a single system, Instruct-to-Act, where we train a world-model controller to act autonomously at high frequency when conditioned on sparse, higher-latency, and high-level text instructions generated by a VLM planner. To train controllers to be language-instructable, we relabel segments of controller policy rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective along with existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. We evaluate our proposed approach across seven embodied environments, including three multi-agent environments where VLM planners coordinate through language while trained controllers serve as their actuators. Under matched observation and action spaces, our decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation variants, preserves fast control, and lets us swap in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Instruct-to-Act, a system combining a VLM planner for high-level instruction generation with a world-model controller for high-frequency, low-latency action execution. Controllers are trained to follow language instructions via relabeled rollouts and a behavior-cloning objective, outperforming controller-only and direct VLM action-generation approaches across seven embodied environments.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained instruction-tuned VLMs excel at high-level planning from instructions and observations but struggle with reliable low-latency action sequences in unfamiliar environments, while world-model controllers handle fast observation-to-action control but lack open-ended task guidance. The goal is to combine these complementary strengths into a single system.
AI.method: (1) Train a world-model controller conditioned on sparse, higher-latency text instructions generated by a VLM planner, acting autonomously at high frequency. (2) Relabel segments of controller rollouts with synthetic instructions and jointly optimize a behavior-cloning objective alongside existing reward-maximizing and world-modeling objectives. (3) The decoupled design allows swapping in different pretrained VLM planners without fine-tuning.
AI.result: Evaluated across seven embodied environments (including three multi-agent ones), the decoupled approach consistently outperforms controller-only and direct VLM action-generation baselines, preserves fast control, supports interchangeable VLM planners without fine-tuning, and remains competitive with strong vision-language-action and multi-agent RL baselines on six of seven tasks.
AI.conclusion: The Instruct-to-Act framework effectively bridges high-level language planning and low-level control by making world-model controllers language-instructable, achieving strong performance and flexibility while maintaining high-frequency control in embodied tasks.

title: ProofEvolve: Neuro-Symbolic Evolution for Formal Automated Theorem Proving
summary: Automated theorem proving offers a natural foundation for recursive self-improvement in scientific discovery. However, existing neural provers do not fully preserve this recursive structure, where the learning process should be self-improving over time. Existing methods either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. In addition, these methods also heavily rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, even when unsuccessful partial attempts contain useful discoveries. To close the gap, we propose ProofEvolve, a neuro-symbolic framework that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures with neural models to decisively expand the knowledge boundary. In this framework, the neural model proposes variation operators, including decompositions, repairs, and schema recombinations. The symbolic Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. Over the evolution loops, ProofEvolve computes verified closure over the resulting proof directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Within each problem, ProofEvolve evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive. Across problems, kernel-checked schema extraction adds newly proved sub-DAGs to a persistent schema library. Proof DAGs inherit the solved results through typed schema recombination, with every residual premise exposed as a new subgoal. This evolutionary process preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness. Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.

AI.tldr: ProofEvolve is a neuro-symbolic framework for automated theorem proving that evolves explicit, formally verified symbolic proof structures (DAGs) with neural models. It preserves verified results from incomplete attempts via kernel-checked schema extraction and behavioral archiving, achieving the highest average solve rate across three competition-level Lean benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural provers do not fully preserve the recursive self-improving structure of theorem proving. They either embed proof experience into model parameters through expensive weight updates, or keep verified intermediate deductions only within the current problem. Moreover, they rely on sparse whole-proof feedback, discarding useful discoveries from unsuccessful partial attempts.
AI.method: ProofEvolve combines neural models with a symbolic Lean kernel. Neural models propose variation operators (decompositions, repairs, schema recombinations) while the Lean kernel verifies every proof transition. It computes verified closure over proof DAGs, evolves partial AND-OR proof DAGs in a behaviorally indexed archive within each problem, and extracts kernel-checked schemas into a persistent library across problems. Typed schema recombination inherits solved results while exposing residual premises as new subgoals.
AI.result: Across three competition-level Lean benchmarks, ProofEvolve achieves the highest average solve rate among the evaluated proof systems.
AI.conclusion: The evolutionary neuro-symbolic approach preserves verified results from incomplete attempts and makes them available for later proofs without weakening formal soundness, enabling decisive expansion of the knowledge boundary in automated theorem proving.

title: Fine-Tuning of Transformer models with Frames
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures
summary: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are effective solutions for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models; however, their memory requirements scale with the size of the model, $\mathcal{O}(dr)$, where $d$ is the model's hidden dimension and $r$ is the rank. Our proposal, FrameFT, models the parameter update $ΔW$ with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis. Fusion Frames can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers, enabling very efficient updates. Only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion are stored/optimized, reducing the memory footprint. The sparse structure of the coefficient matrix in FrameFT and the sparsity in the Fusion Frames give large compute benefits, and our analysis provides formal convergence results. We evaluate the idea across a suite of supervised fine-tuning benchmarks, focusing on language tasks, but also report application to vision models. Our experiments show that FrameFT achieves performance on par with/exceeding state-of-the-art PEFT techniques, but needs far fewer trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: FrameFT is a novel parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that updates model weights using a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis, reducing memory footprint compared to LoRA and achieving state-of-the-art performance with far fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT strategies like LoRA have memory requirements that scale with model size (O(dr)), which limits their efficiency for large-scale pre-trained models. There is a need for a more memory-efficient approach to fine-tuning.
AI.method: FrameFT models parameter updates (ΔW) with a sparse coefficient matrix in a Fusion Frame basis, which can be generated algorithmically and shared across model layers. It stores/optimizes only the sparse coefficients of the basis expansion, and leverages sparsity in both the coefficient matrix and Fusion Frames for compute benefits, with formal convergence guarantees.
AI.result: FrameFT matches or exceeds state-of-the-art PEFT techniques across supervised fine-tuning benchmarks (language tasks and vision models) while requiring far fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: The Fusion Frame-based approach to PEFT provides a memory-efficient alternative to methods like LoRA that scales better with model size while maintaining or improving performance.

title: Don't Overthink, Don't Underthink: Toward Adaptive Reasoning in Agentic AI
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown that increased inference-time reasoning can improve performance on complex tasks. However, many existing approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls, such as fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, or activation-space interventions, and are often evaluated on standalone reasoning benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions may not hold in agentic AI systems, where reasoning requirements evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions. Consequently, reasoning can become either excessive or insufficient, resulting in unnecessary computation, increased latency, planning drift, excessive tool use, or incomplete solutions. We argue that a major challenge for next-generation agentic AI is not merely how much reasoning a language model should perform, but how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands. We characterize over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning and evaluate them on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark. Using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness, our results suggest that cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, whereas cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions. These findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that adaptive reasoning allocation—not just the amount of reasoning—is the key challenge for next-generation agentic AI. It characterizes over-reasoning and under-reasoning as failure modes of misallocated reasoning, evaluating them on MATH-500 and GAIA benchmarks using metrics such as tool-decision latency, token consumption, and answer correctness, finding that over-reasoning incurs high computational cost without proportional accuracy gains while under-reasoning leads to incorrect or incomplete solutions.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM reasoning approaches rely on fixed or preallocated reasoning controls (fixed token budgets, pre-execution difficulty estimates, activation-space interventions) and are evaluated on standalone benchmarks rather than full agentic workflows. These assumptions break in agentic systems where reasoning demands evolve dynamically through planning, tool use, memory retrieval, and agent-to-agent interactions, leading to either excessive or insufficient reasoning.
AI.method: The paper defines and operationalizes over-reasoning and under-reasoning as recurring failure modes of misallocated reasoning in agentic AI. It evaluates these phenomena on MATH-500 and the GAIA public validation benchmark, using tool-decision latency, token consumption, token-limit exhaustion, and answer correctness as evaluation metrics.
AI.result: Cases classified as over-reasoning are associated with higher computational cost without proportional accuracy gains, while cases classified as under-reasoning are consistently associated with incorrect or incomplete solutions.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate future research on adaptive reasoning mechanisms for agentic AI, shifting the focus from how much reasoning an LLM should perform to how it should allocate reasoning according to evolving task demands.

title: PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Long-horizon agent runs generate experience that can improve both the current run and future work. Most self-improvement methods process this experience only after execution ends, so they cannot redirect the active run or immediately apply and validate lessons learned from it. We argue that self-improvement should instead be live, using emerging experience both to redirect the active run and to update the persistent harness. Existing agent architectures do not fully support this goal. Single-agent self-correction combines task execution and trajectory assessment within one context, while subagent delegation separates execution but typically cannot redirect an active subagent. We present PILOT, a supervisor-worker harness for live self-improvement through two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering lets a separate supervisor redirect or abort the active worker during execution; and (2) live self-evolution distils procedures and failure modes revealed during execution into reusable skills and memory. Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, PILOT outperforms counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In the self-improvement setting, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens fall by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens rise by 110.3% and 134.0%, respectively.

AI.tldr: PILOT is a supervisor-worker harness enabling live self-improvement for long-horizon agent runs through live steering (redirecting/aborting active workers) and live self-evolution (distilling procedures and failure modes into reusable skills and memory). Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, it ranks first in five of six configurations, outperforming counterparts by up to 9.8 points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with significant gains in self-improvement settings and token efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing self-improvement methods only process experience after execution ends, preventing redirection or immediate validation of lessons within the active run. Single-agent self-correction conflates execution and assessment in one context, while subagent delegation cannot redirect active subagents. The authors argue that self-improvement should be live—using emerging experience to both steer the ongoing run and update persistent harnesses.
AI.method: PILOT employs a supervisor-worker architecture with two coupled mechanisms: (1) live steering, where a separate supervisor can redirect or abort the active worker mid-execution; and (2) live self-evolution, which distills procedures and failure modes observed during execution into reusable skills and memory components.
AI.result: Across two frozen backbones (GLM-5.1 and Kimi-K2.6) and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six configurations. On Terminal-Bench 2.0 it beats counterpart harnesses by up to 9.8 percentage points. In self-improvement settings, PILOT gains 14.6 points with GLM-5.1 and 12.4 points with Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens drop by 42.9% and 47.4%, while successful evaluations per million output tokens increase by 110.3% and 134.0% for the two backbones respectively.
AI.conclusion: Live self-improvement—combining real-time steering of active runs with ongoing distillation of experience into persistent harness assets—yields superior performance and substantially better token efficiency compared to post-hoc self-improvement approaches.

title: Multi2AV-Safety: Benchmarking Safety in Multimodal-to-Audio-Video Generation
summary: Audio-video generation is rapidly moving from prompt-driven synthesis toward multimodal conditioning, where text, images, audio, and video can jointly shape the generated output. This shift changes the nature of safety evaluation: harmful intent may no longer reside in any single input, but instead emerge from how otherwise benign or weakly harmful conditions interact across modalities and time. Existing safety benchmarks, however, remain largely prompt-centric or tied to fixed conditioning interfaces, leaving such compositional risks difficult to study systematically. To bridge this gap, we introduce Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark, to the best of our knowledge, to cover all 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances. Evaluation on Multi2AV-Safety reveals systematic weaknesses in representative multimodal safety guards across attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures. Our evaluation reveals two complementary failure modes: harmful semantics can emerge from the combination of individually benign inputs, while explicit harmful cues can become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. Together, these results identify \emph{compositional risk perception} as a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation: current safety guards fail to reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time, even when all conditioning inputs are observable. The dataset will be publicly released in October 2026.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark covering all 11 non-singleton text/image/audio/video conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, comprising 11,024 attack instances. Evaluation reveals that multimodal safety guards fail at compositional risk perception—harmful semantics emerge from benign input combinations, and explicit harmful cues become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. The dataset will be released in October 2026.
AI.motivation: Audio-video generation is shifting from prompt-driven synthesis to multimodal conditioning, where safety risks can emerge from interactions across modalities and time rather than residing in any single input. Existing safety benchmarks are prompt-centric and tied to fixed conditioning interfaces, making it impossible to systematically study these compositional risks.
AI.method: The authors construct Multi2AV-Safety, the first safety benchmark spanning all 11 non-singleton T/I/A/V conditioning configurations for audio-video generation, containing 11,024 attack instances. They evaluate representative multimodal safety guards across different attack mechanisms and harm-evidence structures.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals two complementary failure modes: (1) harmful semantics can emerge from combining individually benign inputs, and (2) explicit harmful cues become harder to detect when mixed with benign multimodal context. These findings demonstrate that current safety guards cannot reliably integrate safety evidence across modalities and time even when all inputs are observable.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies compositional risk perception as a central capability gap in safeguarding multimodal-conditioned audio-video generation, and will publicly release the dataset in October 2026 to facilitate further research.

title: DuMateBench: Evaluating Autonomous Agents in Complex Real-World Workflows
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly adopted to complete complex, multi-tool workflows in real-world settings. However, existing benchmarks typically separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate agents in environments that are cleaner and more stable than those encountered in practice. We introduce DuMateBench, a real-session benchmark reconstructed from anonymized and privacy-screened user sessions collected from a large-scale production agent platform. Each task preserves the relevant pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, and is then validated through human verification. The resulting benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning 8 broad scenarios and 17 fine-grained capability categories, with most tasks requiring multiple capability coordination. We execute these tasks in isolated Docker containers injected with three forms of real-world environmental complexity: Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy, and assess performance using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol. Experiments across five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial gaps in strict task completion. Complementary robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses further show that performance under environmental perturbations is jointly shaped by the capabilities of the LLM and the surrounding agent framework. The code and data are publicly available at https://dumatebench.com/.

AI.tldr: DuMateBench is a real-session benchmark for autonomous multi-tool agents, reconstructed from anonymized production user sessions. It comprises 200 human-validated tasks across 8 scenarios and 17 capability categories, executed in isolated Docker containers with three forms of real-world environmental complexity (Insufficient, Unstable, Noisy), and evaluated via a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge protocol. Experiments across five agent frameworks and four LLMs reveal significant gaps in strict task completion.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous agent benchmarks separate tasks by application or capability and evaluate in cleaner, more stable environments than real-world deployments, failing to reflect the practical complexity agents face in production multi-tool workflows.
AI.method: The benchmark is built from anonymized and privacy-screened production user sessions, preserving pre-solution interaction history, persistent configurations, and workspace state, with human verification of each task. Tasks are executed in isolated Docker containers augmented with Insufficient, Unstable, and Noisy environmental perturbations, and scored using a hybrid deterministic and LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Evaluation of five representative autonomous-agent frameworks paired with four state-of-the-art LLMs shows substantial gaps in strict task completion. Robustness, efficiency, and diagnostic analyses reveal that performance under environmental perturbations depends jointly on the LLM's capabilities and the surrounding agent framework.
AI.conclusion: DuMateBench provides a realistic, reproducible benchmark revealing that current agent systems fall short in strict task completion under real-world environmental complexity, and that both the LLM and agent framework co-determine robustness, motivating further research on resilient multi-tool agent design.

title: AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling
comment: 31 Pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables, Accepted as a main conference paper at EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.

AI.tldr: AgentJudgeBench is the first benchmark for systematically studying LLM-as-a-judge reliability on agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, revealing that judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty (1.5x faster without ground truth) and that all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% accuracy band on hard queries without ground truth, exposing structural ceilings that model capacity alone cannot overcome. The study also finds that ground-truth exposure can reduce alignment for some judges (over-anchoring), chain-of-thought and temperature have negligible effects, and structured rubrics help up to 6.5 pp but don't generalize uniformly.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are widely deployed for evaluating agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability specifically on structured, dependency-driven (DAG-based) workflows has never been systematically examined, as existing work focuses on open-ended text or preference evaluation.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances across six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generator models (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judge models (20B to frontier scale), under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions, plus a human validation study and multiple mitigation strategies (chain-of-thought, judge temperature, structured rubrics).
AI.result: Judge alignment degrades monotonically with difficulty and 1.5x faster without ground truth; all six judges converge to a 77-82% band on hard no-ground-truth queries regardless of scale. Ground-truth exposure reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9pp). Chain-of-thought and temperature are negligible; structured rubrics improve up to 6.5 pp but don't generalize. With ground truth QwQ-32B best matches programmatic reference; GPT-OSS-120B is most human-aligned; without ground truth frontier judges lead only marginally.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM judges have fundamental limitations when evaluating agentic tool-calling on structured workflows—primarily driven by task difficulty rather than model scale—and the paper provides practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems, including the nuanced use of ground truth and structured rubrics.

title: SIGMA: Structured Noise-Effect-Aware Grouped Multi-Agent Aggregation
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces significant challenges in maintaining robust coordination under noisy observations. Although observation disturbances are often introduced independently across agents, their downstream effects on cooperative decision-making can become structured through underlying cooperation structures. We characterize this phenomenon as structured noise effects, where noise-induced decision effects exhibit local correlation among agents with stronger task-related dependencies while remaining globally heterogeneous across different agents and local structures. Existing robust MARL methods, however, rarely explicitly characterize or exploit such structure-dependent noise effects. To address this limitation, we propose SIGMA, a hierarchical collaboration framework that exploits cooperation structures to learn robust representations under noisy observations. SIGMA first organizes agents into adaptive local structures through density-based grouping and performs intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific representation deviations. Inter-group attention then adaptively integrates information across different groups to preserve global coordination while accommodating their heterogeneous contributions. Experiments on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II empirically validate the structured noise effects and demonstrate that SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.

AI.tldr: SIGMA is a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that exploits cooperation structures to learn robust representations under noisy observations, using density-based grouping for intra-group consensus aggregation and inter-group attention for global coordination.
AI.motivation: Existing robust MARL methods rarely explicitly characterize or exploit structure-dependent noise effects, where noise-induced decision effects exhibit local correlation among agents with stronger task-related dependencies while remaining globally heterogeneous across different agents and local structures.
AI.method: SIGMA organizes agents into adaptive local structures via density-based grouping, performs intra-group consensus aggregation to preserve shared task-relevant information while smoothing agent-specific representation deviations, and uses inter-group attention to adaptively integrate information across groups for global coordination.
AI.result: Experiments on noisy-observation tasks in StarCraft II empirically validate the structured noise effects and show SIGMA consistently improves robustness under observation noise while maintaining competitive performance in noise-free environments.
AI.conclusion: SIGMA demonstrates that explicitly exploiting cooperation structures can effectively address structured noise effects in cooperative MARL, improving robustness without sacrificing performance in noise-free settings.

title: Relational Over-Regularization: Graph-Based AI-Generated Text Detection via Sentence Transition Deviation
comment: Presented in EMNLP 2026
summary: Detecting AI-generated text (AIGT) remains challenging because existing approaches rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, causing them to overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. We identify a structural signal at the sentence-pair level: LLMs produce inter-sentence transition variance that deviates from human writing through inflated variance driven by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions. We formalize this as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR) and validate it across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). The central contribution is this relational problem formulation, not a novel GNN architecture; CSFG is one concrete instantiation for operationalizing ROR. To exploit this signal, we propose the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework that encodes positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. The per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds and acts as a false-positive calibrator. CSFG achieves 97.14% accuracy under binary detection, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 pp, with a false-positive rate of 1.57% and robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime; detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel structural signal for detecting AI-generated text—inter-sentence transition variance at the sentence-pair level—formalized as Relational Over-Regularization (ROR). The authors propose a graph-based framework, Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), that encodes this signal as learnable GNN edge features, achieving 97.14% accuracy and robust generalization to unseen LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing AIGT detection methods rely on token-level statistical signals or independent stylometric features, which overfit to specific generators and fail under distribution shift. A more structural, relational signal is needed to robustly distinguish AI-generated text from human writing.
AI.method: The paper formalizes Relational Over-Regularization (ROR)—inflated inter-sentence transition variance caused by recurring similarity bursts at paragraph boundaries and templated transitions in LLM text. The authors construct the Cross-Source Stylometric Fingerprint Graph (CSFG), a graph-based framework encoding positional, sequential, semantic, and transition deviation signals as learnable GNN edge features. A per-edge signed deviation δ_ij operationalizes ROR without hand-crafted thresholds, serving as a false-positive calibrator.
AI.result: CSFG achieves 97.14% binary detection accuracy, outperforming the strongest graph-based baseline by 11.14 percentage points, with a false-positive rate of 1.57%. It demonstrates robust generalization to unseen LLMs in the inflated-variance regime, though detection degrades for generators whose transition variance falls at or below the human baseline.
AI.conclusion: The relational problem formulation of ROR is validated across four benchmarks (p < 0.001). CSFG serves as one concrete instantiation for operationalizing this signal. The approach excels in the inflated-variance regime but has limitations for generators with transition variance comparable to or lower than human writing.

title: Five Primitives for Governing Autonomous AI Agents at Runtime
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Describes an implemented system in private pilot deployment; four of five primitives implemented
summary: Enterprise deployments of autonomous AI agents inherit a control model built for human users and long-lived services, and the fit fails in three specific ways: agent principals are ephemeral, appearing and vanishing faster than provisioning; their actions are selected by a model rather than programmed, so the set of things they may attempt is not known in advance; and the population is discovered rather than provisioned, because anyone who can call an API can create one. We argue that governing such agents is a runtime problem -- not a model-alignment problem and not a build-time problem -- and we derive five primitives from the questions that must be answered before an action takes effect and after it has: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain. For each we state what fails if it is absent and why the others cannot structurally supply it. We describe an implementation in which an agent's action is mediated against policy before it takes effect, authorised against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger a third party can verify with the vendor out of the loop. We report what the architecture costs: the enforcement point sits on the request's critical path, identity requires a sidecar per workload, and fail-closed mediation converts availability incidents into denial. We are explicit about implementation status: four primitives are built and running in private pilots, and the fifth is built as separate tooling and not yet integrated into the request path. We keep it in the set deliberately: a five-part decomposition that exactly matches what its authors happened to build is not a taxonomy but a description of a codebase.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that governing autonomous AI agents in enterprise deployments is fundamentally a runtime problem, not a model-alignment or build-time problem. It derives five primitives—discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain—from the questions that must be answered before and after an action takes effect, and describes an implementation where agent actions are mediated against policy, authorized against per-tenant action vocabularies, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger verifiable by third parties.
AI.motivation: Enterprise deployments of autonomous AI agents inherit a control model built for human users and long-lived services, which fails in three specific ways: agent principals are ephemeral and appear/vanished faster than provisioning; their actions are model-selected rather than programmed, so the action set is unknown in advance; and the population is discovered rather than provisioned since anyone who can call an API can create an agent. This mismatch motivates a new governance framework.
AI.method: The authors argue governance is a runtime problem and derive five primitives from questions that must be answered before an action takes effect and after it has: discovery, identity, governance, attestation, and supply chain. They describe an implementation where an agent's action is mediated against policy before taking effect, authorized against a per-tenant action vocabulary, and recorded in a hash-linked signed ledger that a third party can verify without the vendor. They report architectural costs including enforcement on the critical path, sidecar identity per workload, and fail-closed mediation converting availability incidents into denial.
AI.result: The architecture enforces policy mediation before an action takes effect, authorizes against per-tenant action vocabularies, and records actions in a hash-linked signed ledger verifiable by third parties out-of-loop from the vendor. Four primitives are built and running in private pilots; the fifth (supply chain) is built as separate tooling but not yet integrated into the request path. The authors explicitly keep the incomplete primitive in the set to avoid describing a codebase rather than a taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: The five-part decomposition forms a principled taxonomy for runtime governance of autonomous agents, and the authors deliberately retain the not-yet-integrated supply chain primitive to ensure the framework reflects conceptual completeness rather than implementation convenience.

title: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
summary: We present an extension and comprehensive real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system designed to accelerate end-to-end scientific research across hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript generation. Moving beyond in silico hypothesis generation, this specialized configuration transitions Co-Scientist into an execution-grounded research partner advancing closed-loop scientific workflows across materials science, biology, and computer science. In materials science, Co-Scientist interfaced with a semi-automated chemical vapor deposition reactor to design a safe precursor route for MXenes; experimental execution produced a lamellar 2D material sharing key structural similarities with the Ti3C2Tx MXene lattice, although further experiments are needed to confirm the atomic structure. Leveraging Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid, lab-in-the-loop execution, it also tailored growth recipes to laboratory constraints in minutes, enabling single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 semiconductors. In biology, Co-Scientist predicted emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli across inducer (IPTG) gradients from sparse imaging data, quantitatively matching unpublished wet-lab morphological measurements. In computer science, Co-Scientist autonomously discovered an inference-time scaling architecture that outperformed six frontier models on HealthBench (Hard and Professional) while reducing potential clinical harm under blinded physician evaluation. Finally, a double-blind study of end-to-end generated papers with 30 domain experts across 450 reviews demonstrates that Co-Scientist's reliability modules reduce hallucination and plagiarism while improving research safety. Together, these results demonstrate progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an extension and comprehensive real-world validation of Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based multi-agent system for end-to-end scientific research. It demonstrates execution-grounded capabilities across three domains: materials science (MXene synthesis via semi-automated CVD reactor, monolayer MoS2/MoSe2/WS2 growth), biology (predicting E. coli swarming phenotypes matching wet-lab data), and computer science (discovering an inference-time scaling architecture outperforming six frontier models). A double-blind study with 30 experts and 450 reviews shows reliability modules reduce hallucination and plagiarism. Results demonstrate progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI.
AI.motivation: To move Co-Scientist beyond in silico hypothesis generation into an execution-grounded research partner that can advance closed-loop scientific workflows across multiple disciplines, and to comprehensively validate its real-world utility.
AI.method: Extends Co-Scientist with a specialized configuration for execution-grounded research. In materials science, interfaces with a semi-automated CVD reactor for MXene precursor design and uses Gemini 3 Deep Think for lab-in-the-loop growth recipe adaptation. In biology, predicts E. coli swarming phenotypes from sparse imaging data. In computer science, autonomously discovers inference-time scaling architectures. Includes reliability modules evaluated via double-blind peer review.
AI.result: Materials: produced lamellar 2D material similar to Ti3C2Tx MXene lattice (further confirmation needed); single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2. Biology: quantitative predictions matched unpublished wet-lab measurements. CS: discovered architecture outperformed six frontier models on HealthBench while reducing clinical harm. Double-blind study: 30 experts, 450 reviews confirmed reduced hallucination and plagiarism with improved research safety.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate meaningful progress toward closed-loop multi-agent scientific AI systems capable of accelerating real-world scientific discovery across multiple disciplines, with validated reliability in outputs.

title: Style as a Confound: False Positives in AI Detection of Non-Native Academic Writing
comment: Presented in EMNLP 2026
summary: AI text detectors are increasingly employed in academic settings, but it remains unclear whether their outputs reflect AI authorship itself or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. Previous studies have reported high false-positive rates (FPRs) for non-native English writing, but population-level comparisons confound authorship with differences in topic, domain, and writing style. Professional editing provides a useful setting for examining this issue because it changes the linguistic form of manuscripts while preserving authorship and content. We examined 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, to assess how editing affects detector responses controlling for content and authorship. For the 13 AI text detectors, FPRs for human-written texts varied widely, from 0.0% to 100.0%. Responses varied across detectors: the same edits increased AI scores in some detectors but decreased them in others. Notably, score changes correlated with the extent of editing. The findings identify professional editing style as a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs, rather than establishing a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, raising concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings.

AI.tldr: This paper examines 135,389 manuscript pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025) to determine whether AI text detector outputs reflect actual AI authorship or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. By holding authorship and content constant while varying only the linguistic form through professional editing, the study finds that editing style is a key confounding variable in detector outputs, with false-positive rates ranging from 0.0% to 100.0% across 13 detectors.
AI.motivation: Previous studies reported high false-positive rates for non-native English writing in AI detectors, but these population-level comparisons confounded authorship with topic, domain, and writing style. The authors aim to isolate whether detector outputs reflect AI authorship itself or merely linguistic features of polished academic English, which has direct implications for fairness and reliability of AI detectors in academic settings.
AI.method: The study uses a within-subject design leveraging professional editing as a natural experiment: 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018-2025), each consisting of a non-native manuscript and its native-edited version. This controls for authorship and content while varying linguistic form. Thirteen AI text detectors were applied to both versions, and changes in AI scores were analyzed in relation to the extent of editing.
AI.result: False-positive rates for human-written texts varied widely across detectors, from 0.0% to 100.0%. The same edits produced inconsistent directional responses: some detectors showed increased AI scores while others showed decreased scores. Score changes were correlated with the degree of editing applied, indicating that the magnitude of linguistic modification systematically influences detector outputs.
AI.conclusion: Professional editing style is identified as a key confounding variable in AI text detector outputs. The study does not establish a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, meaning detectors cannot reliably distinguish AI authorship from polished human writing. This raises significant concerns about fairness and reliability when AI detectors are used in academic settings.

title: Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training
summary: Large language models offer broad capabilities, but adapting them to evolving domains, tools, and requirements often entails repeated post-training. Autonomous systems automate parts of this process by proposing updates, training candidates, and using evaluation feedback to select subsequent proposals. As evidence accumulates, a central problem emerges: which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training has changed the parent model? An update's effect depends on its parent, data, and training stage. Treating past success as context-free permission can waste compute. If the resulting child is promoted, it can also degrade the subsequent training trajectory. We formulate this problem as conditional experience transfer and introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training. BCIT binds an observed effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed. Fully trained candidates still face a shared adoption rule, and only observed events extend memory. On one 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates exhibit heterogeneous target and retention effects across the evaluated contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives. These results support treating experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a core problem in autonomous post-training of LLMs: when accumulating evidence from past update attempts, an update's effectiveness is conditional on its parent model, data, and training stage. The authors introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training by binding observed effects to their source contexts, checking applicability conditions, vetoing named hard conflicts, and using bounded training trials when needed. Evaluated on a 4B model across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and achieves higher equal-budget final-model quality than alternatives.
AI.motivation: As autonomous systems accumulate evidence from repeated post-training iterations, past update success cannot be treated as context-free permission—the same update may have different effects depending on its parent model, data, and training stage. Misinterpreting past success wastes compute (in non-beneficial retraining) and can degrade subsequent training trajectories if harmful children get promoted.
AI.method: BCIT (Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer) operates before weight-changing training: it binds each observed update effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions for reuse, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and when uncertain, obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial. Fully trained candidates share a single adoption rule, and only observed events extend the memory of what is actionable.
AI.result: On a 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates showed heterogeneous target and retention effects across contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorized fewer harmful updates and achieved higher equal-budget final-model quality compared to the evaluated baseline alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The results support treating experience authorization as a distinct and important problem in autonomous post-training—separate from proposal generation and training—since correctly deciding whether past evidence is still actionable is crucial for compute efficiency and final model quality.

title: Graph-Guided Selective Unlearning for Language Models: Controlling Support Routes Beyond Forget Seeds
summary: Enterprises fine-tune language models on proprietary data that may later require removal due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations. Selective unlearning removes requested knowledge while preserving model utility, offering a practical alternative to full retraining, but existing methods treat the explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope. This is insufficient when target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. We propose GRAPHSU, a graph-guided controller that expands the deletion scope beyond forget seeds by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors. On the Task of Fictitious Unlearning (TOFU), a synthetic author-profile question-answering benchmark, and PISTOL, a structural-unlearning benchmark built around interconnected factual samples, with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over a matched seed-only baseline, demonstrating that effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes, not just forget seeds.

AI.tldr: GRAPHSU is a graph-guided controller for selective unlearning in language models that expands the deletion scope beyond explicitly identified forget examples by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors, achieving up to 49.5 percentage points lower leakage than seed-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing selective unlearning methods treat explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope, which is insufficient because target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. This poses a risk for enterprises required to remove data due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations.
AI.method: GRAPHSU constructs a weighted support-route graph from the forget seeds, propagates deletion pressure through the graph, and applies graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighboring examples, thereby expanding the deletion scope beyond the original forget seeds.
AI.result: Evaluated on TOFU and PISTOL benchmarks with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GRAPHSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points compared to a matched seed-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes in addition to forget seeds, demonstrating that graph-aware expansion of the deletion scope is critical for robust selective unlearning.

title: AgentFold: Closed-Loop Agentic Search for Protein Folding Model Design
summary: Scientific LLM agents have shown promise in literature reasoning, tool use, and experiment planning, but it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific machine-learning systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. We study this question in protein folding, where progress requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation. We present AgentFold, a multi-agent framework that formulates folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, AgentFold proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates model variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores both successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches. On an engineering-scale protein-folding codebase comprising more than 2,000 lines of code, AgentFold explores approximately 80 model variants using approximately 5,000 GPU-hours and 170 million LLM tokens. Under a matched computational budget, AgentFold improves the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperforms a random-search control. Beyond model improvement, the resulting intervention traces reveal recurring empirical design patterns: stable gains tend to arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, whereas direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training. The code and experimental resources are publicly available at https://github.com/lmqfly/AgentFold.

AI.tldr: AgentFold is a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously improves large scientific machine-learning systems by proposing, implementing, and validating executable code changes. Applied to protein folding, it explores ~80 ESMFold variants using ~5,000 GPU-hours and 170M LLM tokens, achieving a 7.5% improvement in best lDDT over baseline methods and revealing empirical design patterns for stable training.
AI.motivation: While scientific LLM agents have shown promise in literature reasoning, tool use, and experiment planning, it remains unclear whether they can autonomously improve large, tightly coupled scientific ML systems through executable code changes and computationally expensive validation. The authors study this in protein folding, where progress requires coordinated architectural modifications, multi-objective evaluation, and domain-aware interpretation.
AI.method: AgentFold is a multi-agent framework that frames folding-model development as a closed-loop search over executable code variants. Starting from ESMFold, it proposes hypotheses, implements and debugs code-level modifications, evaluates variants, analyzes experimental outcomes, and stores successful and failed interventions in structured memory. An MCTS-style policy allocates computational resources across high-scoring search branches.
AI.result: On a 2,000+ LOC protein-folding codebase, AgentFold explored ~80 model variants using ~5,000 GPU-hours and 170M LLM tokens. Under a matched computational budget, it improved the best lDDT by 7.5% over independent Codex proposals and outperformed a random-search control. Intervention traces revealed that stable gains arise from early, soft, learnable priors and gated refinement, whereas direct geometric perturbations and geometry-conditioned feedback often destabilize training.
AI.conclusion: AgentFold demonstrates that LLM agents can autonomously improve complex scientific ML systems through executable code modifications, and the resulting intervention traces provide reusable empirical design insights. The code and resources are publicly released.

title: Discovering Relationships in Data Lakes Using Large Language Models: An Industrial Case
summary: Data lakes rely on metadata to remain usable, yet this meta data is often limited or weakly informative for column relationship discovery, especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels. We propose ColRel, a two-stage method that builds column embeddings from metadata and data available at ingestion time. In difficult cases, such as coded schemata, business dictionaries help better interpret column names and support the generation of short natural-language descriptions used in the second stage. Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset show that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings.

AI.tldr: ColRel is a two-stage method that builds column embeddings from metadata and data at ingestion time for column relationship discovery in data lakes, using business dictionaries to interpret coded schemata and generate natural-language descriptions. It shows particular effectiveness in semantically related, weak-signal settings on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset.
AI.motivation: Data lakes rely on metadata to remain usable, but this metadata is often limited or weakly informative for column relationship discovery—especially in ERP-derived datasets with coded or abbreviated schema labels, where standard approaches struggle.
AI.method: ColRel employs a two-stage approach: (1) building column embeddings from both metadata and data available at ingestion time, with business dictionaries used to interpret coded schemata; and (2) generating short natural-language descriptions of columns to support the second stage of relationship discovery.
AI.result: Experiments on public benchmarks and an industrial ERP dataset demonstrate that ColRel is particularly effective in semantically related, weak-signal settings for column relationship discovery.
AI.conclusion: ColRel addresses the challenge of column relationship discovery in data lakes with limited or weakly informative metadata, especially in ERP contexts with coded schemata, by leveraging business dictionaries and generated natural-language descriptions to build informative column embeddings.

title: DEEPCHART: How Far are LLMs from Faithful Data-Science Chart Generation?
summary: Faithful chart generation in real-world data-science workflows requires grounding visualizations in scattered evidence, computing chart-ready quantities, and rendering them accurately. Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible, instruction-compliant charts, yet data-level hallucinations remain difficult to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts. To measure this gap, we introduce DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 task-conditioned chart-generation instances drawn from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. DEEPCHART formulates chart generation as an Extract--Reason--Visualize pipeline and evaluates source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stage by stage. Experiments with state-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors common in realistic long and multimodal settings. These findings suggest that larger context windows alone are insufficient; faithful chart generation also requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering. Our benchmark and associated resources are available at https://github.com/tangdouer1005/DeepChart.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DEEPCHART, an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,482 chart-generation instances from real-world scientific papers, financial filings, and ecosystem reports. It formulates chart generation as an Extract–Reason–Visualize pipeline and evaluates models stage by stage, revealing that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, and that larger context windows alone are insufficient for faithful chart generation.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs can produce visually plausible, instruction-compliant charts, yet data-level hallucinations remain difficult to detect in long, noisy, and multimodal contexts, highlighting the need for a dedicated benchmark to measure this gap.
AI.method: The benchmark DEEPCHART consists of 1,482 expert-annotated, task-conditioned chart-generation instances drawn from real-world sources. It decomposes chart generation into an Extract–Reason–Visualize pipeline and evaluates source-data extraction, derived-data reasoning, and chart rendering stage by stage.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models show that visually plausible charts often conceal data-level hallucinations, with extraction and reasoning errors being common in realistic long and multimodal settings; larger context windows alone are insufficient to mitigate these issues.
AI.conclusion: Faithful chart generation requires reliable evidence extraction and quantitative reasoning before rendering, in addition to standard LLM capabilities.

title: Categorizer Automata for Discounted-Sum Payoffs
summary: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is a fundamental operation in artificial intelligence. We introduce the categorizer automaton, a deterministic automaton that reads an infinite sequence of rewards and identifies which of finitely many bins contains its discounted sum. Categorizer automata generalize comparator automata, the special case of two bins, which have already proven useful in quantitative synthesis. Our main technical contribution is the construction of a categorizer automaton whose state space is linear in the number of bins, rather than exponential as obtained by a cross-product of comparator automata. We then apply categorizer automata to Markov decision processes, where they allow one to synthesize policies that maximize the expected utility of a discounted-sum payoff for utility functions that may be discontinuous. For piecewise-constant utility functions, the resulting algorithm is exact and runs in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions, a class that includes any utility with bounded slope between finitely many jumps, it again runs in pseudo-polynomial time and yields an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy. We also show that the synthesis problem considered is PSPACE-hard already for piecewise-constant utilities.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces categorizer automata, a deterministic automaton that reads infinite reward sequences and identifies which of finitely many bins contains the discounted sum. They generalize comparator automata (the two-bin case) and offer a linear state space in the number of bins instead of exponential. The automata are applied to Markov decision processes for synthesizing policies maximizing expected discounted-sum utility under discontinuous utility functions, with pseudo-polynomial time algorithms and a PSPACE-hardness result.
AI.motivation: Categorizing continuous data into discrete bins is fundamental in AI. While comparator automata (two bins) have proven useful in quantitative synthesis, handling more than two bins via cross-products leads to exponential blow-up in state space, motivating the need for a more efficient construction.
AI.method: The paper constructs a categorizer automaton whose state space is linear in the number of bins, avoiding the exponential blow-up of cross-product constructions. This is then applied to Markov decision processes for policy synthesis with discounted-sum payoffs under discontinuous (piecewise-constant and piecewise-Lipschitz) utility functions.
AI.result: For piecewise-constant utility functions, the algorithm is exact and runs in pseudo-polynomial time. For piecewise-Lipschitz utility functions (including any utility with bounded slope between finitely many jumps), it also runs in pseudo-polynomial time and yields an epsilon-optimal policy. The synthesis problem is shown to be PSPACE-hard even for piecewise-constant utilities.
AI.conclusion: Categorizer automata provide an efficient (linear in bins) generalization of comparator automata, enabling exact and approximate synthesis of policies for MDPs with discontinuous utility functions in pseudo-polynomial time, while establishing PSPACE-hardness as a complexity lower bound for the general synthesis problem.

title: AI Control Scientist: LLM-driven Agentic System for Automated Control Design
summary: Control system design is critical for modern industry, such as chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control. However,traditional control design workflows rely heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To this end, this paper proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS), the first large language model (LLM)-driven agent capable of automatically generating optimized controller from language design requirements. Specifically, a Task Modeling Agent interprets user requirements to engineering constraints; a Controller Design Agent generate candidate controller structures and executable code; and a Parameter Tuning Agent refine controller parameters under closed-loop performance criteria. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed agentic system can automatically generate multiple representative control systems, outperforms existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency. This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven, paving the way for model predictive control and other advanced control systems design.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AI Control Scientist (AICS), an LLM-driven agentic system that automatically generates optimized controllers from language design requirements, comprising a Task Modeling Agent, Controller Design Agent, and Parameter Tuning Agent. It outperforms existing automated baselines in design success rate and optimization efficiency across multiple control systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional control system design relies heavily on expert knowledge and extensive manual parameter tuning, which limits efficiency and scalability in critical industrial applications such as chemical process temperature regulation and aero-engine control.
