AI.method: AICS consists of three agents: (1) a Task Modeling Agent that interprets user requirements into engineering constraints, (2) a Controller Design Agent that generates candidate controller structures and executable code, and (3) a Parameter Tuning Agent that refines controller parameters based on closed-loop performance criteria.
AI.result: Experiments show that the agentic system can automatically generate multiple representative control systems, outperforming existing automated baselines in both design success rate and optimization efficiency.
AI.conclusion: This work has the potential to transform control system design from human-driven to agent-driven processes, paving the way for model predictive control and other advanced control systems design.

title: SymbolLKG: Towards Verifiable Logical Reasoning via Logical Knowledge Graph and Symbolic Solvers
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in natural language understanding, yet they struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, frequently suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing solutions like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) lack rigorous verification mechanisms, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often misses the complex, structural dependencies inherent in logical tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose a Neuro-Symbolic architecture that integrates a Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with dynamic solver routing. Specifically, we introduce an ontology-based LKG that treats logical rules and constraints as first-class topological nodes, enabling explicit modeling of dependencies extracted from text. We further design a Logic Router to dynamically dispatch tasks to the optimal symbolic engine, which is supported by a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism. Experimental results on logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, delivering higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Neuro-Symbolic architecture integrating a Logical Knowledge Graph (LKG) with dynamic solver routing to address LLMs' limitations in multi-step logical reasoning. The framework models logical rules as graph nodes, uses a Logic Router to dispatch tasks to optimal symbolic engines, and employs topology-aware hybrid retrieval. It outperforms SOTA prompting and RAG baselines on logical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at natural language understanding but struggle with strict multi-step reasoning, suffering from hallucinations and inconsistency. Existing CoT methods lack rigorous verification, and standard RAG fails to capture structural dependencies in logical tasks.
AI.method: The framework consists of: (1) an ontology-based Logical Knowledge Graph treating logical rules and constraints as first-class topological nodes for explicit dependency modeling; (2) a Logic Router that dynamically dispatches tasks to the optimal symbolic engine; (3) a topology-aware hybrid retrieval mechanism supporting the routing process.
AI.result: On logical reasoning benchmarks, the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prompting and RAG baselines, achieving higher accuracy and verifiable reasoning paths.
AI.conclusion: Integrating symbolic knowledge graphs with dynamic solver routing bridges the gap between neural flexibility and symbolic rigor, enabling accurate and verifiable multi-step logical reasoning.

title: LiveSim: Simulating Environment-Shaped Users in Multi-Agent Live-Stream Ecosystems
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables
summary: User behavior simulation with large language models~(LLMs) is increasingly used to support multi-agent ecosystem simulation. Existing simulators typically rely on static user profiles inferred from historical observations, which become inadequate in socially intensive environments such as live streaming where interaction dynamics continuously reshape user behavior. We propose \textbf{LiveSim}, an LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation. It represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses and progressively refines them through trajectory-grounded interactions, where discrepancies between simulated and observed trajectories reveal missing environmental shaping effects. These signals are further extracted as transferable environment-behavior patterns and accumulated in a collective behavioral memory to improve user-level behavioral fidelity and support ecosystem-level simulation. Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data validate the effectiveness of LiveSim in improving user-level behavioral fidelity and enabling ecosystem-level analysis of risk evolution and platform intervention effects.

AI.tldr: LiveSim is an LLM-based framework for live-stream ecosystem simulation that represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses, progressively refines them through trajectory-grounded interactions, and accumulates environment-behavior patterns in collective memory to improve both user-level fidelity and ecosystem-level simulation.
AI.motivation: Existing user behavior simulators rely on static user profiles inferred from historical observations, which are inadequate for socially intensive environments like live streaming where interaction dynamics continuously reshape user behavior.
AI.method: LiveSim represents users as editable behavioral hypotheses and refines them through trajectory-grounded interactions, where discrepancies between simulated and observed trajectories reveal missing environmental shaping effects. These signals are extracted as transferable environment-behavior patterns and accumulated in a collective behavioral memory to support both user-level and ecosystem-level simulation.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world live-stream risk-control data validate LiveSim's effectiveness in improving user-level behavioral fidelity and enabling ecosystem-level analysis of risk evolution and platform intervention effects.
AI.conclusion: LiveSim addresses the limitation of static user profiles in dynamic social environments by dynamically refining behavioral hypotheses through interaction trajectory feedback, demonstrating utility for both user-level fidelity and ecosystem-level simulations including risk analysis and platform interventions.

title: BekchiAI: Measuring, Observing, and Controlling LLM Agents in One Click
comment: 8 pages, 1 Figure, 6 tables
summary: Large language model agents reason, call tools, and act autonomously over many steps, but their agentic skills-correctly sequencing tools, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, and grounding generated arguments-are hard to measure with accuracy-only leaderboards. We present BekchiAI, which addresses both sides: a benchmark for measuring agentic skill and a platform for observing and controlling live agents. The BekchiAI-Benchmark, a suite of 13 tool-using ReAct agents across 7 task categories (arithmetic, structured/SQL, security detection, URL grounding, planning, orchestration, and tool-policy), totalling 2,057 deterministic, committed test tasks. Every task is verifier-checkable gold answers are computed by running canonical SQL against a real database, computing the exact schedule of a directed acyclic graph (DAG), or evaluating closed-form lambdas including adversarial security samples paired with deliberately imperfect signature scanners so a score reflects the model's own judgment, not the copying of an oracle. We define a small set of behavioral metrics beyond accuracy-tool-call adherence, URL hallucination and source-match, and per-model token cost and report a four-model comparison (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b) whose story is in the per-family spread, not the aggregate. The benchmark runs are executed using the provided evaluation scripts. BekchiAI-Platform is a complementary web-based observability and control layer for deployed agents, providing full token and latency telemetry as well as remote run termination. The benchmark, evaluation tools, and platform are publicly released.

AI.tldr: BekchiAI is a dual-purpose framework: a benchmark (BekchiAI-Benchmark) with 13 tool-using ReAct agents across 7 task categories and 2,057 verifier-checkable tasks for measuring agentic skills beyond accuracy, plus a web-based observability platform for monitoring and controlling live deployed agents with full telemetry and remote termination.
AI.motivation: Agentic skills of LLM agents—such as correct tool sequencing, planning under dependencies, judging untrusted inputs, and grounding generated arguments—are not adequately measured by accuracy-only leaderboards. There is a need for a benchmark that captures behavioral aspects of agentic competence and a platform for observing real deployed agents.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 13 tool-using ReAct agents spanning 7 task categories (arithmetic, structured/SQL, security detection, URL grounding, planning, orchestration, tool-policy) with 2,057 deterministic tasks. Gold answers are computed via canonical execution: SQL against real databases, exact DAG scheduling, or closed-form lambdas, including adversarial security samples paired with imperfect signature scanners. Behavioral metrics beyond accuracy include tool-call adherence, URL hallucination/source-match, and per-model token cost. A complementary web platform provides token/latency telemetry and remote run termination for deployed agents.
AI.result: A four-model comparison (Qwen3.7-Max, gemma-4-31B-it, gemma4:26b, gpt-oss-120b) is reported, with findings driven by per-family spread rather than aggregate scores. The benchmark runs are reproducible via provided evaluation scripts, and all artifacts are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: BekchiAI addresses the gap between accuracy-only evaluation and the multifaceted nature of agentic skill by providing verifiable behavioral metrics and a live observability/control platform, enabling more meaningful model comparison and deployment monitoring.

title: C-Unseen: Weak Signal Detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs via LLM Reasoning
comment: Accepted at the AI4SE 2026 Special Track, held within the WISE 2026 Conference
summary: Weak signals are early, low-visibility indicators that precede significant changes before those changes become established. Existing detection methods, based on keyword frequency, topic modeling, or untyped graph topology, fail to capture the semantic and relational structure through which such signals manifest. In this paper, we propose C-Unseen, a self-interpretable framework for weak signal detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs). We define a weak signal as a rare, semantically coherent subgraph that proliferates across consecutive TKG snapshots. The framework operates through two modules: a Rare Subgraphs Extractor, in which an LLM identifies subgraphs whose content is in tension with the dominant snapshot narrative via chain-of-thought reasoning, and a Weak Signal Alerter, in which the persistence of these rare subgraphs is tracked across time steps to isolate true weak signals. Experimental results demonstrate that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes C-Unseen, a self-interpretable framework for weak signal detection in Dynamic Temporal Knowledge Graphs (DTKGs). It defines weak signals as rare, semantically coherent subgraphs that proliferate across consecutive TKG snapshots, detected via an LLM-based Rare Subgraphs Extractor using chain-of-thought reasoning and a Weak Signal Alerter that tracks persistence over time.
AI.motivation: Existing weak signal detection methods (keyword frequency, topic modeling, untyped graph topology) fail to capture the semantic and relational structure through which weak signals manifest in dynamic knowledge graphs.
AI.method: C-Unseen has two modules: (1) a Rare Subgraphs Extractor where an LLM uses chain-of-thought reasoning to identify subgraphs whose content conflicts with the dominant snapshot narrative, and (2) a Weak Signal Alerter that tracks the persistence of these rare subgraphs across consecutive TKG snapshots to isolate true weak signals.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that C-Unseen outperforms keyword-, topic-, and graph-based baselines in weak signal detection.
AI.conclusion: The C-Unseen framework provides a self-interpretable approach to weak signal detection by leveraging LLM-based reasoning on subgraph semantics within dynamic temporal knowledge graphs, surpassing existing detection methods.

title: Evaluating human and LLM screening workflows in a conceptually complex scoping review: Recall--workload trade-offs and run-to-run consistency
summary:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for screening in evidence synthesis, where false negatives can remove relevant studies before full-text assessment. We compared human and LLM title-and-abstract screening workflows in a preregistered study embedded in a conceptually complex scoping review.
  Methods. After a conservative title-only screen, 1,131 records were screened by one review lead, four trained assistants screening non-overlapping subsets, and seven complete LLM runs using different models and processing configurations, including a nominally identical repeat run. We compared retained workload, operational recall against 316 verified eligible records, agreement, run-to-run consistency, and procedural burden. Because eligibility was verified only for records advanced and assessed in the parent review, recall estimates were operational.
  Results. No workflow recovered all verified eligible records. The human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records while achieving 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 file batches achieved the highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7% of records. All-at-once configurations recovered fewer eligible records than corresponding file-batch configurations. Two nominally identical GPT-5.4 file-batch runs agreed on 91.7% of records but differed on 94 records, including 29 verified eligible records retained by only one run.
  Discussion. LLM screening performance depended on the implemented workflow, not model identity alone. Processing configuration, workload, record-level variation, and human-LLM decision integration are therefore substantive properties of deployed systems. For high-recall tasks, LLMs are better suited to validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows than autonomous exclusion.

AI.tldr: A preregistered comparison of human and LLM title-and-abstract screening in a scoping review found that no workflow recovered all verified eligible records. Human workflows and GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42-45% of records with 82-83% recall, while Gemini 3.1 achieved the highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7%. LLM performance depended more on workflow configuration than model identity, with all-at-once runs performing worse than file-batch runs, and nominally identical runs differed on 94 records including 29 eligible ones.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for evidence synthesis screening where false negatives can be consequential, yet their performance as deployed workflows (not just model capabilities) compared to humans remains poorly characterized, especially in complex review contexts.
AI.method: Embedded in a conceptually complex scoping review, 1,131 records post title-only screen were screened by one review lead, four trained assistants over non-overlapping subsets, and seven complete LLM runs (different models and processing configurations, including a nominally identical repeat). Comparisons included retained workload, operational recall against 316 verified eligible records, agreement, run-to-run consistency, and procedural burden.
AI.result: No workflow achieved complete recovery of eligible records. Human workflows and two GPT-5.4 file-batch runs retained 42.2-45.0% of records with 82.3-82.9% recall. Gemini 3.1 file batches achieved highest recall (83.9%) but retained 56.7% of records. All-at-once configurations performed worse than file-batch equivalents. Two nominally identical GPT-5.4 runs agreed on 91.7% of records but differed on 94 records, including 29 verifiably eligible records retained by only one run.
AI.conclusion: LLM screening performance is determined by the implemented workflow (processing configuration, workload, integration decisions) rather than model identity alone. For high-recall tasks, LLMs should be deployed in validated, auditable, human-supervised workflows rather than as autonomous exclusion tools.

title: Learning-Augmented Online Allocation under Unreliable Advice: Robustness, Exposure Fairness, and Distribution Shift
summary: Learning-augmented algorithms improve online decisions using predictions, but unreliable advice may harm efficiency and fairness. We study an online allocation problem with finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints. We propose a robust and fair rule combining advice with a conservative fallback and fairness correction. Under bounded-error assumptions, we prove consistency and robustness with loss proportional to prediction error. Experiments show stability under adversarial advice and significant reductions in exposure disparity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learning-augmented online allocation algorithm with finite candidate sets, irreversible decisions, and exposure constraints. It combines external advice with a conservative fallback and fairness correction, achieving provable consistency and robustness under bounded-error assumptions, with experiments demonstrating stability under adversarial advice and reduced exposure disparity.
AI.motivation: Learning-augmented algorithms rely on predictions to improve online decisions, but unreliable or adversarial advice can degrade both efficiency and fairness. In online allocation problems with irreversible decisions and exposure constraints, there is a need for a rule that safely incorporates advice without sacrificing worst-case guarantees or fairness.
AI.method: The proposed approach combines external predictions with a conservative fallback strategy and a fairness correction mechanism, forming a single decision rule for online allocation. The algorithm is analyzed under bounded-error assumptions, providing theoretical consistency (optimal when predictions are accurate) and robustness (bounded loss under prediction errors proportional to the error magnitude).
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the algorithm remains stable even under adversarial advice and significantly reduces exposure disparity compared to baseline methods, while the theoretical analysis establishes provable consistency and robustness guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a robust and fair framework for learning-augmented online allocation under exposure constraints, balancing the benefits of predictions with safety guarantees against unreliable advice and fairness concerns.

title: AI agents in Algorithmic Electricity Markets: On the Emergence of Tacit Collusion
comment: 10 pages
summary: As electricity market participants increasingly adopt learning-based agents for their bidding strategies, electricity markets are becoming algorithmic. Evidence from algorithmic markets in other domains shows that tacit collusion can arise purely through independent learning. Moreover, electricity markets are typically oligopolistic and feature repeated interaction among a small number of participants, making them structurally susceptible to non-competitive behavior. In the face of these observations, this paper investigates the hypothesis that tacit collusion may emerge in electricity markets where participants' actions are controlled by autonomous learning-based algorithms. We model strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring, and model the participants' emergent behavior using multi-agent reinforcement learning. We propose a multi-dimensional set of criteria (going beyond profit comparisons against Nash equilibria) to assess whether the resulting behavior constitutes tacit collusion. Our experimental results showcase that such a danger is realistic for electricity markets: there are cases where agents do learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes that are supportive of tacit collusion indicators, even though the agents were never instructed to collude.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether tacit collusion can emerge in electricity markets where participants use autonomous learning-based bidding agents, modeling strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring and using multi-agent reinforcement learning to assess collusive behavior through multi-dimensional criteria beyond profit comparisons.
AI.motivation: Electricity markets are becoming increasingly algorithmic as participants adopt learning-based agents for bidding. Evidence from other algorithmic markets shows tacit collusion can arise purely through independent learning, and electricity markets are structurally susceptible to non-competitive behavior due to their oligopolistic nature and repeated interactions among few participants.
AI.method: The paper models strategic bidding as a repeated game with imperfect public monitoring and uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to model emergent agent behavior. It proposes a multi-dimensional set of criteria (going beyond simple profit comparisons against Nash equilibria) to assess whether resulting behavior constitutes tacit collusion.
AI.result: Experimental results show that tacit collusion is a realistic danger for electricity markets: agents can learn to sustain supra-competitive outcomes supportive of tacit collusion indicators in some cases, even though they were never instructed to collude.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous learning-based bidding agents in electricity markets can inadvertently learn collusive behavior, demonstrating a realistic risk that calls for careful design and regulation of algorithmic market participation.

title: Counterfactual Bias Testing for Application Tracking System
summary: Automated candidate-job matching systems are increasingly classified as high-risk AI under emerging regulation, yet auditing them for demographic bias is expensive: classical correspondence-audit studies require hand-crafted resumes and manual submission, which does not scale to fast pipeline retraining cycles. This paper presents a general, reusable methodology that (1) uses task-specialized LLM agents to synthesize identity-neutral base resumes and inject controlled demographic treatments across five protected-characteristic axes (sex/gender, age, residence, language, disability), producing a K x (1+N) correspondence-audit matrix; (2) qualitatively flags inferred protected characteristics per an EU AI Act-aligned prompt; (3) ranks candidates against a job description via a fine-tuned sentence-embedding model and cosine similarity; and (4) computes a nine-metric fairness suite spanning counterfactual (score delta, mean absolute rank change, flip rate), group-fairness (top-K retention, four-fifths/impact ratio), and merit-aware (Recall@K, nDCG@K, equal opportunity, equalized odds) families, each with bootstrap confidence intervals, significance tests, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, culminating in an automated PASS/INVESTIGATE/FAIL report with a composite risk score. On an example corpus of 5 job orders, 100 base candidates, and 10 demographic treatments (90 metric x variant evaluations): score shifts, top-K retention, and merit-aware rate gaps stay within tolerance for every treatment, but a rank-stability metric (MARC) and nDCG@K each surface borderline findings - including one on the neutral baseline itself - that a score- or retention-only view would miss. The results argue for multi-metric, multi-family auditing over any single aggregate score, and for LLM-agent-generated audits as a practical, low-cost complement to human-curated audits for any candidate-job matching pipeline.

On an example corpus, most metrics pass, but rank-stability (MARC) and nDCG@K surface borderline findings that score- or retention-only views would miss, arguing for multi-metric auditing as a practical complement to human-curated audits.
