title: A Table Is Worth 64 Tokens: Pixel-level Compression for Multi-Table Document Question Answering
summary: Answering questions over real-world documents requires processing long inputs that interleave text with tables. Optical context compression, which represents context as images, promises to reduce token cost, but its effect on table understanding remains unclear. We study pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, evaluating five VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets. Representing tables as images at native resolution matches text in both performance and efficiency, but downscaling them makes models compensate the loss in readability with longer, less effective reasoning traces that cancel the expected savings. Highly downscaled tables, however, preserve enough signal to identify whether they are relevant to a question. We exploit this asymmetry with a training-free, two-step method: the model first identifies the tables needed to answer a question from a pixel-compressed context, and then reasons over those at native resolution. On long documents, our method saves 41% of total tokens and gains 7 accuracy points over single-step QA with native resolution tables. It also uses 15% fewer tokens than the most efficient single-step compressed configuration, with no accuracy loss.

AI.tldr: This paper studies pixel-level table compression for question answering over documents with multiple tables, finding that native-resolution table images match text in performance/efficiency, while downscaling degrades readability and reasoning. The authors propose a training-free two-step method that first identifies relevant tables from compressed context, then reasons over those at native resolution, saving 41% of tokens and gaining 7 accuracy points over single-step native-resolution QA.
AI.motivation: Optical context compression (representing documents as images) promises to reduce token costs for long-document QA, but its impact on table understanding—a critical component of real-world documents—is not well understood. The paper aims to clarify this trade-off.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five VLMs across two benchmarks and five visual-token budgets for pixel-level table compression. They then exploit the asymmetry that highly downscaled tables preserve enough signal for relevance identification but not for detailed reasoning, proposing a training-free two-step method: (1) identify needed tables from pixel-compressed context, (2) reason over those tables at native resolution.
AI.result: Native-resolution table images match text in performance and efficiency. Downscaling causes models to produce longer, less effective reasoning traces that negate expected savings. The two-step method saves 41% of total tokens and gains 7 accuracy points over single-step native-resolution QA on long documents, while using 15% fewer tokens than the most efficient single-step compressed configuration with no accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Downscaled tables retain enough signal for table relevance identification but not for fine-grained reasoning. A training-free two-step pipeline that leverages this asymmetry yields significant token savings and accuracy gains over single-step approaches, demonstrating an effective strategy for pixel-compressed multi-table document QA.

title: From Atomic to Agentic: Towards Interpretable Evaluation of LLMs' Agentic Mathematical Capabilities
comment: EMNLP 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are evolving from performing end-to-end mathematical reasoning to integrating agentic intelligence. However, most existing math benchmarks evaluate only final answers. This outcome-oriented evaluation provides limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic, failing to guide the transformation of LLMs into robust agents. To bridge this gap, we present a process-level benchmark designed to evaluate the inherent agentic mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Our framework aligns problem-solving agentic behaviors with a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. We design a comprehensive suite of planning, action, and feedback tasks across both textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations via controlled LLM rewriting. Experiments reveal that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles. This demonstrates that process-level evaluation is crucial for interpreting the true potential of LLMs and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a process-level benchmark for evaluating agentic mathematical reasoning in LLMs, moving beyond outcome-only evaluation. It aligns agentic problem-solving behaviors with a taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities, incorporating planning, action, and feedback tasks in both textual and multimodal settings, with an automated pipeline for trajectory synthesis and fine-grained annotation. Experiments show models with similar end-to-end accuracy can differ significantly in process-level agentic capability profiles, highlighting the need for process-oriented evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing math benchmarks predominantly evaluate only final answers, offering limited diagnostic value for identifying process-level failures or rigorous logic in LLMs as they evolve from end-to-end reasoning to agentic intelligence. This outcome-oriented approach fails to guide the development of robust mathematical agents.
AI.method: The framework constructs a process-level benchmark by mapping agentic problem-solving behaviors to a structured taxonomy of reusable mathematical atomic capabilities. It includes planning, action, and feedback tasks across textual and multimodal contexts, supported by an automated pipeline that synthesizes high-quality trajectories and produces fine-grained annotations via controlled LLM rewriting.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that models with similar end-to-end accuracy can exhibit markedly different agentic capability profiles, demonstrating that process-level evaluation provides crucial diagnostic information beyond outcome-based metrics.
AI.conclusion: Process-level evaluation is essential for interpreting the true potential of LLMs and guiding the development of next-generation mathematical agents, as it uncovers capability differences that end-to-end accuracy alone cannot reveal.

title: GraphMemix: Query-Aware Evidence Forests for Long-Term Multimodal Agent Memory
comment: Project page with code: https://github.com/ligeng0197/graphmemix
summary: Organizing long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging because existing methods either suffer from expensive question-agnostic offline summaries or naive embedding similarity matching that introduces incomplete and redundant context. To address these issues, we propose GraphMemix, a combinatorial-optimization graph memory framework that models memory organization as query-aware evidence-forest construction. Specifically, our method consists of three key components:(1) candidate graph construction, which expands multi-view seed memories through schema and semantic relations to acquire query-aware original context; (2) evidence utility and activation costs, which decouples direct memory support from anchor-conditioned relation verification to suppress redundant or conflicting information; and (3) forest optimization, which jointly selects a forest-format memory context under a maximum evidence budget and its reliable relational structure. By organizing memory into a query-relevant subgraph, the method avoids substantial lifecycle cost and recovers low-similarity complementary evidence. Experimental results across four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements with different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.

AI.tldr: GraphMemix is a query-aware graph memory framework for multimodal agents that models long-term memory organization as combinatorial-optimization evidence-forest construction, surpassing prior methods on accuracy and lifecycle cost across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory methods for multimodal agents either rely on expensive question-agnostic offline summaries or naive embedding similarity matching, which introduces incomplete and redundant context. This creates a gap between retrieval quality and computational efficiency.
AI.method: GraphMemix comprises three components: (1) candidate graph construction that expands multi-view seed memories via schema and semantic relations for query-aware context; (2) evidence utility and activation costs that decouple direct memory support from anchor-conditioned relation verification to suppress redundancy/conflict; and (3) forest optimization that jointly selects a forest-format memory context under a maximum evidence budget with reliable relational structure.
AI.result: Experiments on four long-term multimodal memory benchmarks show significant improvements across different foundation models and establish a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and lifecycle cost.
AI.conclusion: By organizing memory into a query-relevant subgraph, GraphMemix avoids substantial lifecycle cost and recovers low-similarity complementary evidence, offering an efficient and effective alternative to prior memory organization strategies.

title: DSA: Evidence-Aware LLM-Agent Orchestration for Multi-Market Stock Research
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Code available at https://github.com/ZhuLinsen/daily_stock_analysis
summary: Large language models can summarize financial information, but an operational stock-research system must first assemble heterogeneous evidence, expose unavailable data and model capabilities, and control how generated opinions affect a final report. We present DSA, an evidence-aware orchestration framework for multi-market stock research with large language model (LLM) agents. DSA organizes the workflow into evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation with selected context and diagnostics. A default report profile and an optional agentic profile share evidence and model-routing services but use profile-specific output validation and risk safeguards. In the agentic profile, core role outputs are processed by role-specific parsers, whereas Strategy Skill opinions undergo an additional signal-eligibility partition before synthesis; disagreement is supplied explicitly to the decision agent, followed by a conservative risk override. The reference implementation includes six regional market paths, fifteen bundled Strategy Skills, hosted and local model routes, and multiple execution and delivery surfaces. At a frozen software snapshot, a selected manifest of 1,457 portable offline backend contract tests passed; 596 cases were retrospectively mapped to six contract families central to the reported LLM-agent architecture. This evidence establishes implementation conformance for the tested software contracts, not superior report quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.

AI.tldr: DSA is an evidence-aware orchestration framework for multi-market stock research using LLM agents, organizing workflows into evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, role/Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation with profile-specific safeguards.
AI.motivation: Operational stock-research systems must assemble heterogeneous evidence, expose unavailable data and model capabilities, and control how generated opinions affect final reports—capabilities that raw LLM summarization alone cannot provide.
AI.method: DSA organizes workflow into evidence acquisition, structured context construction, model-routed analysis, optional role and Strategy Skill reasoning, and report generation. It features a default report profile and an agentic profile sharing evidence and model-routing services but with distinct output validation and risk safeguards. The agentic profile uses role-specific parsers, signal-eligibility partitioning for Strategy Skill opinions, explicit disagreement signals to the decision agent, and a conservative risk override. The reference implementation includes six regional market paths, fifteen bundled Strategy Skills, hosted/local model routes, and multiple execution surfaces.
AI.result: At a frozen software snapshot, 1,457 portable offline backend contract tests passed, with 596 retrospectively mapped to six contract families central to the LLM-agent architecture.
AI.conclusion: The evidence establishes implementation conformance for tested software contracts only—not superior report quality, forecasting accuracy, or investment returns.

title: ASIL: Replacing Screenshot-and-Click with Structured State and Semantic Actions
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 19 pages, 7 figures: 9-page main paper followed by limitations, ethics, acknowledgments, references, and appendices A-E. Project page: https://sharryxr.github.io/ASIL/
summary: Powerful code agents can execute scripts, call tools, and manage files, yet many important applications remain accessible primarily through graphical user interfaces. We argue that screenshot-and-click is an inefficient interface for software-operating agents: screenshots are state-incomplete, and GUI actions are brittle, semantically weak, and poorly matched to long-horizon planning. We introduce ASIL (Agent-Software Interaction Layer), an agent-native interface that exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, realized through the deepest feasible access path for each application. We instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and a benchmark of 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks. ASIL reaches above 80 with closed models while executing fewer than five actions per task. Under a repaired runtime and a 50-step screenshot budget, the same tasks yield 6.6 and 26.6 strict success under screenshot-and-click control, rising to 15.0 and 53.3 on an easier OSWorld-comparable band. Against application-native interfaces on matched tasks, ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 strict points but only matches draw.io's MCP content contract. The structured modality also suits training: small-scale SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4, and resource-limited on-policy RL further raises them to 74.4 and 82.2.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ASIL (Agent-Software Interaction Layer), an agent-native interface that replaces screenshot-and-click control with structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions. ASIL is instantiated across 15 applications with 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks, achieving >80% success with closed models while using fewer than 5 actions per task—far outperforming screenshot-based control (6.6% vs 26.6% strict success) and matching or exceeding application-native interfaces. The structured modality also enables efficient training, with SFT and on-policy RL improving Qwen3.5 models substantially.
AI.motivation: Powerful code agents can execute scripts and tools, but many important applications remain primarily GUI-accessible. Screenshot-and-click interaction is argued to be an inefficient interface for software-operating agents because screenshots are state-incomplete and GUI actions are brittle, semantically weak, and poorly matched to long-horizon planning.
AI.method: ASIL exposes software through structured JSON observations and code-executable semantic actions, realized through the deepest feasible access path for each application (e.g., APIs, protocols, or internal interfaces). The authors instantiate ASIL across 15 applications and evaluate on 300 single-application and 80 multi-application tasks, comparing against screenshot-and-click baselines and application-native interfaces, as well as testing fine-tuning with SFT and on-policy RL on small models.
AI.result: ASIL achieves >80% success with closed models using fewer than 5 actions per task. Under a repaired runtime and 50-step screenshot budget, the same tasks yield only 6.6% and 26.6% strict success under screenshot-and-click control (15.0% and 53.3% on an easier band). ASIL exceeds LibreOffice's UNO API by 28-38 strict points and matches draw.io's MCP content contract. SFT raises Qwen3.5-2B from 58.0 to 72.1 and Qwen3.5-9B from 66.6 to 80.4; on-policy RL further raises them to 74.4 and 82.2.
AI.conclusion: Structured agent-native interfaces like ASIL are substantially more effective and efficient than screenshot-based interfaces for software-operating agents, both for inference with strong closed models and for training smaller open models. The structured modality is well-suited to both zero-shot agent evaluation and model fine-tuning.

title: A Multi-Modal AI Framework for Real-Time Queue Prediction, Management and Optimisation in Intelligent Border Control Systems
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, conference
summary: In the present work an efficient border control management procedure is proposed. Compared to operational queue management systems, whose operations are based on mostly static data, the proposed work takes into account dynamic traffic conditions, thus enabling optimal performance, even in cases of uncertainty. To this end, we are proposing a multi-modal Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework, tailored to th needs of border control systems, which enables real-time queue prediction, management, and resource optimization. The novel proposed approach integrates heterogeneous data sources and presents them through a unified representation by employing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for queue forecasting. Furthermore, it leverages Model Predictive Control (MPC) and scheduling optimization to derive actionable control policies, which in turn can be presented to border control officers. The proposed work has been evaluated using synthetic data simulating realistic traffic. The evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces queue prediction error by up to 35% and average waiting time by 30%. Accordingly, the average throughput increases by nearly 20%, compared to ARIMA and rule-based methods. The abovementioned results show the effectiveness and efficiency of combining AI architectures with optimization techniques for proactive and adaptive border traffic management.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an efficient border control management procedure using a multi-modal AI framework that integrates LSTM networks for real-time queue prediction, Model Predictive Control (MPC), and scheduling optimization for proactive and adaptive border traffic management. Evaluated on synthetic data, the method reduces queue prediction error by up to 35%, average waiting time by 30%, and increases throughput by nearly 20% compared to ARIMA and rule-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing operational queue management systems for border control rely mostly on static data and fail to perform optimally under dynamic traffic conditions and uncertainty. There is a need for a framework that accounts for real-time traffic dynamics to enable optimal border control performance.
AI.method: The proposed approach is a multi-modal AI framework that: (1) integrates heterogeneous data sources into a unified representation, (2) employs Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for real-time queue forecasting, and (3) leverages Model Predictive Control (MPC) combined with scheduling optimization to derive actionable control policies for border control officers.
AI.result: Using synthetic data simulating realistic traffic conditions, the proposed method reduces queue prediction error by up to 35%, decreases average waiting time by 30%, and increases average throughput by nearly 20%, compared to ARIMA and rule-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that combining AI architectures (LSTM) with optimization techniques (MPC and scheduling) is effective and efficient for proactive and adaptive border traffic management, outperforming traditional static-data-based approaches.

title: Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder
comment: Preprint
summary: Multimodal representation learning has been shifting from traditional two-tower architectures to large language model (LLM)-based embedders due to their strong instruction-following capabilities. Despite this progress, existing approaches primarily focus on language and image modalities, which also remain the dominant modalities for user-conditioned interactions in current embedders. In this paper, we propose the first Omni-Interactive Universal Embedder (OmniUE), which not only learns a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio by leveraging intermediate-layer representations from dedicated learnable tokens, but also supports omni-interactive querying, enabling users to provide inputs in the form of text, visual regions of interest, and audio spans. Within OmniUE, visual and audio segmenters process diverse user interactions and integrate them with an omni-LLM to produce user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation. To evaluate OmniUE's omni-interactive capabilities, we introduce OmniCHOIR, benchmarking models for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval based on the given text, video, and audio as well as unimodal or multimodal interaction prompts. OmniUE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, with average improvements of 10.5% on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on our omni-interactive OmniCHOIR benchmark. We believe that jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying paves the way toward universal embedders.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OmniUE, the first omni-interactive universal embedder that learns a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio while supporting user interactions via text, visual regions, and audio spans. The authors also propose OmniCHOIR, a new benchmark for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval. OmniUE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all modalities, with notable gains of 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks and 24.1% on the new OmniCHOIR benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multimodal embedders primarily focus on language and image modalities, lacking support for omni-modal (text, video, audio) representation learning and omni-interactive querying that allows users to condition retrieval through diverse input forms beyond just text.
AI.method: OmniUE employs dedicated learnable tokens and leverages their intermediate-layer representations to create a unified embedding space across text, video, and audio. It uses visual and audio segmenters to process diverse user interactions, integrates them with an omni-LLM, and produces user-conditioned any-to-any embeddings via context aggregation. A new benchmark, OmniCHOIR, is introduced for omni-interactive compositional audio retrieval.
AI.result: OmniUE consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, achieving average improvements of 10.5% on textual-interactive video benchmarks (MMEB-v2-video), 1.1% on audio tasks (MAEB), 83.7% on visual-interactive benchmarks (SCaR), and 24.1% on the new OmniCHOIR benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that jointly advancing omni-modal representation learning and omni-interactive querying is a promising direction toward developing universal embedders that can handle arbitrary modalities and interaction types.

title: A Contract-Centered Architecture for Scalable and Manageable Agentic Runtimes
comment: 48 pages, 7 figures
summary:
Enterprise AI deployment is a coordination problem across business units, application and AI teams, testing, platform engineering, infrastructure, security, operations, and data governance. Use-case benchmarks show whether one agent completes one task, but not how changing capabilities, models, runtime mechanisms, capacity, and enterprise data should be owned, changed, admitted, or evidenced together.
  We present four responsibility objects as shared organizational contracts: Skill (reusable, versioned capability and workflow asset), Harness (runtime compiler and governor), Scaffold (execution/control boundary and NFR owner), and a stack-external data substrate under independent CIO-governed semantics and telemetry. The runtime core is A = <S, H, X>, with the data substrate outside that stack.
  The central contribution is one bounded, falsifiable hypothesis, P1 (cost-aware capability-capacity separability): within a declared operating region, changing activated capability preserves the capacity-response interaction within a preregistered equivalence margin, while changing compatible Scaffold capacity preserves capability semantics up to a non-inferiority margin, and the required controls stay within a declared enforcement budget. Six design conditions become measured obligations whose coverage, violations, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions determine whether P1 is decidable.
  We propose a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment (balanced order, reset/washout, repeated seeds and failure regimes, cluster-aware uncertainty) with a four-state verdict: supported, falsified, conditional-engineering, or inconclusive. This paper contributes a contract-bounded runtime architecture, a source-preserving data substrate, and a falsifiable measurement protocol. It reports no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured result.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a contract-based architectural framework for enterprise AI deployment, introducing four "responsibility objects" (Skill, Harness, Scaffold, and a CIO-governed data substrate) as organizational coordination contracts. The central contribution is a bounded, falsifiable hypothesis P1 (cost-aware capability-capacity separability) with six design conditions as measurable obligations, evaluated via a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment with a four-state verdict. The paper reports no implementation or empirical results.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI deployment is fundamentally a multi-party coordination problem spanning business units, AI teams, platform engineering, security, and governance. Existing use-case benchmarks only measure single-agent task completion and fail to address how capabilities, models, runtime mechanisms, capacity, and enterprise data should be jointly owned, changed, admitted, or evidenced.
AI.method: The paper defines four responsibility objects as shared organizational contracts: Skill (reusable versioned capability/workflow asset), Harness (runtime compiler and governor), Scaffold (execution/control boundary and NFR owner), and a stack-external data substrate under CIO-governed semantics. The runtime core is A = <S, H, X>. It formalizes P1, a falsifiable hypothesis about cost-aware capability-capacity separability, operationalized through six design conditions as measured obligations (coverage, violations, uncertainty, cost, exclusions). Evaluation uses a cluster-period randomized crossover experiment with balanced order, reset/washout, repeated seeds/failure regimes, and cluster-aware uncertainty, yielding a four-state verdict.
AI.result: The paper presents no completed implementation, experiment, dataset, or measured result. Its contributions are architectural and methodological: a contract-bounded runtime architecture, a source-preserving data substrate, and a falsifiable measurement protocol for testing separability between capability and capacity in enterprise AI systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper reframes enterprise AI deployment as an organizational coordination problem addressable through explicit responsibility contracts and a preregistered, falsifiable experimental protocol. It sets up a rigorous evaluation framework but explicitly defers empirical validation to future work, positioning its contribution as architectural and methodological groundwork rather than demonstrated results.

title: pro-team at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship and Reuse: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Vocabulary-Constrained Filtering for Ontology Learning
summary: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite significant progress in Large Language Models (LLMs), which can hallucinate domain terms, produce inconsistent formats, and favor hierarchical over associative relations. In the LLMs4OL 2026 Challenge, we address both the End-to-End Flagship Task (Task A) and Ontology Extension Reuse Task (Task B) using an offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline. Our system employs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval, selecting the top-5 examples for Task A and top-2 for Task B. A left-truncated context-windowing strategy preserves task instructions within long prompts. For Task B, generated triples undergo deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering, retaining triples when at least one endpoint belongs to the sample's closed term/type vocabulary and removing duplicates of the initial ontology. The approach achieves Semantic Graph Similarity of 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 of 0.9200, and Taxonomy Discovery F1 of 0.8540 on Task B, while Task A achieves 0.7416 Semantic Graph Similarity. However, no non-taxonomic relations are extracted, highlighting limitations of closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabularies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline using Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for the LLMs4OL 2026 Challenge Tasks A and B, achieving strong scores on Task B but failing to extract non-taxonomic relations due to closed relation vocabularies.
AI.motivation: Ontology learning from text remains challenging despite LLM advances due to hallucinations, format inconsistencies, and a bias toward hierarchical over associative relations.
AI.method: An offline retrieval-augmented few-shot prompting pipeline: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as the LLM, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for demonstration retrieval (top-5 for Task A, top-2 for Task B), left-truncated context-windowing to preserve task instructions, and deterministic vocabulary-constrained filtering for Task B that retains triples with at least one endpoint in the closed vocabulary and removes duplicates.
AI.result: Task B achieves Semantic Graph Similarity of 0.8692, Term-Typing F1 of 0.9200, and Taxonomy Discovery F1 of 0.8540. Task A achieves 0.7416 Semantic Graph Similarity. However, no non-taxonomic relations are extracted.
AI.conclusion: The system performs well on taxonomy-focused ontology learning, but the closed, taxonomy-oriented relation vocabulary limits its ability to extract associative (non-taxonomic) relations, highlighting a key limitation of the approach.

title: LAAF: A Layered Accountability Architecture Framework for LLM Applications
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) operate in hospitals, courtrooms, banks, and public service desks, where fluent, confident outputs are treated as authoritative even when ungrounded or incorrect. When such an output contributes to harm, who is answerable, and through what mechanisms can responsibility be traced, explained, and acted upon? Following PRISMA guidance, five databases were searched from January 2022 to March 2026 against four review questions; of 4,512 records identified, 122 primary studies were included, together with 12 regulatory and standards documents analysed as primary sources. The review consolidates a sociotechnical account of accountability as an actor-forum relation resolved into five dimensions, and synthesises mechanisms across four families: technical controls, human oversight, organisational governance, and documentation and traceability, each with a maturity assessment. The corpus is read through a four-layer classification device spanning provenance, application logic, human oversight, and governance and redress, cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring. Both are mapped onto the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations have applied since 2 August 2026, the NIST AI RMF with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance in healthcare, consumer finance, education, and the public sector. Four persistent gaps emerge: under-specification of human oversight, absence of shared accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, and limited empirical evaluation, alongside five structural tensions that no surveyed instrument resolves. The review closes by consolidating the classification device into an integrated accountability architecture, LAAF, with cybersecurity aligned to the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025); it is a synthesis of the surveyed evidence rather than a validated artefact.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA-guided systematic review (122 primary studies, 12 regulatory documents) consolidating a sociotechnical accountability framework for LLM deployment in high-stakes domains, resolving accountability into five dimensions across four mechanism families, and mapping them onto the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance. Identifies four persistent gaps and five structural tensions, culminating in a proposed LAAF accountability architecture aligned with OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025).
AI.motivation: LLMs are deployed in high-stakes settings (hospitals, courts, banks, public services) where confident but ungrounded or incorrect outputs can cause harm, yet there is no consolidated account of who is answerable and through what mechanisms responsibility can be traced, explained, and acted upon.
AI.method: A systematic review following PRISMA guidance: five databases searched from January 2022 to March 2026 against four review questions; 4,512 records screened to 122 primary studies plus 12 regulatory/standards documents. Analyses use a four-layer classification device (provenance, application logic, human oversight, governance and redress) cross-cut by traceability, role clarity, and continuous monitoring, with findings mapped onto EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF + GenAI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and sectoral guidance.
AI.result: Accountability is modelled as an actor-forum relation resolved into five dimensions, with mechanisms synthesised across four families (technical controls, human oversight, organisational governance, documentation and traceability), each with a maturity assessment. Four persistent gaps emerge: under-specified human oversight, absence of shared accountability metrics, disciplinary disconnection, and limited empirical evaluation. Five structural tensions remain unresolved by any surveyed instrument.
AI.conclusion: The classification device is consolidated into an integrated accountability architecture, LAAF, aligned with the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025). The authors emphasize LAAF is a synthesis of surveyed evidence rather than a validated artefact, indicating the next step is empirical validation.

title: TransMeme: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Cultural Meme Transcreation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Internet memes are a pervasive form of multimodal online communication; however, such communication often involves users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Therefore, adapting memes across cultures and languages is a central challenge for enabling mutual understanding in online communication. Unlike ordinary translation or standalone text rewriting, cross-cultural meme transcreation must jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning for the target audience, and maintain coherence between text and image. In this work, we first provide an explicit task analysis of cross-cultural meme transcreation and identify three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent and tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. Based on this analysis, we propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents that are coordinated to address these challenges through cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment. The framework strengthens target text adaptation with coordinated feedback to handle difficult cases that require deeper cultural or visual intervention. We evaluate the framework on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation using both human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge. Our method consistently outperforms all baselines across both evaluation settings. In human evaluation, it achieves the best performance on all four dimensions and delivers a 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline, while in LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains the highest Top-1 ranking rate (60% versus 26% for the second-best baseline). Further analysis indicates that each component contributes to the performance. Our error analysis suggests that the remaining bottlenecks lie in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than simple cultural knowledge gaps, pointing to future work on humor transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses cross-cultural meme transcreation—adapting internet memes across languages and cultures—by proposing a multi-agent framework with four specialized agents (cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment) that jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culture-dependent meaning, and maintain text-image coherence. Evaluated on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation, the method outperforms all baselines in both human evaluation (33.1% average improvement) and LLM-as-a-Judge (60% Top-1 ranking rate). Error analysis reveals remaining bottlenecks in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than cultural knowledge gaps.
AI.motivation: Internet memes involve users from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds, making cross-cultural adaptation essential for mutual understanding online. Unlike ordinary translation or text rewriting, meme transcreation must jointly preserve communicative intent, adapt culturally dependent meaning, and maintain multimodal coherence between text and image—a task not adequately addressed by existing methods.
AI.method: The authors first provide an explicit task analysis identifying three core challenges: culture-specific knowledge understanding, intent and tone preservation, and multimodal consistency. They then propose a multi-agent framework with specialized agents for cultural adaptation, target text rewriting, revision, and conditional visual adjustment, coordinated with feedback loops to handle difficult cases requiring deeper cultural or visual intervention.
AI.result: The framework is evaluated on bidirectional Chinese-English meme transcreation using both human evaluation and LLM-as-a-Judge. It consistently outperforms all baselines: in human evaluation, it achieves best performance on all four dimensions with a 33.1% average improvement over the strongest baseline; in LLM-as-a-Judge, it attains a 60% Top-1 ranking rate versus 26% for the second-best baseline. Ablation analysis confirms each component contributes to performance.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent framework effectively addresses cross-cultural meme transcreation, with remaining challenges concentrated in humor reconstruction and image-text alignment rather than cultural knowledge gaps. This points to future research directions on humor transfer in multimodal content adaptation.

title: GRAIN: Bridging Name and Narrative Shifts in Real-World Graph Reasoning through Invariance-Rewarded Agentic RL
summary: Despite their potential in standardized graph tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulation. While deterministic graph tools are invariant to such shifts, extracting topological structures from noisy text is highly fragile for LLMs, which often overfit to surface patterns. Moreover, mitigating these parsing failures via multi-agent systems incurs prohibitive latency. To address this, we propose GRAIN, a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. GRAIN models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward. By validating extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies, this reward forces the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts. We also introduce GRIT, a benchmark evaluating sensitivity to such linguistic shifts. GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45\% in accuracy with approximately 24\% lower latency. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap of SFT models (from 15.77\% to 7.80\%) and maintaining robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.

AI.tldr: GRAIN is a single-agent LLM framework trained via reinforcement learning with a Structure Invariance Reward for robust graph reasoning. It outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45% in accuracy with ~24% lower latency, and halves the OOD generalization gap of SFT models from 15.77% to 7.80%.
AI.motivation: LLMs are brittle to real-world shifts in node identifiers and task formulations on graph tasks. They overfit to surface patterns when extracting topological structures from noisy text, while deterministic graph tools are shift-invariant. Multi-agent systems that mitigate parsing failures incur prohibitive latency.
AI.method: GRAIN is a single-agent framework optimized via reinforcement learning. It models reasoning as a semantic parsing and tool-execution pipeline, guided by a Structure Invariance Reward that validates extracted intermediate graphs against ground-truth topologies. The authors also introduce GRIT, a benchmark for evaluating sensitivity to linguistic shifts.
AI.result: GRAIN outperforms multi-agent baselines by 16.45% in accuracy with approximately 24% lower latency. It demonstrates superior structural generalization, halving the OOD gap of SFT models from 15.77% to 7.80%, and maintains robustness on large-scale graphs beyond the training distribution.
AI.conclusion: GRAIN's reinforcement learning with structure invariance reward enables the LLM to learn robust text-to-structure mappings rather than memorizing linguistic artifacts, achieving both higher accuracy and lower latency than multi-agent approaches while generalizing better to out-of-distribution graph settings.

title: Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering for Graph Anomaly Detection
summary: In recent years, graph anomaly detection (GAD) based on frequency-domain filtering have achieved promising results. However, existing approaches still face three major challenges: First, they use static basic function to constructed graph filter which cannot effectively adapt to the frequency-domain distribution of graph data. Second, they fail to adequately consider the importance information of each attribute in the node feature vector, leading to the loss of fine-grained information. Third, they insufficiently utilize node labels for GAD. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel graph anomaly detection method called JPGFN (Feature Transformation Enhanced Jacobi Polynomial Graph Filtering Network). First, a Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) is developed to better learn fine-grained node features by feature separation and applying nonlinear transformations to node features across different dimensions. Second, an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module is constructed based on Jacobi polynomials to adaptively capture complex frequency-domain features of graph signals. Finally, a node label constraint module is developed to facilitate the use of node labels and enhance the performance of GAD. Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms mainstream approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes JPGFN, a graph anomaly detection method that combines feature separation transformation, adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering, and node label constraints to address limitations in existing frequency-domain GAD approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing frequency-domain graph anomaly detection methods face three challenges: (1) they use static basis functions for graph filters that cannot adapt to the frequency-domain distribution of graph data, (2) they neglect the importance of individual attributes in node feature vectors causing loss of fine-grained information, and (3) they insufficiently utilize node labels for anomaly detection.
AI.method: JPGFN consists of three key modules: (1) a Feature Separation Transformation Network (FSTNN) that learns fine-grained node features by separating and applying nonlinear transformations across different feature dimensions, (2) an adaptive Jacobi polynomial graph filtering module that leverages Jacobi polynomials to adaptively capture complex frequency-domain features of graph signals, and (3) a node label constraint module that facilitates the use of node labels to enhance detection performance.
AI.result: Experimental results on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that JPGFN significantly outperforms mainstream graph anomaly detection approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed JPGFN method effectively resolves the three identified challenges in frequency-domain GAD by combining fine-grained feature transformation, adaptive polynomial graph filtering, and label-aware constraints, achieving superior performance over existing methods.

title: When Tool Outputs Become Commands: Separating Action Induction from Runtime Authorization in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented LLM agents must rely on untrusted runtime Observations to complete open-ended tasks; however, when tool outputs no longer merely provide data but begin to specify concrete actions, they effectively become ``commands'' that can drive real-world side effects beyond user intent. We argue that this risk arises from conflating action induction with execution authorization. To address this distinction, we propose SARA, which treats action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles and separates action provenance from execution authority. On the Observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics and persistently records action-origin provenance across steps as a review signal; on the execution side, actual tool calls are authorized only against the user objective and audited evidence from authorized successful executions, while satisfying goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support. To preserve this separation across multi-step execution, SARA applies No-History-Promotion to prevent historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority. Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn, SARA limits ASR to no more than \(0.63\%\) across four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional Agent backbones.

AI.tldr: SARA is a framework that distinguishes action induction from execution authorization in tool-augmented LLM agents, preventing tool outputs from driving unintended side effects by separating action provenance from execution authority.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented LLM agents rely on untrusted runtime observations, but when tool outputs begin specifying concrete actions rather than just providing data, they effectively become "commands" that can cause real-world side effects beyond user intent. This risk stems from conflating action induction with execution authorization.
AI.method: SARA separates action induction and execution authorization as distinct runtime roles. On the observation side, a context-isolated Action Probe exposes action-inducing semantics and persistently records action-origin provenance as a review signal. On the execution side, actual tool calls are authorized only against the user objective and audited evidence from authorized successful executions, requiring goal, execution-chain, and argument-level support. Additionally, No-History-Promotion prevents historical recurrence from laundering action origins into execution authority across multi-step execution.
AI.result: Across AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks, SARA limits Attack Success Rate (ASR) to no more than 0.63% across four primary evaluation settings while maintaining competitive task utility, and consistently reduces ASR across additional agent backbones.
AI.conclusion: SARA effectively mitigates the security risk of tool outputs driving unintended actions by enforcing a strict separation between action induction and execution authorization, achieving near-zero attack success while preserving task performance.

title: Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
comment: Open-weight model: https://huggingface.co/thomsonreuters/Thomson-1.0-Small
summary: The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid- & post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values & data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax & multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $π$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that frontier-level AI performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on open-weight models, rather than requiring massive compute budgets. The authors introduce a mid- and post-training stack with safeguards preserving plasticity and stability, enabling minimal high-impact parameter interventions. They demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model focused on high-stakes professional work, which performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic, safety, legal, tax, multilingual, and Deep Research tasks, exhibiting a distinctive "π-shaped" improvement pattern with negligible forgetting.
AI.motivation: To address the information, economic, and power asymmetry between frontier model developers and the diverse AI user base, by providing concrete advice on how SovereignAI (independent building, deployment, and governance of AI) can be achieved short-term under diverse funding settings.
AI.method: Continual Learning applied to readily available open-weight models, using a modern mid- and post-training stack with safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact parameter interventions.
AI.result: Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work, performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax, multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. It shows a π-shaped improvement pattern: gains across a wide range of capabilities (including untargeted ones) while nearly eliminating catastrophic forgetting common in narrow domain adaptation. Gains are comparable to multiple successive model generations at substantially lower compute/personnel budgets.
AI.conclusion: Making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values, and data privacy) viable for far more actors, democratizing frontier AI development beyond a small number of heavily funded players.

title: BPMN4CAI: A BPMN Extension for Modeling Dynamic Conversational AI
comment: Presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), September 2025, Münster, Germany
summary: Conversational AI systems, such as chatbots and virtual assistants, are becoming increasingly important to digital business processes. However, the established Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) standard faces challenges when representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions. This paper addresses this methodological and practical research gap by developing a standard-compliant BPMN extension (BPMN4CAI). Using Design Science Research methodology, this paper develops an approach that systematically extends existing BPMN elements and incorporates specialized components. The applicability and relevance of the BPMN4CAI framework are demonstrated and evaluated through a case study. The results show that the BPMN4CAI extension facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.

AI.tldr: The paper develops BPMN4CAI, a standard-compliant extension of the BPMN notation, to model dynamic and context-sensitive conversational AI interactions within business processes, evaluated through a case study.
AI.motivation: The established BPMN standard faces challenges when representing dynamic, context-sensitive interactions characteristic of conversational AI systems, creating a methodological and practical research gap.
AI.method: Design Science Research methodology is used to systematically extend existing BPMN elements and incorporate specialized components, followed by a case study for demonstration and evaluation.
AI.result: The BPMN4CAI extension facilitates adaptive decision-making processes, robust context management, and transparent interactions for Conversational AI within business processes.
AI.conclusion: The BPMN4CAI framework successfully addresses the representation gap for conversational AI in business processes through a validated, standard-compliant modeling extension.

title: Calibrated Enough to Know, Not Calibrated to Act: Fabricated Evidence Makes LLM Agents Commit to the Unknowable
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, pre-registration and all cached model outputs: https://github.com/Pranav-1100/confidence-calibration-evaluation . Also archived at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22043517
summary: An LLM agent shown a professional-looking market panel commits to a directional call on a provably unpredictable question far more often than one asked the bare question: across 12 frontier models, commitment rises from 6.5% to 54.0% as evidence is escalated. It commits just as readily when every number on the panel is invented: fabricating the entire display, so nothing the model can see is true except the question itself, still lifts commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%, statistically indistinguishable from the 37.6% produced by genuine market data. What unlocks confident action is not information but the authority of its packaging. The failure is narrow and locatable. Incapacity is not the answer: on matched answerable questions attached to the same panels, the same models answer essentially always, at near-perfect accuracy. Nor is it belief - stated probabilities barely move across the gradient that swings action by 48 points, and score worse than a climatological baseline. Missing judgment isn't it either: asked to classify a question's knowability before acting, models call it irreducible 90% of the time and then commit on just 0.4% of those. The act/don't-act gate is what fails, and the effect is concentrated in a few models rather than universal. Because the gate is separable, it can be trained. Supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases, predominantly dice, coins, jars and timers, drives commitment to 0.0% on the original cases and transfers to three unseen domains. It does not survive everything: the gate holds exactly when the response format leaves room to reason, and rigid formats that remove that room leave the model confident and wrong on questions it otherwise answers correctly. The gate is trainable and context-fragile, and deployment needs both halves of that sentence.

AI.tldr: LLM agents commit to directional calls on provably unanswerable questions when the question is presented in a professional market panel (54.0%) versus a bare question (6.5%). The effect persists even when all panel data is fabricated, showing it's the packaging/authority rather than information that drives commitment. The failure is a narrow act/don't-act decision gate, not incapacity, belief, or missing judgment. It's concentrated in a few models and trainable via supervised fine-tuning on synthetic cases, but holds only when response format allows reasoning.
AI.motivation: To understand why LLM agents commit to confident directional predictions on provably unpredictable questions when presented with professional-looking market evidence, and to locate the specific cognitive/systems failure underlying this behavior.
AI.method: Behavioral experiments across 12 frontier models with escalating evidence conditions (bare question to full market panel), including fabricated-panel control conditions, matched answerable questions, stated probability measurements, and knowability classification probes. Additionally, supervised fine-tuning of a 3B model on 540 synthetic cases followed by transfer testing across three unseen domains.
AI.result: Commitment rises from 6.5% to 54.0% with evidence escalation; fabricated data lifts commitment from 24.5% to 36.8%, statistically indistinguishable from genuine data (37.6%). Stated probabilities barely move and are worse than climatological baseline. Models classify questions as irreducible 90% of the time yet commit on 0.4% of those. Fine-tuning drives commitment to 0.0% on original cases and transfers to unseen domains, but rigid response formats that remove reasoning room break the gate.
AI.conclusion: The act/don't-act decision gate is the specific failure point, is separable and trainable, but context-fragile—the gate holds when reasoning room exists in the response format and fails when it doesn't. Deployment must account for both its trainability and fragility.

title: What Makes Good Agentic Data? An ACE Lens on Data Generation for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on generated interaction data to learn how to interact with external environments. Agentic data generation must maintain consistency among environments, tasks, interactions, and success signals while producing experience that is useful rather than merely abundant. Existing work spans many agent domains, but domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation often obscure common generation mechanisms and conflate candidate construction with verification and selection. This work develops a two-level framework for the field. First, we represent agentic data as a common factorized object $(E,q,τ,v)$, comprising an environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier. We organize generation paradigms by their primary anchor and dependency structure. Second, we formulate generation as constrained distribution design through the Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity (ACE) lens. Accuracy establishes the feasible support of grounded and internally consistent data. Within this support, Complexity places learning mass relative to the capability of a declared learner and execution configuration, while divErsity controls coverage and redundancy of data. Using this framework, we explore how prior work verifies generated experience, constructs and calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage. The literature reveals a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and diversity beyond surface variation or dataset size. We further discuss broader directions and emerging trends in agentic data generation through the ACE lens, including their implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes and adaptive learning. Overall, the central challenge is not simply to generate more data, but to continually allocate valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-level framework for unifying the field of agentic data generation for LLM agents. Agentic data is represented as a factorized object (E,q,τ,v) covering environment, task, interaction, and verifier. Generation is formulated as constrained distribution design via an Accuracy-Complexity-diversity (ACE) lens, revealing a shift toward execution-grounded accuracy, learner-relative complexity, and meaningful diversity.
AI.motivation: Existing work on agentic data generation spans many domains but lacks a unified organizing principle. Domain-centered organization and heterogeneous evaluation obscure common generation mechanisms, and conflate candidate construction with verification and selection. A common framework is needed to reveal underlying patterns and guide future work.
AI.method: The paper develops a two-level framework. Level 1 represents agentic data as a factorized object (E,q,τ,v): environment specification, task signal, interaction realization, and optional verifier, organizing generation paradigms by primary anchor and dependency structure. Level 2 formulates generation as constrained distribution design through the ACE (Accuracy-Complexity-divErsity) lens: Accuracy defines feasible support of grounded data, Complexity places learning mass relative to learner capability, and diversity controls coverage and redundancy.
AI.result: Applying the framework to prior work reveals three key shifts: (1) execution-grounded accuracy over purely synthetic generation, (2) learner-relative complexity rather than absolute difficulty calibration, and (3) diversity that goes beyond surface variation or dataset size into behavioral coverage. The framework also exposes how prior work verifies generated experience, constructs and calibrates difficulty, and expands behavioral coverage.
AI.conclusion: The central challenge in agentic data generation is not simply producing more data but continually allocating valid, informative, and non-redundant experience as agents and environments evolve. Broader directions include implications for scaling, data sources, training regimes, and adaptive learning through the ACE lens.

title: Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures
summary: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a simple single-lineage prompt optimization method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO matches or outperforms more complex optimizers like GEPA with fewer rollouts, and its advantage grows with stronger teacher models. It remains competitive in interactive games, and optimized prompts transfer across student models within the same family.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to counter the trend toward increasingly complex prompt optimizers in agentic AI, arguing that simple methods may rival sophisticated search procedures for improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks, particularly in the context of recursive self-improvement.
AI.method: NPO is a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. The authors compare it against GEPA (a more complex optimizer) and GRPO across various tasks, including interactive games, and test cross-model transfer of optimized prompts.
AI.result: NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts. Its advantage increases with stronger teacher models. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA, while GRPO outperforms on some tasks less amenable to prompt optimization. NPO-optimized prompts transfer effectively to other student models, especially within the same family.
AI.conclusion: Simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning can partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity.

title: BrailleBench: Investigating Multi-Criteria Braille Comprehension in Large Language Models
summary: Although Large language models (LLMs) mediate access to knowledge and computational assistance, their capabilities should benefit vulnerable groups in the same way. However, it is unclear whether existing AI systems are inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users to access the same functionality through Braille, whose indicators, contractions, and digital representations introduce distinct requirements for model comprehension. To this end, we introduce BrailleBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs in Braille comprehension from different Criteria. BrailleBench aligns 5,570 instances from five datasets, including mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop question answering across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Different configurations are designed to understand whether the systems can comprehend Braille-authored content, express answers in Braille, and complete end-to-end Braille interaction. To ensure the quality and prevent evaluation bias, the benchmark is built through a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline via a self-created Braille Toolkit without using any data instances generated by LLMs. We evaluate six representative LLMs from various aspects. The results reveal a persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric, where Grade 2 is especially fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille requests further reduce performance. The experimental observations provide valuable guidance for the development of future Braille AI systems. All related resources in BrailleBench are publicly available for future research.

AI.tldr: BrailleBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' Braille comprehension across Grades 1 and 2, comprising 5,570 instances from five datasets covering mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop QA, with deterministic expert-reviewed construction. Evaluation of six representative LLMs reveals a persistent performance gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility, with asymmetric understanding/expression abilities and Grade 2 being particularly fragile on input.
AI.motivation: While LLMs mediate access to knowledge and computational assistance, their capabilities should equally benefit vulnerable groups. However, it is unclear whether existing AI systems are inclusive enough for blind and deafblind users to access the same functionality through Braille, whose indicators, contractions, and digital representations introduce distinct requirements for model comprehension. This motivates a systematic benchmark for evaluating LLMs in Braille comprehension.
AI.method: The paper introduces BrailleBench, a benchmark built by aligning 5,570 instances from five datasets (mathematics, commonsense, and multi-hop QA) across English and Braille Grades 1 and 2. Multiple configurations are designed to test comprehension of Braille-authored content, expression of answers in Braille, and end-to-end Braille interaction. The benchmark is constructed through a deterministic, expert-reviewed pipeline using a self-created Braille Toolkit, without any LLM-generated data instances, to ensure quality and prevent evaluation bias.
AI.result: Evaluation of six representative LLMs reveals a persistent gap between print-English capability and Braille accessibility. Braille understanding and expression are asymmetric, where Grade 2 is especially fragile on the input side compared to Grade 1, and fully Braille requests further reduce performance. All resources in BrailleBench are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The experimental observations provide valuable guidance for the development of future Braille AI systems, highlighting the need to improve LLMs' inclusive access for blind and deafblind users through better Braille comprehension capabilities.

title: LLMs Can Design Near-Optimal OR Algorithms
summary:
We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research (OR) problems. We study inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization. We evaluate two levels of LLM use: at level 1, the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution for that instance; at level 2, it receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, and returns an algorithm that maps instance parameters to solutions. Human input is minimal: we give one untuned prompt that describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget.
  The strongest model we test, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances. This holds even at level 2, where the returned algorithm is fixed before seeing the evaluation instances. Performance also improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, suggesting that this capability is moving quickly. Thus, for the well-specified operations problems we study, a single untuned LLM query can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized methods. These results suggest that frontier LLMs can be a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models can design effective algorithms for well-specified operations research problems (inventory control, queueing network control, and assortment optimization). The strongest model tested, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms existing specialized methods with minimal human input, even when asked to produce a class-level algorithm before seeing evaluation instances. The capability is improving rapidly across recent model releases.
AI.motivation: To determine whether frontier LLMs can serve as serious empirical baselines for algorithm design in well-specified OR problems, given that existing specialized methods require significant domain expertise and engineering effort.
AI.method: The authors evaluate LLMs at two levels: (1) instance-level solution generation where the model receives one problem instance and returns a solution, and (2) class-level algorithm design where the model receives only the problem class description and broad parameter ranges, then returns an algorithm mapping parameters to solutions. A single untuned prompt describes the problem, and the model has access to a Python sandbox tool with a fixed compute budget.
AI.result: The strongest model, gpt-5.6-sol, matches or outperforms the best existing method on almost all evaluated instances, including at level 2 where the algorithm is fixed before seeing evaluation instances. Performance improves sharply across models released less than eight months apart, indicating rapid capability growth.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs can already produce algorithms competitive with specialized OR methods using a single untuned query, suggesting they should be considered a serious empirical baseline for algorithm design in well-specified operations research problems.

title: Verify Smarter, Evolve Further: Efficient Harness Evolution through Behavior-Aware Verification
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures
summary: Agent harnesses shape how language-model agents use instructions, tools, and runtime components, but adapting these harnesses requires costly verification. Existing propose-and-verify methods typically score every candidate on a fixed task set, wasting rollouts on unrelated behaviors and allowing aggregate scores to obscure specific regressions. We introduce HarnessLens, a budget-aware framework for automated harness evolution. HarnessLens jointly explores the task space and user-configurable components, derives candidate modifications from execution trajectories, and selectively verifies each candidate on behavior-relevant tasks using an attributable-evidence gate. These results demonstrate that behavior-aware verification with explicit attribution enables more reliable and sample-efficient harness evolution under constrained interaction budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/jhxu5214/HarnessLens.
