title: Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance
comment: 5 pages (14 appendices), 5 figures, presented at 2026 ICML Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Steering interventions targeting eval-awareness, a model's recognition that it is being tested, are increasingly used in safety evaluation pipelines, where evaluation-awareness is treated as a single quantity to be suppressed. We show that verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought can be identified as capabilities-flavored ("the user is testing my ability to follow instructions"), safety-flavored ("the user is testing my boundaries"), both, or neither: framings that predict compliance very differently. On Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset, capabilities-framing predicts compliance with a +24 to +46 percentage-point gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions. A CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts suggests the link is causal, with 10 of 11 prefills shifting compliance in the predicted direction. Then, eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform: aggregate suppression rates can move while the safety-relevant component does not, and the same "X% suppression of eval-awareness" can correspond to qualitatively different behavioral outcomes.

AI.tldr: Eval-awareness in LLMs is not a single uniform quantity but decomposes into capabilities-flavored and safety-flavored framings that predict compliance very differently (capabilities-framing yields a +24 to +46 percentage-point compliance gap over safety-framing). Steering interventions that suppress eval-awareness can shift aggregate metrics without changing the safety-relevant component, meaning identical suppression rates can produce qualitatively different behaviors.
AI.motivation: Steering interventions targeting eval-awareness are increasingly standard in safety evaluation pipelines, yet they treat eval-awareness as a single uniform quantity to suppress. The authors question this assumption, proposing that eval-awareness is behaviorally heterogeneous and that its internal framing (capabilities vs. safety) predicts compliance outcomes differently.
AI.method: The authors analyze verbalized eval-awareness in chain-of-thought on Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset. They classify eval-awareness into capabilities-flavored, safety-flavored, both, or neither, and compare compliance across steering conditions. They also apply a CoT-prefill intervention to eval-awareness-negative rollouts to test causality.
AI.result: Capabilities-framing predicts a +24 to +46 percentage-point compliance gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions. A CoT-prefill intervention on eval-awareness-negative rollouts showed 10 of 11 prefills shifting compliance in the predicted direction, indicating a causal link. Aggregate suppression rates can change while the safety-relevant component does not, and identical suppression percentages can correspond to qualitatively different behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Eval-awareness is not behaviorally uniform. Steering interventions that report aggregate suppression rates may be misleading, since only the safety-relevant framing matters for safety outcomes. Evaluation pipelines need to account for the compositional nature of eval-awareness rather than treating it as a single quantity.

title: Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm
comment: 59 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Includes Appendix A (variable definitions), Appendix B (supplementary tables), and Online Appendix C (meta prompts)
summary: We study how sophistication in generative AI (genAI) use varies among the back-office workforce of a large firm. Using proprietary data, we observe 713,564 employee prompts and their corresponding large language model responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025. We document three main findings. First, senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, consistent with domain expertise complementing genAI capabilities. Second, sophistication varies considerably across functions and is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management, three groups that share a focus on firmwide strategic initiatives and organizational change. Third, we observe neither improvements in sophistication over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training, suggesting that sophisticated use can be difficult to change. Together, our study provides measures of and insights into sophisticated genAI use that managers can use to improve outcomes and that researchers can use in future research.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 713,564 employee prompts and corresponding LLM responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025 to examine how sophistication in generative AI use varies. The authors find that (1) senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, (2) sophistication varies by function—highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management—and (3) no improvements over time or lasting gains from formal AI training, suggesting sophisticated use is hard to change.
AI.motivation: To understand how sophistication in generative AI use varies among back-office workers, providing empirical measures and insights that managers can leverage to improve outcomes and that researchers can build upon.
AI.method: Using proprietary data from a large firm, the study analyzes 713,564 employee prompts and LLM responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over an eight-month period in 2025, examining variation in genAI use sophistication by seniority, function, and time/training effects.
AI.result: Senior employees show more sophisticated genAI use; sophistication is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management; neither improvements over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training were observed.
AI.conclusion: Sophisticated genAI use correlates with domain expertise and functional focus, but is difficult to change through time or formal training alone, indicating that more targeted or structural interventions may be needed to improve genAI sophistication in the back-office workforce.

title: CorporateBench: Large-Scale Q&A Benchmarking with Temporal Knowledge Bases
comment: Accepted to EMNLP Findings
summary: LLMs are increasingly able to answer complex questions about enterprise-scale document collections. But evaluation is hard: companies don't want to share internal communications, and synthetic datasets have been overly simple. We present CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark whose scale approaches the conditions LLMs encounter in corporate communication networks, with evaluation corpora surpassing 230,000 documents. CB evaluates LLMs across two dimensions (information extraction and knowledge base querying) through four synthetically generated firms ranging from 12 to 10,000 employees. Each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, guaranteeing cross-document logical consistency even across hundreds of thousands of documents. We evaluate five LLMs on CB, revealing increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic scales. CB provides LLM developers a metric for corporate communication reasoning, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CorporateBench (CB), a human-validated multi-task Q&A benchmark for evaluating LLMs on enterprise-scale document collections, with corpora exceeding 230,000 documents across four synthetic firms. Evaluation of five LLMs reveals performance degrades significantly as input scales approach realistic corporate sizes.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for enterprise document Q&A are inadequate: real corporate data cannot be shared due to confidentiality, and existing synthetic datasets are overly simplistic, failing to reflect the scale and complexity of real corporate communication networks. There is a critical gap in benchmarking LLMs under realistic enterprise-scale conditions.
AI.method: CorporateBench is constructed as a human-validated multi-task benchmark covering two dimensions: information extraction and knowledge base querying. It contains four synthetically generated firms (12 to 10,000 employees) where each corpus is sampled from a temporally evolving knowledge base describing a consistent world, ensuring cross-document logical consistency across hundreds of thousands of documents. Five LLMs are evaluated on this benchmark.
AI.result: Evaluation of five LLMs on CorporateBench reveals increasingly poor performance as input size approaches realistic enterprise scales, indicating current models struggle with large-scale corporate communication reasoning despite performing adequately on smaller benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CorporateBench provides LLM developers a metric specifically for corporate communication reasoning at realistic scale, filling a crucial gap in the benchmarking ecosystem and highlighting the scalability limitations of current LLMs on enterprise document collections.

title: Learning a Continuous Sepsis Severity Score Without Hour-by-Hour Supervision: A Two-Site Retrospective Study
summary:
Currently used sepsis severity indices rely on fixed variables and weights established decades ago, which are coarsely discretized and calibrated to a cohort that no longer reflects contemporary critical care. No alternative learned directly from patient trajectories is in routine use. We conducted a retrospective two-cohort study on a total of 29,116 and 7,691 adult patients meeting Sepsis-3 criteria from two hospital systems in Massachusetts and Georgie, respectively.
  We developed a sepsis index using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Unlike previous studies, we use mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than a per-state target, allowing credit to be redistributed non-uniformly across timesteps. Evaluation was done on a permanent 20% test holdout, using clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation. Uncertainty intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling of whole patients. Under this ranking scheme, non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher than survivors on a 0-10 scale within all strata of baseline SOFA-2, with similar results stratifying within lactate, mean arterial pressure (MAP), and creatinine. Within-patient change in the index correlated with change in lactate (Spearman rho = 0.39; n = 1,854). Similar, weaker correlations were found for MAP and creatinine. On a cohort level, cross-institutional agreement measured by Spearman correlation between models trained on different sites, were 70-77% of same-site correlation. External within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 against ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. Our index also correlated with established indices, while null controls stayed near zero.
  Our index demonstrated hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and is consistent with clinical expectation, indicating potential as a decision support tool complementing clinical judgement.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a novel sepsis severity index learned directly from patient trajectories using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour window, incorporating mortality as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than per-state target. Validated on two large retrospective cohorts (29,116 and 7,691 patients), the index demonstrates meaningful separation of survivors and non-survivors across all SOFA-2 strata, clinically consistent within-patient correlations with lactate/MAP/creatinine, moderate-to-strong cross-institutional generalizability, and hourly prognostic information complementary to clinical judgment.
AI.motivation: Existing sepsis severity indices rely on fixed variables and weights established decades ago, are coarsely discretized, and are calibrated to outdated cohorts. No alternative learned directly from patient trajectories is in routine clinical use, motivating the need for a data-driven, trajectory-based severity score that reflects contemporary critical care.
AI.method: A retrospective two-cohort study using 43 routinely charted variables over a 72-hour treatment window. Mortality is used as a treatment-level ranking signal rather than a per-state target, enabling non-uniform credit redistribution across timesteps. Evaluation uses a permanent 20% test holdout with clinical vignettes and Spearman correlation, with uncertainty intervals from bootstrap resampling of whole patients. Cross-institutional validation was performed by training models on separate hospital systems.
AI.result: Non-survivors scored 1.19-1.64 points higher on a 0-10 scale across all SOFA-2 strata and similar stratification by lactate, MAP, and creatinine. Within-patient index change correlated with lactate change (Spearman rho=0.39; n=1,854), with weaker correlations for MAP and creatinine. Cross-institutional Spearman correlation was 70-77% of same-site correlation; external within-patient correlations were 0.54 and 0.59 against ceilings of 0.92 and 0.90. The index correlated with established indices while null controls stayed near zero.
AI.conclusion: The sepsis index provides hourly prognostic information that meaningfully separates patient outcomes and aligns with clinical expectations, demonstrating potential as a decision support tool to complement clinical judgment in real-time sepsis severity assessment.

title: Mechanistic Reaction Prediction via Discrete Flow Matching on Graph-Structured Electron Occupation
summary:
Chemical reactions are fundamentally transformations in electron space, yet most machine learning approaches model them either through \textit{de novo} generation of product molecules or through heuristic graph edits that operate directly on molecular topology.
  We introduce MAELLE (\textbf{M}ech\textbf{A}nistic \textbf{E}dit f\textbf{L}ow-matching on e\textbf{L}ectron r\textbf{E}arrangements), which instead models reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors.
  Concretely, we formulate the reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over the graph-structured integer-valued electron occupation space defined on all bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites.
  To construct the intermediate edit trajectories, we generalize the discrete flow matching mixture path to discrete electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, yielding a sequence of mechanistically interpretable edit moves without requiring elementary step annotations.
  MAELLE achieves competitive performance on the USPTO-480K benchmark compared with leading reaction prediction models.
  Beyond in-distribution accuracy, we evaluate robustness across two out-of-distribution settings - structural complexity and reaction type - and find that MAELLE maintains strong performance where existing methods degrade.
  Finally, because the learned flow operates over the full electron redistribution, MAELLE naturally recovers mechanistic trajectories that align with known chemistry and can predict side products of a reaction.

AI.tldr: MAELLE is a novel reaction prediction model that frames chemical reactions as discrete flow matching over electron occupation vectors, treating reactions as continuous-time Markov chains over graph-structured electron space rather than operating on molecular topology or generating products de novo.
AI.motivation: Chemical reactions are fundamentally electron rearrangements, yet existing ML approaches either generate product molecules de novo or apply heuristic graph edits to molecular topology, neither of which explicitly models the underlying electron-space transformations that define chemistry.
AI.method: MAELLE formulates reactant-to-product mapping as a Continuous-time Markov Chain (CTMC) over integer-valued electron occupation vectors defined on bonding, non-bonding, and hydrogen sites. It extends discrete flow matching mixture paths to electron rearrangements using Optimal Transport, producing mechanistically interpretable edit trajectories without requiring elementary step annotations.
AI.result: MAELLE achieves competitive performance on USPTO-480K against leading reaction prediction models, maintains strong performance under out-of-distribution settings (structural complexity and reaction type) where existing methods degrade, and recovers mechanistic trajectories consistent with known chemistry while predicting side products.
AI.conclusion: Modeling reactions at the electron occupation level via discrete flow matching yields both competitive accuracy and improved robustness/interpretability, enabling mechanistic insight and side-product prediction that topology-based or generative approaches cannot naturally provide.

title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution
summary: Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

AI.tldr: WikiSkill is a framework that co-evolves AI agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki), separating raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods across benchmarks and models, demonstrating that systematic knowledge consolidation enables more effective, transferable skill development.
AI.motivation: Existing agent skill discovery methods extract skills from experience but leave insights scattered across optimization histories, preventing systematic reuse across iterations. The knowledge that guides skill development is lost rather than accumulated, limiting the effectiveness and transferability of evolved skills.
AI.method: WikiSkill introduces a framework that maintains three separated components: raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge in a persistent wiki, and executable skills. It continuously consolidates experience into the wiki, and subsequent skill updates build on this accumulated knowledge, enabling iterative co-evolution of skills and knowledge.
AI.result: WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods across diverse benchmarks and models, and improves over no-skill baselines in most settings. Larger models benefit more from evolved skills; smaller models with skills outperform larger models without them. Evolved skills transfer across models and families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Ablations confirm persistent knowledge accumulation is critical.
AI.conclusion: Systematically accumulating and refining agent experience is crucial for developing reusable and transferable skills. The persistent wiki provides a principled mechanism for knowledge consolidation that complements model scaling and enhances skill evolution effectiveness.
